assumptions: MOBIBuffer contract: buf->data points to an allocation of at least buf->maxlen readable bytes, so data + maxlen is one-past-end.
The entry-number guard at line 10 is effective, so all indx->entries[entry_number] accesses are in bounds.
tagx->tags is a valid array of tagx->tags_count MOBITag elements.
limitations: Label over-read via strncpy (line 42) and the helpers at lines 29/31: whether label_length can exceed the stack buffer text (INDX_LABEL_SIZEMAX + 1) depends on the unshown constant and on mobi_getstring_ordt/mobi_indx_get_label honoring the passed length; not confirmable from this snippet.
idxt.offsets[curr_number + 1] at line 7 has no bounds check in the shown code; whether curr_number + 1 is always < index_count depends on the caller's contract.

Unsigned wrap of buf->offset + entry_length at line 16 (e.g., entry_length underflow from decreasing offsets) can bypass the guard only on narrow/huge size_t; the subsequent bounded reads error out in the non-ordt branch (lines 32-34), so this is a robustness concern, not a confirmed exploit.

Multiplication in malloc at lines 56/101 (tagx->tags_count * sizeof(...)) could in principle overflow for absurd tags_count values, but tags_count is bounded by realistic file size, so no confirmed vulnerability.
ordt is dereferenced at line 28 without a NULL check; a NULL ordt would require an out-of-scope caller contract violation.

Practical exploitation of the confirmed OOB read depends on the record buffer being allocated exactly at maxlen; if data aliases a larger backing buffer, the reads remain a logic/entry-bound violation rather than a heap over-read.

verdict.summary: When parsing a crafted MOBI file, control_bytes is derived from the attacker-controlled record buffer (line 41) and advanced once per tag with control_byte==1 (line 62) with no bound check against the entry end or the heap allocation; the first subsequent tag dereferences control_bytes[0] at line 66, producing an out-of-bounds heap read that can crash the parser or disclose one heap byte.

evidence.reason: control_bytes aliases a position inside buf->data, whose allocation size is buf->maxlen (record size, attacker-controlled). The entry-end bound (buf->offset + entry_length set at line 20) is never recorded for this pointer, and the pointer is advanced at line 62 solely from attacker-controlled tagx->tags[i].control_byte values.

Sink: control_bytes[0] is dereferenced without any check against buf->maxlen or the entry region. From near the record end (offset equal to entry end, or after K leading control_byte==1 tags), the read lands at or beyond buf->data + buf->maxlen, i.e. past the heap allocation. The guards at lines 16 and 22 only bound helper-based reads and label_length (0-255), not this raw pointer dereference, so a crafted file reaches the OOB read directly.

assumptions: Line numbers are relative to the provided snippet.
mobi_buffer_get8 returns exactly one octet, so label_length is bounded by 255; combined with INDX_LABEL_SIZEMAX >= 256 this makes the label text[INDX_LABEL_SIZEMAX] path safe.
buf->data points to an allocation of exactly buf->maxlen bytes; the temporary maxlen shrink at line 20 does not resize the allocation.
indx->entries has total_entries_count elements (enforced by the line 10 check), tagx->tags has tags_count elements, and idxt.offsets includes the trailing sentinel for the caller's curr_number range.
mobi_indx_get_label and mobi_getstring_ordt write at most label_length bytes into text.
limitations: idxt.offsets[curr_number + 1] (line 7) may read one element past the array if the caller does not allocate the sentinel offset; caller allocation is outside this snippet (unconfirmed).

Non-monotonic idxt.offsets could make entry_length wrap to a huge size_t, and the unsigned sum at line 16 could theoretically wrap past the guard; no concrete value was found that survives all subsequent checks into a memory-safety failure (robustness concern).
The (int) cast of tagx->control_byte_count at line 42 and the exact behavior of mobi_buffer_seek are not shown, so any impact of seek failure/truncation cannot be confirmed.
ordt is dereferenced at line 28 without a NULL check; a NULL ordt would require a caller contract violation, which is out of scope.

Malloc failure paths return early without restoring buf->maxlen (lines 34-37, 53-56, 98-102, 128-132, plus free(ptagx) paths), leaving a reduced maxlen on later retries; noted as a robustness concern, not a confirmed vulnerability.

verdict.summary: gopherToHTML has an off-by-one stack out-of-bounds write at line 96: when a gopher response line (including trailing newline) reaches TEMP_BUF_SIZE-1 bytes, line[llen + 1] = '\0' writes one byte past the local 'line' array (CWE-121/CWE-787), enabling remote denial of service / memory corruption from a malicious gopher server. Additionally, host and port fields parsed from the same attacker-controlled line are emitted into HTML attributes without escaping (CWE-79), allowing HTML/script injection in the proxy-generated page.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds write sink: 'line' has size TEMP_BUF_SIZE (declared line 6), valid indices 0..TEMP_BUF_SIZE-1, but the terminator index is llen+1. Whenever the final line length is exactly TEMP_BUF_SIZE-1 (a response line of >= TEMP_BUF_SIZE-2 data bytes plus '\n'), 'llen + 1' equals TEMP_BUF_SIZE and this write lands one byte past the array. The clamp at lines 75-78 caps copies at TEMP_BUF_SIZE-1 but never corrects the +1 terminator index, so the overflow occurs in both the clamped and unclamped outcomes.

Reachability enabler: attacker-controlled 'llen' (line 71/73) passes the guard when total >= TEMP_BUF_SIZE; the clamp caps content at TEMP_BUF_SIZE-1, after which line 96 writes index TEMP_BUF_SIZE. With no clamp (total == TEMP_BUF_SIZE-1, e.g. llen == 4095 with gopherState->len == 0), the guard is bypassed entirely and line[4096] = 0 still executes. Confirms taint of the inbuf-derived line length and the insufficient bound on the follow-on write.

evidence.snippet: outbuf.appendf(" %s\n", icon_url, host, rfc1738_escape_unescaped(selector + 5), html_quote(name));
evidence.reason: HTML injection sink: 'host' is a substring of the attacker-controlled gopher line (lines 122-126), truncated only at TAB/CR/LF/NUL, and is inserted raw into the href attribute. A host value containing '"' + '>' plus event handlers breaks out of the attribute and executes script in the proxy's page origin (CWE-79). The same raw-insertion pattern exists for 'port' in the telnet branch (lines 219-225).

Secondary HTML injection sink: the attacker-controlled 'port' field (line 127) is emitted raw (only TAB/CR/LF are chopped at lines 134-145). Characters such as '"', '>', '<' pass through and can inject markup/attributes into the rendered gopher page.

assumptions: TEMP_BUF_SIZE is the declared size of the local 'line' array via LOCAL_ARRAY (line 6); Squid ships TEMP_BUF_SIZE = 4096, and the off-by-one holds identically for any value >= 1.

inbuf/len are populated by the caller from network response bytes of the upstream gopher server (this function's stated role), making the input remotely attacker-controlled even though the calling path is not shown.
gopherState->buf has capacity at least TEMP_BUF_SIZE, matching the residue accumulation at lines 83-84.
limitations: The stack overflow is a single NUL-byte write; code execution is not demonstrated. On stack-protector builds it overwrites the canary word and aborts (remote DoS); exploitability depends on compiler options and surrounding stack layout.
CWE-79 impact is deployment-dependent: it requires the proxy-generated page to be a meaningful trust boundary for the victim (malicious gopher server serving crafted host/port).
atoi(NULL) concerns in the CSO branch are unreachable: strtok returns NULL on the first call only when no further tokens exist, so 'result != NULL' implies the preceding token pointers are non-NULL.
Reads of port[1]/port[2] (lines 149-150) and the strchr scans are bounded by the NUL-terminated, in-bounds copy of the line; no separate overflow is confirmed for them.

verdict.summary: reg_match_visual is a match-gating predicate with no allocation, indexing, or state mutation. The only memory-touching call (win_linetabsize at line 68) receives a length that is a within-line pointer offset (rex.input - rex.line), whose upper bound the shown code never exceeds absent an out-of-scope regex-engine contract violation. The MAXCOL arithmetic on lines 55 and 69 can only misclassify a match inside/outside the visual area (it is never used as a size or index), which is a robustness/logic concern, not a memory-safety vulnerability. No concrete attacker-controlled value can be shown to reach a dangerous sink in this function.

evidence.snippet:
cols = win_linetabsize(wp, rex.line, (colnr_T)(rex.input - rex.line));
	if (cols < start || cols > end - (*p_sel == 'e'))
evidence.reason: Only dereferencing sink in the function. Its length argument is the byte offset rex.input - rex.line, which all reachable paths (lines 14-48) leave within [0, STRLEN(rex.line)] by the regex-engine invariant; the guard on line 69 then bounds cols against the merged selection columns. Any OOB scenario requires rex.input placed past the line allocation by an out-of-scope caller, which is not reachable from the shown code.

assumptions: colnr_T is 64-bit long with MAXCOL = 2147483647 in the build under analysis, so bot.col + 1 (line 55) and end - 1 (line 69) cannot overflow.
The regex engine guarantees rex.line <= rex.input <= rex.line + STRLEN(rex.line) when reg_match_visual is invoked, so the length passed to win_linetabsize (line 68) is a valid in-line offset.
rex.reg_win, if non-NULL, is kept alive for the duration of the match by the engine, and curbuf->b_visual is editor-validated state.
limitations: Unconfirmed: an out-of-bounds read in win_linetabsize (line 68) would occur if some caller invoked the match with rex.input one-past or beyond the line allocation; no such path exists in the shown code, so this is classified as a robustness concern (CWE-125 hypothesis only).

Unconfirmed: on a 32-bit int colnr_T build, bot.col + (*p_sel != 'e') at line 55 with bot.col == MAXCOL could wrap (CWE-190), and end - (*p_sel == 'e') at line 69 with end == 0 and exclusive selection could underflow; in both cases the value is used only in a comparison gate, so the impact is incorrect match acceptance/rejection in the visual-selection search, not memory corruption.

Unconfirmed: use of wp = rex.reg_win (line 6) and curbuf->b_visual (lines 34-45) presumes the engine holds a stable reference; a concurrent window/buffer teardown would be a caller-contract violation outside this function's scope.
Unconfirmed: truncation of ptrdiff_t (rex.input - rex.line) when narrowing to colnr_T (lines 53, 68) matters only for lines >= 2 GiB, which cannot be exercised through the shown checks.

verdict.summary: No confirmed, fully-reachable attacker-triggerable vulnerability in the shown code. The line-index check at snippet lines 48-49 bounds all subsequent line-based access, col is derived from the engine invariant rex.input in [rex.line, rex.line+line_len] (line 51), and lines 69-71 re-fetch rex.line/rex.input after getvvcol flushes the cached line, mitigating the historical stale-pointer issue. Remaining concerns (NULL from reg_getline, content change between fetch and re-fetch, ptrdiff-to-int truncation on >INT_MAX lines) depend on unshown code/invariants and are recorded as limitations.

evidence.reason: Guard fully covers the line-index domain used by every subsequent operation: lnum is bounded to [top.lnum, bot.lnum], and top/bot are derived solely from Vim-maintained VIsual/window positions in the buffer that was already verified equal to rex.reg_buf at line 14. No later statement indexes a line without passing this check.

The known stale-pointer hazard (rex.line invalidated by getvvcol) is mitigated here: the line is re-fetched before any use, and col was computed at line 51 from the original pair rex.input - rex.line, which the engine keeps within [rex.line, rex.line + strlen(line)]. Under the assuming invariants (reg_getline returns the same line content; no buffer mutation), rex.line + col stays in-bounds, so no OOB read is confirmed from the shown code.

Single narrowing conversion (ptrdiff_t to colnr_T/int). The value is a byte offset within the current line by the engine invariant (rex.input never precedes rex.line and never advances past the line's trailing NUL), and Vim caps line lengths well below INT_MAX, so the cast is value-preserving; a truncation-driven OOB would require an out-of-scope >2GB line and is not a confirmed finding.

assumptions: rex.input always lies within [rex.line, rex.line + strlen(line)] (engine invariant of the regexp matcher).
reg_getline(rex.lnum) returns the same line content and length as the pre-flush rex.line for the validated lnum, and returns non-NULL because lnum <= bot.lnum was checked while reg_buf == curbuf.
getvvcol is read-only and cannot mutate the buffer between the col computation at line 51 and the re-fetch at line 70.
Vim caps buffer line lengths below INT_MAX, making the ptrdiff_t-to-colnr_T cast at line 51 value-preserving.
Snippet line numbers start at 1 with 'reg_match_visual(void)'.
limitations: NULL dereference at 'rex.input = rex.line + col' (line 71) would occur if reg_getline returned NULL; reachability depends on unshown reg_getline bounds logic and is not established by the shown code.

Out-of-bounds read at 'win_linetabsize(wp, rex.line, col)' (line 73) would require rex.line's content/length to change between lines 51 and 70 (concurrent buffer mutation or a differing line returned by reg_getline), which depends on out-of-scope behavior and is not confirmed.
Integer truncation at line 51 for lines longer than INT_MAX is theoretical; Vim line-length limits prevent it in practice.
Logic edge at line 74 ('end - (*p_sel == "e")' underflowing to -1 when end == 0 with exclusive selection) only causes a spurious FALSE return; no memory-safety impact.
The historical use-after-free in this function (fixed in Vim 8.0.0322 era) is not present here because lines 69-71 re-fetch rex.line and rex.input after getvvcol.

verdict.summary: Attacker-controlled #define width/height values flow unvalidated into a 32-bit unsigned multiplication (size = bytes_per_line * hh), wrapping to a negative signed int; g_malloc then receives a huge size_t and GLib aborts the process, giving a reachable denial of service via a crafted cursor definition file.

evidence.reason: ww and hh are attacker-controlled guint values parsed from '#define width %d' / '#define height %d' lines (lines 33, 40-43) with only a nonzero check (line 77). bytes_per_line is int; hh is guint, so the multiply at line 87 is performed in 32-bit unsigned and stored into signed int size. With ww=0xFFFFFFF8 (bytes_per_line=536870911) and hh=5, size=0xA0000003 = -1610612741 as int; g_malloc (line 88) promotes it to an ~18EB size_t and GLib aborts on the failed allocation — a reachable crash triggered solely by file content.

assumptions: MAX_SIZE is a fixed compile-time constant >= 2, so the fgets truncation guard at line 31 and the %s token lengths keep line/name_and_type in bounds.
int and guint are 32-bit; GLib g_malloc aborts the process on allocation failure (documented GLib behavior).
fstream refers to a caller-opened file whose contents are attacker-controllable.
limitations: If g_malloc returned NULL instead of aborting, the 'if (!bits) RETURN (FALSE)' path would fail cleanly and the only remaining impact would be wrapped small/zero allocations with huge ww/hh surfaced to out-of-scope callers (lines 117-119): unconfirmed here.

If the oversize allocation somehow succeeded, both data loops (lines 94-100, 105-109) are bounded by the wrapped (negative => skipped) size, so no in-function out-of-bounds write is confirmed; downstream overflows would depend on code not shown.

The 'hot' parse at lines 45-51 can read one stack byte before name_and_type when '_' is at index 1; no observable output and a full strcmp match is impossible, so it is a robustness concern, not a vulnerability.
(ww+7) itself wraps mod 2^32 for ww >= 2^32-6 (e.g., ww=0xFFFFFFFF gives bytes_per_line=0), producing 0/small allocations; same overflow class, subsumed by the confirmed finding.

verdict.summary: No attacker-controlled input reaches a dangerous sink. The loop index i is bounded by the compile-time constant MAX_LOADED_OBJECTS via a strict inequality, so the maximum index (MAX_LOADED_OBJECTS-1) stays within s_objects; MemorySet writes exactly sizeof(OBJECT_ATTRIBUTES) bytes into the attributes member of an in-bounds slot; the optional out parameter handle is null-checked before dereference; and the arithmetic i + TRANSIENT_FIRST involves only internal, non-attacker values.

evidence.reason: The only index used, i, is produced solely by the loop guard i < MAX_LOADED_OBJECTS (line 7) and is not attacker-controlled, so &s_objects[i] (line 9) stays in bounds against an array of MAX_LOADED_OBJECTS elements; MemorySet (line 15) writes only sizeof(OBJECT_ATTRIBUTES) bytes into that in-bounds slot; handle is dereferenced (line 13) only under the explicit if(handle) null check (line 12), and i + TRANSIENT_FIRST uses no attacker data.

assumptions: s_objects is declared with exactly MAX_LOADED_OBJECTS elements, and MAX_LOADED_OBJECTS / TRANSIENT_FIRST are compile-time constants (declarations not shown).
OBJECT_ATTRIBUTES.occupied uses CLEAR=0, so zeroing attributes marks the slot as free for the next owner.
limitations: If TRANSIENT_FIRST + (MAX_LOADED_OBJECTS-1) could exceed the TPMI_DH_OBJECT range (e.g., an extreme MAX_LOADED_OBJECTS), the handle arithmetic could overflow; both operands are internal constants, so this is a robustness concern with no attacker control in the shown code.

Only OBJECT_ATTRIBUTES is cleared; stale public/sensitive data in other OBJECT fields would persist if the slot-reclaim path does not wipe them. Whether that occurs depends on caller lifecycle code not shown, so it is an unconfirmed residue-handling concern, not a confirmed vulnerability.
Returning NULL when the table is full relies on callers to check the result; any NULL dereference would occur in caller code that is out of scope of the shown snippet.

verdict.summary: No attacker-reachable memory-safety or logic vulnerability is confirmed within the shown eval7 fragment. Every single-byte expression read (lines 31, 100, 139-151, 181-182) lands at or before the NUL terminator of the in-bounds, NUL-terminated expression buffer; recursion is capped at 1000 balanced active frames (lines 44-49, 281) with a project-stated safe margin; and the name-length guard (lines 211-212) fully covers all downstream uses of s/len, which are additionally protected by exact-length STRNCMP comparisons (lines 233, 240, 247). Residual concerns (partial deref at line 164, deep-recursion stack usage, unshown callees) are recorded as limitations.

evidence.reason: The only base+1 read in the numeric/dot path executes only when **arg is '.', so *arg points at a non-NUL in-bounds byte and *arg+1 is at worst the NUL terminator of the NUL-terminated expression buffer. No allocation size is enforced here, but the read cannot exceed the buffer; terminator read is in-bounds, so no OOB vulnerability.

Recursion guard: the static counter is incremented only after this check (line 49) and decremented exactly once at line 281; there are no returns between lines 50 and 280. The equality check therefore caps active eval7 frames at 1000, fully covering the recursion depth. Whether 1000 frames exhaust the stack is environment-dependent and stated by the project comment (lines 42-43) to be safe, so it is a limitation, not a confirmed finding.

Length guard for the name path: all later uses of s and len (lines 217, 222-226, 233, 240, 247, 256, 263) execute only when len >= 1, and the STRNCMP calls are additionally protected by exact-length checks (len == 4/5/4 matching n=4/5/4), so no read can exceed the name buffer. This is a verified covering guard, supporting the not-vulnerable verdict.

assumptions: The expression string behind *arg is NUL-terminated and resides in a valid allocation, so reading at or before the terminator is in-bounds.
in_vim9script(), evalarg, and evalarg->eval_flags are framework-internal trusted state with no attacker path through this fragment.
get_name_len returns a length consistent with the actual name bytes and an alias buffer of len + NUL when alias is non-NULL.
Evaluation is single-threaded per Vim instance, so the static `recurse` counter is not subject to races in this context.
get_lambda_tv, when returning OK in vim9script mode for a leading '(', produces a valid partial with pt_func set (callee invariant).
limitations: The genuinely bug-prone parsing and evaluation logic (eval_number, eval_string, eval_lit_string, eval_list, eval_dict, get_lambda_tv, get_name_len, eval_func, eval_variable, check_vars, handle_subscript, eval7_leader, compile_def_function, get_reg_contents) is not shown; any vulnerability inside those callees is out of scope for this analysis.

Line 164 dereferences rettv->vval.v_partial->pt_func without a NULL/type check; if a future or alternate get_lambda_tv returned OK with a non-partial value, this would be a null/type-confusion, but no such reachable path exists in the shown code, so it is an unconfirmed robustness concern.

An attacker-controlled deeply nested expression can drive up to 1000 active eval7 frames (plus nested eval1..eval6 frames); stack overflow at that depth is environment-dependent and the project comment (lines 42-43) indicates 1000 was chosen as safe, so this is an unconfirmed DoS/robustness hypothesis rather than a confirmed finding.
The static `recurse` variable is not reentrant-safe if eval7 could be invoked concurrently from multiple threads; no such concurrent invocation path is shown here.

verdict.summary: No confirmed, reachable, attacker-triggerable vulnerability in FindEmptyObjectSlot. The loop index is bounded by MAX_LOADED_OBJECTS with strict inequality, the handle dereference is NULL-guarded, and MemorySet uses exactly sizeof(*object). Remaining concerns (callers re-marking the slot as occupied, and the s_objects array-size invariant) are outside the shown code.

evidence.reason: Attacker-controlled input is absent; i is a loop-local UINT32. The strict inequality i < MAX_LOADED_OBJECTS bounds the largest reachable index at MAX_LOADED_OBJECTS-1, which is in-bounds for a global array declared with MAX_LOADED_OBJECTS elements (standard TPM invariant). No out-of-bounds access is reachable.

The NULL check at the start of the span fully guards the dereference of handle; a NULL handle never reaches the write. Worst-case value i + TRANSIENT_FIRST = (MAX_LOADED_OBJECTS-1) + 0x40000000 fits in UINT32, so no wraparound.

evidence.snippet: MemorySet(object, 0, sizeof(*object)); // libtpms added: Initialize the whole object
evidence.reason: The write length equals sizeof(*object) exactly and starts at object, so the memset cannot overflow the slot. It does clear attributes.occupied; the returned slot's occupied state is solely a caller-contract concern, not a memory-safety flaw in this function.

assumptions: s_objects is declared with exactly MAX_LOADED_OBJECTS elements (standard TPM 2.0 reference declaration), since the declaration is outside the shown snippet.
TRANSIENT_FIRST and MAX_LOADED_OBJECTS have their conventional values (0x40000000 and 16), making i + TRANSIENT_FIRST overflow-free.
MemorySet behaves like memset with correct bounds semantics.
Callers of FindEmptyObjectSlot set object->attributes.occupied = SET after the call, and TPM command dispatch serializes access to s_objects.
limitations: If s_objects were declared smaller than MAX_LOADED_OBJECTS, line 9 could go out of bounds, but that depends on a declaration not shown and contradicts the standard invariant; unconfirmed.

MemorySet zeroes attributes.occupied, so the slot is returned with occupied == CLEAR; a (not shown) caller that failed to re-mark the slot could receive the same slot twice. Not attacker-controlled and not reachable within this code; robustness/logic concern only.
No thread-safety analysis is possible from this snippet; concurrent callers of FindEmptyObjectSlot could race on the same slot, but TPM command serialization is assumed and no such path is shown.

verdict.summary: NULL pointer dereference in inflate() while parsing a gzip header extra field: line 144 reads state->head->extra_len before the state->head != Z_NULL guard at line 145. A gzip stream with FEXTRA (FLG 0x0400) and nonzero XLEN forces copy > 0 and crashes consumers that decompress without inflateGetHeader (head == Z_NULL), enabling attacker-controlled denial of service.

evidence.reason: Attacker-controlled gzip FLG bit 0x0400 (parsed at lines 85-87) and the 16-bit XLEN (line 128) select case EXTRA; copy = min(state->length, have) with have >= 1 makes copy > 0. When state->head == Z_NULL (inflateGetHeader not called), line 144 dereferences state->head->extra_len before any NULL check, crashing the process.

evidence.snippet:
if (state->head != Z_NULL &&
                        state->head->extra != Z_NULL &&
                        len < state->head->extra_max) {
                        zmemcpy(state->head->extra + len, next,
evidence.reason: The only NULL guard (line 145) appears after the dereference at line 144, so it cannot prevent the crash. The guard bounds only the zmemcpy, which is additionally capped by extra_max - len; therefore no overflow is confirmed when head != Z_NULL, and the confirmed defect is the out-of-order dereference.
When state->head == Z_NULL, extra_len is never assigned; the first access to it is the line 144 dereference, confirming the tainted EXLEN -> EXTRA path that reaches the NULL pointer sink.

assumptions: LOAD()/RESTORE(), NEEDBITS(), PULLBYTE(), DROPBITS(), INITBITS(), BYTEBITS(), BITS(), and UPDATE_CHECK() behave as in zlib and preserve the have/left bounds (macro bodies are not shown).
state->wrap includes bit 1 (gzip) and bit 2 (CRC) for gzip decoding, e.g. inflateInit2(47) or inflateInit2(-15).
state->head is Z_NULL unless the application called inflateGetHeader(); that is a legal, common configuration per the zlib contract.
Window/state bookkeeping (window, wsize, whave, wnext) maintained by updatewindow() is correct; inflate_table() and inflate_fast() are outside the shown code.
limitations: No heap buffer overflow is confirmed for the gzip extra field when head != Z_NULL, because lines 145-150 cap the copy at extra_max - len; a CVE-2022-37434-style OOB write cannot be substantiated from the shown code alone.
The NULL dereference requires head == Z_NULL; deployments that always call inflateGetHeader() with a valid header buffer do not trigger it.
Potential issues in inflate_table(), inflate_fast(), or updatewindow() are out of scope because those functions are not shown.

verdict.summary: No confirmed attacker-reachable memory-safety or input-validation vulnerability within the shown code. All writes into NameBuff are size-bounded (guard `len < MAXPATHL - 1` at line 54-55 plus `vim_snprintf(..., MAXPATHL - len, ...)` at lines 58, 64, 72, 77), and both truncation paths are fully covered by the `this_ru_col <= 1` guard (line 84) and by the loop guard `p[i] != NUL` (line 98), which keep the `'<'` writes inside the buffer. The mbyte truncation can write '<' into the last byte of a multibyte character (display corruption only), and the keymap/file-name/cell-count calls rely on unshown callee invariants; these are recorded as limitations.

evidence.reason: This guard bounds this_ru_col from below (>= 2 in every else branch). Without it, a non-positive this_ru_col from `ru_col - (Columns - wp->w_width)` (line 81) would make `len - (this_ru_col - 1)` exceed `len`, advancing `p` past the NUL in the non-mbyte branch (lines 112-113). The guard fully covers that operation, so the write cannot leave NameBuff.

The `len < MAXPATHL - 1` check before `*(p + len++) = ' '` guarantees `len <= MAXPATHL - 1` afterward, so the following (and subsequent) `vim_snprintf(p + len, MAXPATHL - len, ...)` calls always have size >= 1 and can never write past index MAXPATHL - 1 of NameBuff, even when vim_snprintf truncates; the subsequent `len += STRLEN(p + len)` re-clamps len to <= MAXPATHL - 1.

The loop index i is a byte offset advanced only while `p[i] != NUL`, so the maximum reachable value is `STRLEN(p)`; the write at `p + i - 1` (line 104) is therefore confined to `[p, p + strlen - 1]` inside NameBuff and cannot go out of bounds. The write may land on the final byte of a multibyte character, which is a display/robustness issue, not a memory-safety defect.

assumptions: NameBuff is exactly MAXPATHL bytes per line 44 and NUL-terminated by the unshown get_trans_bufname/get_keymap_str implementations (required for `STRLEN` at lines 46, 59, 73, 78, 122 to be in-bounds).
vim_snprintf behaves like snprintf: with a size >= 1 it writes at most size-1 bytes plus a NUL terminator.
mb_string2cells/mb_ptr2len/mb_ptr2cells read no further than the NUL terminator of the (bounded) string, per Vim's encoding contract.
ru_col, Columns, and wp->w_width are non-negative ints with wp->w_width <= Columns, so line 81 cannot overflow.
screen_puts/screen_fill/win_redr_ruler clip columns to the screen and tolerate inverted or zero-length fill ranges (unshown implementations).
Line numbers refer to the supplied snippet, numbered from the function header.
limitations: The multi-byte truncation at lines 104-105 writes '<' at `p + i - 1`, which can be the last byte of a multibyte character, producing a split/invalid character on screen. This is an in-bounds display corruption concern, not a confirmed memory-safety or CWE-classified vulnerability.

If any unshown callee violates its contract (get_trans_bufname/get_keymap_str writing more than MAXPATHL bytes, mb_ptr2len reading past NUL, screen_puts/screen_fill accepting out-of-range columns), memory-safety issues could manifest at the call sites on lines 44, 106, 117-119, 121-124; these are outside the shown code and not confirmable here.

`clen` can transiently become -1 when a two-cell character straddles the `this_ru_col - 1` boundary (loop at lines 98-100), and `len = clen` at line 101 is only made non-negative by `++len` at line 106 when `i > 0`. The downstream arithmetic (`len + wp->w_wincol` at line 118) remains in range, but the odd accounting is a robustness concern.

All attacker-influenced input entering the shown code is confined to buffer-name bytes already constrained inside NameBuff; no argv, socket, or file-derived numeric input is parsed directly in this function.

verdict.summary: prealloc_elems_and_freelist computes the preallocation size in 32-bit arithmetic: elem_size (u32) * smap->map.max_entries (u32) wraps modulo 2^32 before being passed to bpf_map_area_alloc, while pcpu_freelist_populate later writes max_entries freelist nodes at elem_size strides. Attacker-controlled value_size/max_entries (BPF_MAP_CREATE) can make the wrapped allocation far smaller than the populated span (e.g., elem_size 8192, max_entries 524289 -> 8192-byte allocation, node i=1 written at offset 8192), yielding a kernel heap out-of-bounds write due to integer overflow (CWE-190 -> CWE-122).

evidence.reason: Sink of the integer overflow: elem_size and smap->map.max_entries are both u32 (Phase 1, attacker-controlled via BPF_MAP_CREATE), so the product is computed in unsigned 32-bit arithmetic and wraps mod 2^32 before zero-extension to size_t. elem_size=8192 with max_entries=524289 gives true product 0x1_0000_2000 but allocates only 8192 bytes.

OOB write trigger: the callee writes a pcpu_freelist_node (>=8 bytes) at mem + i*elem_size for i in [0, max_entries). With the wrapped 8192-byte allocation from the L6 sink and max_entries=524289, node i=1 writes at offset 8192, immediately past the buffer; the shown L8 null check does not bound the size. Impact: kernel heap buffer overflow (CWE-122).

Origin of the vulnerable size: the size_t sum is narrowed into a u32, and elem_size (user-controlled via value_size) is the multiplicand whose wrap at L6 truncates the allocation while the un-truncated count max_entries is passed at L16, creating the size/count mismatch.

assumptions: smap->map.value_size and smap->map.max_entries originate from the user-supplied BPF_MAP_CREATE attributes via the caller stack_map_alloc (standard eBPF map-creation dataflow).
sizeof(struct stack_map_bucket) is a fixed compile-time constant (528 bytes in upstream with MAX_STACK_DEPTH=64); the exact value does not affect the overflow conclusion.
pcpu_freelist_populate writes one pcpu_freelist_node (at least 8 bytes) at each mem + i*size offset for i in [0, nr), per its in-kernel contract (kernel/bpf/percpu_freelist.c).
limitations: The caller stack_map_alloc is not shown; upstream bounds it may impose (e.g., value_size <= KMALLOC_MAX_SIZE, cost checks) are not part of the shown code, so the widest reachable attacker values are inferred from BPF map-creation semantics rather than verified against the caller.
The exact bucket and freelist-node struct sizes are defined in unshown headers; they change the OOB write extent, not the overflow or the undersized allocation.
Unprivileged triggering depends on BPF capability configuration (CAP_BPF/CAP_SYS_ADMIN, unprivileged_bpf_disabled); this affects exploitability, not the presence of the bug.

verdict.summary: No attacker-reachable memory-safety or logic vulnerability in addBinding. The attacker-controlled URI length (len) is capped by 'len > INT_MAX - EXPAND_SPARE' checks (lines 68, 96) and by the SIZE_MAX/sizeof(XML_Char) checks (lines 76-80, 103-107) before any allocation arithmetic, the memcpy size is derived from the same NUL-terminated uri and fits the (len + EXPAND_SPARE) allocation, and the prefix->name reads are bounded by the chained literal-match conditions. Remaining concerns (unbounded URI length for large allocations, stored URI non-termination when m_namespaceSeparator is set) depend on parser-level limits and consumers outside the shown code.

evidence.reason: Guard before the size computations (lines 83, 110): len is the attacker-controlled URI length from the line 45 loop plus optional separator increment (lines 63-64). This check ensures len + EXPAND_SPARE never overflows int, so sizeof(XML_Char) * (len + EXPAND_SPARE) cannot wrap on 64-bit; candidate integer-overflow finding C1 is not reachable.

On 32-bit size_t platforms this caps (len + EXPAND_SPARE) at SIZE_MAX/sizeof(XML_Char), preventing size_t overflow of the allocation product at lines 83 and 110; on 64-bit the earlier INT_MAX cap already bounds the product far below SIZE_MAX. Sink for candidate C1 is therefore unreachable in every build configuration.

memcpy length equals len, which is strlen(uri) or strlen(uri)+1 (when the separator increment at lines 63-64 is taken); the +1 case copies uri's NUL element, still inside the source string, and the destination was allocated with len + EXPAND_SPARE XML_Chars (lines 87, 115). The write at b->uri[len-1] uses index >= 0 and < capacity. Candidates C2 and C3 are not reachable.

Each read prefix->name[k] (k = 1..5) is only evaluated after prefix->name[0..k-1] matched the literal, which guarantees the NUL-terminated name string is at least k+1 chars long, so index k is inside the string storage. Candidate C4 is not reachable for any NUL-terminated prefix name (framework invariant).

assumptions: uri is a NUL-terminated XML_Char string whose storage contains at least strlen(uri)+1 elements (standard Expat string representation).
prefix->name is a NUL-terminated XML_Char string (parser-internal invariant).
EXPAND_SPARE is a small positive compile-time constant (e.g., 20), so len + EXPAND_SPARE cannot overflow between the guard and the allocation.
XML_Char is 1 or 2 bytes in the builds under consideration; even with 4-byte XML_Char the guards at lines 76-80 / 103-107 cap the product below SIZE_MAX on 32-bit.
Parser-level limits on attribute/URI buffer sizes (outside this function) keep realistic len values feasible.
limitations: The allocation size grows linearly with the attacker-controlled URI length up to INT_MAX; a denial-of-service via very large namespace URIs cannot be confirmed because parser-level size limits are not shown in this code.

When m_namespaceSeparator is set, the separator overwrites the copied NUL terminator (line 120), so the stored b->uri is not NUL-terminated; safety then depends on all consumers honoring b->uriLen, which is outside the shown code.

Integer-overflow and size checks depend on SIZE_MAX/UINT_MAX semantics of the build platform; a platform where unsigned int cannot represent all size_t values was assumed to have size_t <= 32 bits, matching the #if UINT_MAX >= SIZE_MAX guard.

If a caller supplied a non-NUL-terminated uri or prefix->name (violating the internal contract), the loop at lines 45-52 and the memcpy at line 118 could misbehave; this is out of the shown code's reachable scope.

verdict.summary: addBinding contains no confirmed, reachable vulnerability. Static-array reads in the reserved-URI comparison loop are bounded by the len > xmlLen / len > xmlnsLen short-circuit guards against arrays sized xmlLen+1 / xmlnsLen+1; allocation arithmetic in both the realloc and malloc paths is protected by INT_MAX - EXPAND_SPARE and size_t product overflow guards before the sizeof(XML_Char) * (len + EXPAND_SPARE) MALLOC/REALLOC calls; the memcpy at the end copies at most through the NUL terminator of the pool-allocated uri, which is in bounds.

evidence.reason: Potential CWE-125 read of xmlNamespace/xmlnsNamespace is fully guarded: xmlLen==35 and xmlnsLen==27 are computed from array sizes including the terminator (lines 12, 19-20), and the `||` short-circuit ensures `uri[len] != xmlNamespace[len]` / `uri[len] != xmlnsNamespace[len]` executes only while `len <= xmlLen` / `len <= xmlnsLen`, i.e. index 35/27 at most, which is the in-bounds NUL element.

Potential CWE-190/CWE-680 in the attacker-length-driven `sizeof(XML_Char) * (len + EXPAND_SPARE)` is blocked before `REALLOC`: line 79 bounds `len` to `INT_MAX - EXPAND_SPARE`, and line 88 (where `size_t` can overflow on the platform) bounds the byte product, so no wrapping value reaches the allocation size.

The fresh-allocation path repeats the same two overflow guards (lines 107 and 115) before `MALLOC` (line 121), so attacker-controlled `uri` length cannot overflow `len + EXPAND_SPARE` (int) or the `sizeof(XML_Char) * (len + EXPAND_SPARE)` byte count (size_t), keeping the later `memcpy` (line 129) and `b->uri[len - 1]` write (line 131) within the `len + EXPAND_SPARE`-element buffer.

assumptions: `uri` is NUL-terminated and its storage includes the terminator (parser string-pool invariant).
`prefix->name` is NUL-terminated (parser/Dtd invariant).
`strlen(uri)` cannot reach `INT_MAX` because parser-level input length limits (not shown here) bound attribute value sizes.
Downstream namespace-aware consumers use `b->uriLen` rather than treating `b->uri` as a NUL-terminated string after the separator is written.
limitations: If a caller passed a non-NUL-terminated or undersized `uri`, the `memcpy` at line 129 (which copies `len == strlen(uri)+1` elements when `m_namespaceSeparator` is set) could over-read; this depends on violating the string-pool contract and is not reachable within the shown code.

If `strlen(uri) == INT_MAX` while `m_namespaceSeparator` is set, `len++` at line 74 would wrap `int`; no guard in this function prevents it, but it depends on parser-level input-size invariants outside this function.
After line 131, `b->uri[len]` is left uninitialized and the binding string is not NUL-terminated; this is only a robustness concern if some not-shown consumer scans `b->uri` past `uriLen`.
Only `addBinding` was analyzed; callers and the namespace-splitting consumer logic were not in scope.

verdict.summary: win_redr_status() reads the translated buffer name into len without ever re-checking it against MAXPATHL before appending status suffixes. For a buffer whose name fills NameBuff to MAXPATHL-1 bytes (crafted long path), the unguarded `*(p + len++) = ' '` advances len to MAXPATHL; the subsequent `len += (int)STRLEN(p + len)` calls then read one byte past the end of NameBuff (out-of-bounds read), and the inflated len later feeds `p += len - (this_ru_col - 1); *p = '<'` (single-byte mode) and `vim_snprintf(p + len, MAXPATHL - len, ...)` with a negative size, producing out-of-bounds writes into memory adjacent to NameBuff.

evidence.reason: Root cause: len is taken solely from STRLEN(NameBuff) with no MAXPATHL bound check, and line 54 unconditionally executes *(p + len++) = ' ' when any flag on lines 48-53 is set. With an attacker-supplied translated name of exactly MAXPATHL-1 bytes, the append writes the final legal byte and sets len = MAXPATHL, after which every p + len expression addresses NameBuff + MAXPATHL (one-past-end).

evidence.snippet:
vim_snprintf((char *)p + len, MAXPATHL - len, "%s", "[+]");
	    len += (int)STRLEN(p + len);
evidence.reason: Confirmed OOB read sink (same pattern at lines 57-58, 63-64, 78-79): with len == MAXPATHL, vim_snprintf receives remaining size 0 and writes nothing, then STRLEN(p + len) reads from NameBuff + MAXPATHL, past the end of the MAXPATHL-byte buffer, and adds the number of adjacent non-NUL bytes to len, inflating it beyond the buffer.

Confirmed OOB write sink for has_mbyte == 0: the len inflated by the OOB reads at lines 58/64/74/79 is used as a byte offset; line 113 advances p to NameBuff + MAXPATHL + g - (this_ru_col - 1), and line 114 writes '<' outside the MAXPATHL-byte buffer (g >= 1 non-NUL bytes found past the buffer). If b_p_ro is set, line 78's vim_snprintf also receives MAXPATHL - len as a negative int widened to a huge size_t, writing "[RO]" out of bounds.

assumptions: NameBuff is a static buffer of exactly MAXPATHL bytes and get_trans_bufname()/trans_characters() guarantees a NUL-terminated result of byte length <= MAXPATHL-1 (caller contract not shown in the snippet).
MAXPATHL equals PATH_MAX (4096) on the target platform, so OS-level file names can produce translated names of exactly MAXPATHL-1 bytes.
vim_snprintf(str, 0, ...) performs no write (snprintf-family size-0 contract).
The default statusline path is reached: *p_stl == NUL and *wp->w_p_stl == NUL, redrawing() is true, and no popup menu overrides the redraw.
The 'changed' (bufIsChanged) flag is set by editing the buffer, and b_p_ro by a read-only file or 'ro' option.
limitations: The exact truncation bound inside get_trans_bufname()/trans_characters() is not shown; if it caps the name strictly below MAXPATHL-1, the len == MAXPATHL edge is unreachable.

The post-corruption behavior of out-of-scope callees (screen_puts, screen_fill, win_redr_ruler, get_keymap_str internals) with the corrupted pointer/length was not verified; the write magnitude/gap depends on the layout of globals adjacent to NameBuff.

If (*mb_ptr2len)(p + i) could return 0 for an invalid byte, the multibyte truncation loop (lines 99-101) would not terminate; no concrete attacker-controlled encoding value is shown to produce that, so it is recorded as a robustness concern only.
Setting a custom 'statusline' option bypasses this code path entirely.

verdict.summary: No attacker-triggerable memory-safety flaw is confirmable within the shown code. All accesses to the heap buffer b are confined to [0, size) with size >= 32 enforced at line 11, and both r_buf_read_at call sites are guarded by 'available != size' checks (lines 19, 56) that return NULL on read failure, so no out-of-bounds access is reachable inside this function. The strongest residual concern is the missing off >= 0 validation: a negative off passes the off >= size guard (line 4), inflates size (line 7), and is promoted to a huge ut64 at the r_buf_read_at calls (lines 18, 55) and forwarded as off + 16 (line 72), but any resulting OOB would occur inside the unshown callee implementations, which is out of scope for a confirmed finding and is recorded as a limitation.

evidence.reason: The guard only rejects off >= size; a negative int off (e.g., off = -8) passes it. Then size -= off grows size beyond buf_size. There is no off >= 0 check, so the negative value flows to the r_buf_read_at call at line 18, where int-to-ut64 promotion turns it into a ~2^64 address. Within the shown code the only defense is the follow-up 'available != size' check, so no in-function OOB is reachable; the unchecked lower bound is the root of the unconfirmed callee-address concern.

This is the first dangerous call site: off (possibly negative) is passed as the ut64 address parameter and size (st64, possibly > INT_MAX) as the int length parameter. The guard fully covers subsequent use of b inside this function: any callee failure returns NULL before b is touched. A wrapped-address OOB could only materialize inside r_buf_read_at itself, whose implementation is not shown, so the negative-offset path is a limitation, not a confirmed finding.

The retry re-read uses off - 8, which is negative whenever off < 8 (and reachable because the first read at line 18 succeeded with positive off in [0, 7] satisfying off < size and size >= 32). The same int->ut64 promotion applies; the only in-function protection is the 'available != size' bailout, and any read past the buffer would occur inside the unshown r_buf_read_at. This confirms the missing-lower-bound pattern repeats on a second reachable path, still without an in-scope sink.

assumptions: r_buf_read_at reports failure (returns a value != the requested length) when it cannot read a requested range; the code itself encodes this contract via the 'available != size' checks.
size (st64) is within the int range accepted by r_buf_read_at's length parameter; any narrowing for size > INT_MAX would trip the 'available != size' check and return NULL.
off originates from caller parsing logic, so attacker-control of its value cannot be traced within the shown code; it is treated only as a potentially attacker-influenced parameter.
limitations: Missing off >= 0 validation: negative off passes the line 4 guard, inflates size at line 7, and reaches the unshown r_buf_read_at at lines 18 and 55 as a huge ut64 address (also off + 16 at line 72 into r_coresym_cache_element_new). Any OOB read or wrapped addr+len arithmetic would take place inside those unshown callees; unconfirmed per the scoping rules (would otherwise be CWE-125 with CWE-681).
Integer overflow of off - 8 (line 55) and off + 16 (line 72) requires off near INT_MAX, i.e., a buffer larger than 2 GiB; theoretical worst case, not demonstrated.
st64-to-int narrowing of the length argument at lines 18 and 55 for size > INT_MAX would fail the 'available != size' checks; robustness concern only.

A negative off inflates the malloc(size) request (line 14) beyond the file size, bounded by |INT_MIN| + buf_size; malloc failure is handled, so this is at most a resource/robustness concern, not a confirmed vulnerability.

verdict.summary: nft_flow_rule_create() sizes the flow rule from num_actions, which counts only expressions whose offload_action is set and returns true (L11-13), but then fills the rule by calling expr->ops->offload() for every expression with an offload op (L35-45) and unconditionally invokes nft_flow_rule_transfer_vlan() (L46). Nothing shown bounds the number of appended actions by num_actions, so a crafted nftables rule can drive more action slots than were allocated, producing a heap out-of-bounds write (CVE-2021-45469 pattern).

evidence.reason: Action capacity is counted from the offload_action predicate only: expressions without a true-returning offload_action are not counted, even though they may still append actions later via their offload callback. This under-count flows directly into nft_flow_rule_alloc() at L21.

Sizing sink: the flow rule's action storage is allocated with capacity num_actions derived from the L10-13 predicate. The actual number of actions appended (L40/L46) is not constrained by this value, so the allocation can be smaller than the fill volume (CWE-131 leading to CWE-787).

Fill phase: offload() is invoked for every expression with an offload op, regardless of the counting predicate used at L11-13, and the appends it performs inside are not bounded by num_actions from L21.

Unconditional additional append path: the VLAN action transfer runs after the offload loop and is not reflected in the num_actions count (L13/L21), providing at least one extra potential action slot write beyond the allocated capacity.

assumptions: nft_expr_first/nft_expr_more/nft_expr_next correctly bound iteration to the validated expression area of rule.
nft_flow_rule_alloc() sizes the flow rule's action storage from its num_actions argument (standard upstream implementation).
The per-expression offload() callbacks and nft_flow_rule_transfer_vlan() append action records into flow's action array.
rule contents originate from the nf_tables netlink interface, making the expression mix attacker-influenced.
limitations: The exact byte-level out-of-bounds write instruction and the action-array layout live in nft_flow_rule_alloc(), the per-op offload() callbacks, and nft_flow_rule_transfer_vlan(), none of which are in the shown excerpt; the overflow offset is therefore inferred, not pinned to a shown line.
Triggering requires the nf_tables rule-creation caller path (CAP_NET_ADMIN in a network namespace), which is only referenced implicitly by this function's contract, not shown here.
No kernel build/repro was run in this environment to validate the exact appended-action count for a concrete rule.
The historical CVE-2021-45469 attribution is from prior knowledge of this function and is consistent with, but not provable solely from, the shown code.

verdict.summary: r_bin_java_inner_classes_attr_new reads the 2-byte number_of_classes field (buffer+6) before any bounds check against sz. A crafted InnerClasses attribute whose payload is truncated to 0-1 bytes after the 6-byte header (sz=6 or 7) causes a 1-2 byte out-of-bounds read of attacker-controlled file data, in violation of the code's own size discipline established by the later `offset + 8 > sz` guard.

evidence.reason: Sink: R_BIN_JAVA_USHORT reads buffer[offset] and buffer[offset+1] with offset=6 (line 8) and no prior check that offset+2 <= sz. Taint: buffer/sz originate from the untrusted class file; truncation makes sz=6 or 7. Reachability: the only prior branch (attr == NULL, line 9) does not fire for a header-present 6/7-byte region, and the loop guard at line 19 executes an iteration too late. Impact: 1-2 byte OOB read past the region end (CWE-125): info disclosure and potential ASan/SEGV crash on crafted input.

assumptions: r_bin_java_default_attr_new succeeds whenever at least the 6-byte attribute header is present (sz >= 6), so control reaches line 14 for sz=6 and sz=7.
R_BIN_JAVA_USHORT(a, b) reads exactly two consecutive bytes a[b] and a[b+1].
sz is the exact accessible size of the buffer/region passed by the caller, matching the code's own use of sz as a bound at line 19.
limitations: Impact magnitude depends on caller allocation granularity; if the underlying allocation is larger than sz (e.g., full-file mmap), the OOB read may stay within the allocation and only violate the region bound, reducing severity to robustness.
Lines 43/49 call r_bin_java_get_item_name_from_bin_cp_list with obj possibly NULL (lines 40-48); any NULL dereference would occur in that unshown callee, so it is unconfirmed here.
Line 53 frees icattr without freeing icattr->flags_str (allocated at line 35), leaking memory on the error path; robustness only, no security impact.
If default_attr_new itself fails or reads OOB for sz < 6, that behavior is outside the shown code and was not evaluated.
offset + 8 cannot wrap ut64 (max ~524288), so no integer-overflow concern in the loop math.

verdict.summary: Out-of-bounds read in the CP950 PUA lookup: after the search loop over cp950_pua_tbl exits without a match, k equals the row count N and lines 57-61 unconditionally dereference cp950_pua_tbl[k][...]. Attacker-controlled lead/trail byte pairs admitted by the line-45 guard (e.g., 0x81 0x3A) can exhaust the loop, causing a one-past-the-end read in the Big5/CP950 converter.

evidence.reason: The loop bound N = sizeof(cp950_pua_tbl)/(sizeof(unsigned short)*4) allows k to reach N when no row satisfies c2 in [row[2], row[3]]. The following lines dereference cp950_pua_tbl[k][2] and cp950_pua_tbl[k][0] with no k < N guard, so an exhausted search reads one row past the table. k derives from attacker-controlled c2 (lines 20/30/50); a guard-passing pair such as c1=0x81, c=0x3A (c2=0x813A) can reach this sink.

This guard admits c1 = 0x81 (range [0x81,0x8d]) with trail c = 0x3A (range (0x39,0x7f)) when the main table lookup yields w = 0 (line 40 after line 37 fails for the negative w computed at line 33). It also admits trail bytes 0x3A-0x3F, below the 0x40 row-start the code itself tests at line 57, so a no-match loop exit is not excluded. c2 is formed from these attacker-controlled bytes at line 50 and drives the search in lines 51-55.

Taint source for the lead byte: any attacker-supplied byte c with c1 < c < 0xff (for CP950, c1 = 0x80 from line 9, so c = 0x81 qualifies) is cached and later read back at line 30, entering the PUA path that leads to the out-of-bounds table read.

assumptions: The filter is fed bytes one at a time in the range 0x00-0xFF from the string being converted (standard mbfl decoder contract).
filter->from->no_encoding is trusted framework-internal data selecting CP950 vs Big5.
big5_ucs_table_size correctly bounds big5_ucs_table, and the line-37 guard fully covers the line-38 access.
cp950_pua_tbl is a static array of N rows of 4 unsigned short values with range in columns [2],[3].
limitations: The exact input that misses every cp950_pua_tbl row cannot be proven from the shown code because the table contents are not displayed; the confirmed defect is the unconditional post-loop dereference with no k < N guard, and the concrete trigger is data-dependent on table gaps.
CK(...) and filter->output_function are not shown; their failure modes (error propagation, buffer writing) are out of scope.

Impact is limited to an out-of-bounds read (potential crash or information disclosure); whether a specific input crashes or only corrupts w depends on heap/static-data layout and is not determinable from the shown code.

verdict.summary: No confirmed, reachable attacker-triggerable vulnerability in the shown code. The historically dangerous mb_ptr2len call (line 99) is protected by the new_cursor_col >= 0 guard (line 98) and by the loop's NUL break (lines 102-103), keeping all reads within [0, len]; the space-buffer writes (lines 114-120) and VREPLACE NUL write (line 196) are within their allocations. Remaining concerns (mb_ptr2len boundary behavior on truncated multi-byte sequences, out-of-scope helper functions) are unconfirmed robustness matters.

evidence.reason: The only negative index, new_cursor_col == -1 set at line 93, is excluded from the sink at line 99 by the guard at line 98, so mb_ptr2len is never invoked at ptr-1. After the first iteration new_cursor_col is in [0, len] and each position passed to mb_ptr2len (line 99) was validated non-NUL at line 102 in the prior iteration, so the subsequent ptr[] reads at lines 102 and 104 stay within the NUL-terminated line buffer ([0, len]). No concrete value reaches line 99 with an out-of-bounds pointer.

When the branch is entered, vcol == last_vcol <= virtcol (set at lines 97 and 106) and vcol != virtcol (line 110), so i = virtcol - vcol >= 1. alloc(i + 1) at line 114 allocates indices [0, i], and the writes at lines 118-120 cover exactly those indices; no write exceeds the allocation. The NUL write at line 196 is likewise bounded because cursor col never exceeds the new line length.

assumptions: ml_get_curline() returns a NUL-terminated buffer with at least len+1 bytes (standard Vim line-buffer invariant).
mb_ptr2len, for the active encoding, reads only valid character bytes plus the terminating NUL when called on a position previously validated as non-NUL within the line.
lbr_chartabsize returns at least 1 for any non-NUL byte, guaranteeing loop progress and termination.
beginline(BL_WHITE) leaves curwin->w_cursor.col within [0, len].

If mb_ptr2len for the configured encoding read past the terminating NUL for a truncated trailing multi-byte sequence, a small OOB read would occur at lines 99/102; this depends on the library's boundary contract, which is not shown, and the validated-character invariant makes it unconfirmed.

Helper functions called but not shown (set_indent, shift_line, ins_str, ins_bytes, backspace_until_column, ml_replace, replace_join, replace_push) could contain issues of their own, but they are outside the analyzed code.

verdict.summary: No confirmed, reachable, attacker-triggerable vulnerability in the shown code. The dereference of priv->ndev->nfc_dev at line 6 occurs before any free in this function (nci_free_device is at line 14), the GPIO release is fully guarded by gpio_is_valid, and kfree(priv) is the last statement. The only suspicious constructs depend on unshown callees/callers (nci_unregister_device semantics, registration-lifetime invariant, nfcmrvl_fw_dnld_* bodies) and are recorded as limitations, not findings.

evidence.reason: Examined sink candidate: priv->ndev->nfc_dev is dereferenced after nci_unregister_device(ndev) (line 5). Both pointers originate from driver registration (priv->ndev = nci_allocate_device(...), not shown) and are not attacker-controlled; no free of ndev or ndev->nfc_dev occurs between line 5 and line 6 in the shown code, since nci_free_device (the ownership transfer) is at line 14. Possible UAF/NULL-deref would require unshown nci_unregister_device semantics or a caller violating the registration invariant, so this is not a confirmed vulnerability.

assumptions: nfcmrvl_nci_unregister_dev is invoked only after successful registration, so priv, priv->ndev and priv->ndev->nfc_dev are non-NULL
nci_unregister_device(ndev) does not free ndev or ndev->nfc_dev; freeing is deferred to nci_free_device(ndev)
kfree(priv) at line 15 is the final access to priv, and no concurrent accessor is considered within the shown function
limitations: NULL-pointer dereference of priv->ndev->nfc_dev (line 6) is only reachable if a caller violates the registration invariant or if nci_unregister_device frees the device; both depend on code outside the shown snippet and are unconfirmed hypotheses

Use-after-free between line 5 and line 6 cannot be confirmed because nci_unregister_device's body is not shown; the NCI-core contract (free only in nci_free_device) supports the not-vulnerable reading
nfcmrvl_fw_dnld_abort (line 7) and nfcmrvl_fw_dnld_deinit (line 9) are unshown; any double-free, race, or stale-access concern involving them cannot be substantiated from this code
Attacker influence over fw_download_in_progress is not demonstrated by the shown code; it is treated purely as a kernel-managed flag
The GPIO release ordering/lifetime relative to drive-request APIs outside this function is not verifiable from the shown code

verdict.summary: No attacker-triggerable vulnerability is confirmed within the shown code. The permission gate (maywrite), the length-bounded memcmp equality check, the userid==NULL rejection, and the quota arithmetic are guarded/valid as far as the shown lines establish. The remaining concerns (key buffer safety and keylen validation, memcmp NULL-safety, quota-diff integer behavior) all depend on out-of-scope callees or type invariants (make_key, struct buf representation, cyrusdb retry contract) and are recorded as unconfirmed limitations.

evidence.reason: The stack buffer is MAX_MAILBOX_PATH+1 bytes and is filled only through make_key(..., key, sizeof(key)) at line 26. The shown code never validates the returned keylen before it flows into read_old_value/cyrusdb_delete/cyrusdb_store (lines 29/68/93); whether this is safe is determined entirely by make_key, which is not shown, so no overflow or negative-length path can be confirmed from the visible code.

memcmp is short-circuited when value->len == 0 and otherwise reads exactly value->len bytes from both sides, so the comparison is fully length-bounded. A NULL-deref would require a struct buf with len > 0 and s == NULL, which violates the Cyrus buf invariant and is not constructible from the shown code.

With struct buf.len typed int (Cyrus lib/buf.h) and quota_t a signed 64-bit type, value->len and oldval.len both promote to 64-bit signed and the difference lies in [-2^31+1, 2^31-1], so no integer overflow or unsigned wrap occurs for any reachable len. A wrap-based failure would require an unsigned len representation that the shown code does not establish.

For non-empty annotation values, a NULL userid aborts the write, closing the historical path that would create prefix-ambiguous keys. The empty-value branch (lines 74-76) is intentionally left open for tombstone/cleanup, so no unauthorized-write path is reachable from this guard.

assumptions: struct buf.len is int (Cyrus lib/buf.h), so line 44 arithmetic is performed in signed 64-bit and cannot overflow.
quota_t is a signed 64-bit type.
make_key honors its capacity argument (sizeof(key)) and returns a length within the buffer.
struct buf invariant: s is non-NULL whenever len > 0.
MAX_MAILBOX_PATH is on the order of 900, constraining the key buffer size used in Phase 2.
limitations: keylen from make_key (line 26) is consumed unvalidated at lines 29/68/93; if make_key can return -1 or a value exceeding sizeof(key), attacker-controlled entry/userid/mboxname would drive an out-of-bounds or negative-length DB access. Not confirmed because make_key is out of scope.

If make_key silently truncates long mailbox names/entries/userids, distinct annotations could collide on the same DB key, enabling cross-user overwrite. Unconfirmed; depends on make_key's truncation semantics.
memcmp at line 33 would dereference NULL if a caller supplied a buf with len > 0 and s == NULL; the shown code does not enforce this, relying on the framework invariant.
If struct buf.len were an unsigned size_t, line 44 would wrap for oldval.len > value->len and cause spurious quota denials (availability), but the visible code and Cyrus buf.h contradict that type.
The cyrusdb_delete/cyrusdb_store retry loops (lines 67-69, 92-94) could spin indefinitely on persistent CYRUSDB_AGAIN; termination relies on the cyrusdb backend contract.

verdict.summary: The octet-count accumulator (iOctetsRemain) is a signed int that grows unboundedly from attacker-supplied digits (line 33). Sending more than INT_MAX worth of digits (e.g. '2147483648 ') wraps it negative after an unchecked signed-overflow; the negative value is only logged about (lines 40-53), left in place, and on the next invocation is assigned to octatesToCopy (line 98), passes both size guards (lines 100-106) unchanged, and is converted to a huge size_t for memcpy (line 108), causing an out-of-bounds heap write and a remotely triggerable crash.

evidence.reason: Attacker-controlled digit c (line 10) is accumulated into the signed int iOctetsRemain with no digit-count cap and no range check. Repeated bytes like '2','1','4','7','4','8','3','6','4','8' drive the value through INT_MAX and wrap it to -2147483648 (CWE-190), the taint origin for the memcpy OOB write.

Both bounds checks only log; they neither reset iOctetsRemain nor abort the frame, so the negative (wrapped) value survives and line 54 sets inputState=eInMsg while eFraming remains TCP_FRAMING_OCTET_COUNTING, directing the next invocation into the copy path.

Sink: octatesToCopy was assigned from the negative iOctetsRemain at line 98; the guards at lines 100 and 103 only shrink positive values, so the negative int is converted to a huge size_t and passed to memcpy, writing far past the pMsg heap buffer (CWE-787) and crashing: reachable with the input '2147483648 ' followed by any further byte.

assumptions: iOctetsRemain and iMsg are signed 32-bit ints with two's-complement wraparound at line 33.

Three-part reachability assumes the caller re-invokes processDataRcvd per received byte with buffLen >= 1, as the persistent inputState/iOctetsRemain state machine implies (rsyslog-style streaming driver).
pMsg is a heap buffer of capacity iMaxLine (+terminator) and iMaxLine is a positive int, so a length >= 0x80000000 on 32-bit / 0xFFFFFFFF80000000 on 64-bit is out of bounds.
limitations: isdigit(c) at line 32 is called with c promoted directly (no (unsigned char) cast), which is undefined behavior for wire bytes >= 0x80; no exploitable impact could be confirmed, so it is not reported.
The iOctetsRemain == 0 case moves *buff backward by one (line 111, '- 1') and relies on an unshown caller offset contract; potential re-processing was not confirmed as exploitable.
A buffLen == 0 or empty *buff invocation is not handled; a caller-supplied non-empty buffer invariant is assumed.
Beyond the guaranteed crash, deterministic corruption/exploitation depends on allocator layout, which is outside the shown code.

verdict.summary: Heap-based buffer overflow in unix_expandpath(): buf is allocated as STRLEN(path)+BASENAMELEN+5 (line 32) and directory entry names returned by readdir() (up to NAME_MAX=255 bytes) are copied into it with STRCPY(s, dp->d_name) (line 150) without any length check. A single file/directory entry whose name exceeds the ~104-byte free space (e.g., >=104 chars with pattern "*", >=105 with "**") writes past the heap allocation; the '**'-append writes at lines 157-158 and 164 compound the overflow. Reachable via any wildcard expansion (e.g., :e *, :find, filename completion) over a directory containing a crafted long file name.

evidence.reason: Fixed-size heap allocation: with BASENAMELEN=100 this is STRLEN(path)+105 bytes. After copying path (p-buf <= STRLEN(path), line 45-73), the free space starting at the component pointer s is only BASENAMELEN+4 = 104 data bytes, yet the sink copies up to 256 bytes of dirent name.

Sink: attacker-influenced dp->d_name from readdir() (line 138) is copied at s with no length validation. Pattern "*": buf=106 bytes, s=buf, a 255-char directory entry name writes 256 bytes -> ~150-byte heap overrun. The match guard at lines 141-148 checks only dot-prefix and regex/ncmp match, never d_name length, so it cannot prevent overflow.

Secondary overflow sites in the starstar branch: len (line 151) already includes a long d_name, and path_end is the un-validated tail of the pattern; buf is the same fixed-size allocation (line 32), so the appended "/**" and remaining pattern bytes can extend past the heap object.

Additional overflow site: after a long entry is copied at s, STRCPY(buf+len, path_end) writes the original pattern tail beyond the remaining buf capacity (buf_size - len - 1 < strlen(path_end)+1 when d_name length is large).

assumptions: BASENAMELEN is not defined in the shown snippet; Vim's os_unix.h defines it as 100. The verdict does not depend on this exact value: with BASENAMELEN=255 the line 157-158/164 append path would still overflow for long entries plus a non-empty pattern tail.
NAME_MAX on the target filesystem is 255 (Linux), so readdir() may return 255-char names; this is the concrete value used to demonstrate the overflow magnitude.
Line numbers refer to the provided code block starting at 'unix_expandpath(' as line 1 (no repository file was available in the workspace).
wildoff, flags, and recursion inputs (lines 125/160/169) are framework-internal and bounded by the caller's own buffer, consistent with Vim's wildcard-expansion call sites.
limitations: The MACOS_CONVERT block (lines 183-193) can also overrun buf if mac_precompose_path returns longer output; it is compiled only under a macro not shown here, so it is an unconfirmed hypothesis rather than a reported finding.
The ptroff_t-to-int casts at lines 125/160/169 are theoretically narrowing but cannot change values at reachable pattern lengths (< INT_MAX); robustness concern only.
alloc(SIZE) arithmetic at line 32 could in principle wrap, but no reachable path supplies a multi-GB pattern (recursion bounds path at the caller's buffer), so this is not exploitable in-context.
Recursion depth is capped by stardepth < 100 (lines 24/120/153); deep-recursion stack exhaustion is bounded and not reported.

verdict.summary: Heap buffer overflow in gzip extra-field parsing: an attacker-chosen 16-bit extra length (E) stored in state->length/head->extra_len can exceed the application-provided head->extra buffer size (extra_max). With chunked input, the already-copied offset len = extra_len - state->length grows past extra_max because state->length is reduced by the full copy even when the write is clamped; the size expression extra_max - len then underflows to ~2^32-1 and zmemcpy performs a massive out-of-bounds heap write.

evidence.reason: Taint origin: 16 input bits (attacker-controlled gzip FEXTRA length, range 0..65535) are stored verbatim into persistent state->length with no cap relative to head->extra_max; it survives across inflate() calls and drives the size arithmetic at the sink (lines 141-149).

Sink: with E=65535, extra_max=100, and 100-byte chunks, after two calls len=200 (> extra_max) and the guard still takes the clamped branch, computing size = 100 - 200 = 0xFFFFFF9C (unsigned underflow, CWE-191) passed to zmemcpy at extra+200, producing a confirmed out-of-bounds heap write (CWE-787). The guard covers only len <= extra_max; no check bounds len or E.

Mechanism enabling the underflow: state->length is decremented by the full clamped copy (up to have) even when only extra_max-len bytes were written, so the offset len = extra_len - state->length (line 146) strictly increases past extra_max on subsequent resumed iterations (line 157 returns mid-field), making the next extra_max - len computation wrap.

assumptions: The application is a zlib consumer that registered a gzip header via inflateGetHeader (state->head != Z_NULL) and supplied a heap buffer head->extra of size extra_max smaller than the stream's 16-bit extra length.
Input is delivered to inflate() incrementally (avail_in limited per call), which is the zlib-documented streaming contract; the shown code explicitly resumes via goto inf_leave at line 157.
state->sane is initialized to 1 and state->wbits/wsize set by inflateInit2/inflateReset2 (not shown); MATCH relies on this for its distance checks.
Bit-buffer macros (NEEDBITS/BITS/DROPBITS/PULLBYTE/LOAD/RESTORE) and helpers (inflate_table, inflate_fast, updatewindow, fixedtables) are the standard zlib implementations (not shown).
limitations: Reachability of the overflow requires the inflateGetHeader integration (head and extra registered); consumers that never parse gzip headers into a caller buffer cannot reach the sink.

If the entire gzip header (all E extra bytes) is supplied in a single inflate() call with have >= E, state->length reaches 0 before len can exceed extra_max and this path is safe; the bug requires chunked input.
The inflate_fast fast path (have >= 6 && left >= 258) is not shown; its internal bounds are assumed correct and were not part of this analysis.
Severity rated high rather than critical because exploitability depends on the inflateGetHeader usage pattern and heap layout; with full layout control the write could enable code execution.

verdict.summary: No attacker-reachable memory-safety or logic vulnerability is confirmed in the shown code. The only attacker-indexed access, param->string[i] in the name-validation loop, is fully covered by the guards at lines 63 and 65 (0 < size <= 255), and the fs_parameter contract guarantees at least size+1 readable bytes. All string stores transfer ownership via param->string = NULL, loop indices in the subsystem path derive from the static subsys table, and errors from fs_parse are handled before the switch. Remaining concerns (signed char to isalnum, (1 << i) for large i, unchecked NULL string for source/release_agent, reliance on the unshown kmemdup_nul invariant) fail taint, reachability, or impact and are recorded as limitations.

evidence.reason: The only attacker-influenced index is i in the loop at line 68. The guard at line 65 rejects any size > MAX_CGROUP_ROOT_NAMELEN - 1 (255), so the maximum reachable index is size-1 <= 254, and the fs_parameter buffer holds size data bytes plus a terminating NUL (kmemdup_nul invariant). The guard fully covers the access at line 69; no value passes the check yet reads out of bounds.

Ownership transfer pattern: param->string is moved into the fs_context and NULLed so the fs-layer cleanup will not free it while the context still references it. No dereference or copy of the stored pointer occurs in the shown code, so the absence of a length check here has no memory-safety impact within this function.

i originates from the static subsystem table, not from attacker input, so it is bounded well below 31; the (1 << i) shift at line 23 cannot overflow an int or reach undefined behavior. Even if the total subsystem count exceeded 16, u16 truncation of the mask would be a logic limitation, not a memory-safety issue in this code.

assumptions: fs_parse/vfs_parse_fs_string fills param->string with kmemdup_nul(value, size), guaranteeing size data bytes plus NUL and string == NULL only when size == 0.
cgroup_fc2context() returns a valid context pointer for any fc passed to this parser (fs_context private-data invariant).
for_each_subsys iterates the static, boot-time-constructed subsystem table with ids well below 31.
cgroup_no_v1_named is a read-only boot parameter in this kernel context.
limitations: Candidate A (OOB read in name loop) depends on the unshown kmemdup_nul/fs_parameter buffer invariant; if a caller ever built a fs_parameter whose size exceeded the actual string allocation, line 69 could read past it. Not confirmable from the shown code.

Candidate B (signed char c passed to isalnum at line 69-70) would read before a ctype table only under a ctype implementation that indexes by the raw signed value; the kernel's isalnum macro casts to unsigned char, and no such table is shown, so impact cannot be confirmed.
Candidate C ((1 << i) at line 23) would be undefined behavior only for i >= 32, which is unreachable because i comes from the static subsystem table (~13 entries).

Candidate D (no size/NULL validation on source and release_agent at lines 13 and 55) has no dereference or copy sink in the shown code; downstream use in cgroup1_get_tree / cgroup1_mount is outside this function's scope.
isalnum(c) with high-bit bytes simply fails the whitelist (returns 'Invalid name'), so no non-ASCII name is accepted even in the benign case.

verdict.summary: No confirmed attacker-reachable memory-safety or integer-overflow vulnerability in the shown code. The overflow guard at lines 94-95 provably detects every 32-bit wraparound of bytes_per_line*hh for all reachable ww/hh (hh in [1,INT_MAX], bpl in [1,2^28+1]), so no wrapped or negative size reaches g_malloc. The version-10 loop writes at most the allocated size (bytes_per_line is always even in the version10p branch, giving exactly size bytes with padding=0 and size-hh with padding=1), and the non-version10 loop writes exactly size bytes. Residual concerns (huge legitimate allocations near INT_MAX, sscanf %d out-of-range literal UB, unshown next_int) are recorded in limitations.

evidence.reason: Attacker-controlled fall-through values give hh in [1,2^31-1] (lines 40-49, 83-84) and bytes_per_line in [1,2^28+1] (line 91). If P=bytes_per_line*hh wraps 32-bit unsigned at line 93, the stored S=P mod 2^32 satisfies S <= P-2^32 < P-bytes_per_line, so S/bytes_per_line <= hh-1, and if S >= 2^31 the int value is negative; both outcomes make the int division differ from hh, so every wraparound is rejected and no truncated/negative size reaches g_malloc(size) at line 96.

In the version10p branch, padding=1 (line 86) exactly when ww%16 in 1..8, where (ww+7)/8 is odd, so bytes_per_line is even; for ww%16 in {0,9..15} padding=0 and (ww+7)/8 is even. Either way bytes_per_line is even, size is even, and the loop runs size/2 iterations writing at most 2 bytes each: exactly size bytes with padding=0, or size-hh bytes (high byte skipped at end of each scanline) with padding=1. The maximum pointer offset is size-1 (or size-hh-1), inside the g_malloc(size) allocation at line 96; loop terminates at bytes >= size.

The non-version10 loop increments ptr once per iteration and runs exactly size iterations (bytes goes 0..size-1, terminates when bytes == size), writing indices 0..size-1 into the size-byte allocation from line 96. No write can exceed the buffer.

The continue at line 53 fires whenever either post-decrement comparison is true, i.e., whenever type would be decremented to or below &name_and_type[0]; the fall-through that reaches strcmp at lines 54/56 requires both comparisons false, which forces the final type to remain at or after name_and_type[0]. No out-of-bounds read of type occurs.

assumptions: int is 32-bit two's complement and usual arithmetic conversions make bytes_per_line*hh (int x guint) modular unsigned 32-bit arithmetic.
MAX_SIZE is large enough that 'static...' format strings and token lengths (bounded by strlen(line) < MAX_SIZE-1) fit in line/name_and_type.
g_malloc aborts on allocation failure (GLib contract), which bounds the impact of the large-allocation path.
next_int is a file-format hex token reader returning a non-negative value on success and < 0 on failure; its exact body is outside the shown code.
limitations: Attacker-controlled dimensions that pass the overflow guard can request legitimate allocations up to ~2^31-1 bytes (e.g., ww=INT_MAX, hh=7 -> ~1.88 GB at line 96); on memory-constrained hosts g_malloc may abort, a resource-exhaustion/DoS concern (CWE-770/CWE-400) that depends on out-of-scope allocation failure and is not a confirmed corruption vulnerability.

sscanf %d on out-of-int-range numeric literals is undefined per the C standard; libc-specific clamping is not verified here, though both the value<=0 rejection and the proven-safe ranges neutralize the practical outcomes.
Forming &name_and_type[-1] during the post-decrement comparisons at lines 51-52 is formally UB pointer arithmetic, but the pointer is never dereferenced on that path; not exploitable.
Because next_int is not shown, malformed-hex parsing behavior could not be analyzed; however, any such effect cannot exceed the proven write-count bounds of the fill loops.

verdict.summary: No attacker-reachable vulnerability is confirmed within the shown code: every candidate (memcmp length misuse at the no-op check, unchecked keylen into cyrusdb_*, absent authz on the mailbox==NULL write path, pre-authz equality/quota side effects) depends on an out-of-scope caller or on a framework/library buf invariant not established in these lines.

evidence.reason: Candidate OOB read: value->len (int, caller-constructed buf) is the memcmp length. The guard proves oldval.len == value->len only; the read is bounded iff value->s and oldval.s each hold >= value->len valid bytes, which is the struct buf invariant (s NULL iff len==0, alloc>=len) maintained by code outside this snippet. A negative or oversized len already violates that invariant, and no path inside the shown code can create it, so reachability fails; demoted to limitation.
