This is the only authz check on the shown path and it sits inside the mailbox!=NULL branch. When mailbox==NULL, lines 60-96 delete/store without evaluating maywrite, and the equality early-out (34-35) returns before the check. Exploitation requires an unshown caller to invoke this static function with mailbox==NULL (or an equal-value no-op) while maywrite==0; that is an out-of-scope caller contract, so the CWE-863/285 hypothesis is unconfirmed.

Both operands are int before the (quota_t) cast promotes to signed 64-bit, so the difference stays within int range (no CWE-190) and negative deltas (deletion) are representable; QUOTA_ANNOTSTORAGE is a compile-time index into a QUOTA_NUMRESOURCES-sized array. No confirmed failure.

assumptions: struct buf invariant: s is NULL iff len==0 and at least len valid bytes exist at s; maintained by the buf API used by callers (not shown).
read_old_value sets oldval.s and oldval.len consistently from stored DB bytes.
make_key honors the sizeof(key) bound and returns a length that fits key, and callers never invoke write_entry with mailbox==NULL while maywrite==0.
Line numbers are 1-based counts from the start of the provided snippet.
limitations: memcmp at line 34 reads out of bounds only if a caller supplies a buf whose len exceeds the valid memory at s, or a negative len; not reachable through the shown code.
keylen from make_key (line 26) is passed unchecked to cyrusdb_delete/cyrusdb_store (lines 68, 93); an out-of-range return (e.g., -1) would be a vulnerability in the unshown callee.
The mailbox==NULL write path (lines 60-96) performs no maywrite/authz check; a confirmed authz bypass needs an unshown caller passing maywrite==0.

The equality early-out (34-35) and quota check (40) run before the maywrite check (44-47), letting an unauthorized caller trigger DB reads and observable equality/quota side effects; low-impact information/robustness concern, not a confirmed vulnerability.
The do/while retry loops on CYRUSDB_AGAIN (69, 94) and the DEBUG-only syslog printing value->s with %s (88-89) rely on DB behavior and NUL termination respectively; robustness/logging-only concerns.

verdict.summary: No attacker-reachable memory-safety or validation vulnerability can be confirmed from the shown tc_new_tfilter body alone. All dangerous operations (string copy of TCA_KIND into name[IFNAMSIZ], chain/proto lookup, refcount put, chain deletion) are performed by unshown helpers whose contracts decide correctness, and the label ordering (IS_ERR(tp) jumps to errout_tp past tcf_chain_tp_delete_empty) plus the tca/chain/flags initializations and bounds checks are internally consistent. The closest in-snippet defect is the use of the possibly uninitialized 'name' stack buffer at the tcf_proto_is_unlocked(name) call when TCA_KIND is omitted, but its impact is confined to an rtnl-locking decision and cannot be tied to a concrete memory error or disclosure, so it is recorded as a limitation (CWE-457/CWE-200 candidate), not a confirmed vulnerability.

evidence.reason: Attacker-controlled input: absence of the TCA_KIND attribute (optional netlink attribute). When it is absent, tcf_proto_check_kind(tca[TCA_KIND], name) at line 67 returns success without writing the 16-byte stack buffer char name[IFNAMSIZ] (line 6), leaving it uninitialized; line 79 then passes name to tcf_proto_is_unlocked() whenever rtnl_held is false and q is NULL or unlocked. This is a provable uninitialized-read path from the shown code, but the value only selects whether rtnl_lock() is taken (line 81), so no concrete memory-safety failure, crash, or attacker-visible disclosure can be confirmed from the shown code alone.

assumptions: rtm_tca_policy (unshown) enforces TCA_KIND as a bounded string (<= IFNAMSIZ-1) and TCA_CHAIN as NLA_U32, and nlmsg_parse_deprecated minlen sizeof(*t) guarantees the tcmsg fields are in-bounds (line 31).
nlmsg_parse_deprecated/nla_parse zero-initializes the tca[] array so absent attributes read as NULL.
tcf_proto_check_kind() returns 0 and leaves 'name' untouched when the kind attribute is NULL.
tcf_proto_is_unlocked() and tcf_proto_lookup_ops() are string lookups whose out-of-name reads stay on stack memory (no unpaged access).
tcf_chain_tp_delete_empty() unlinks the proto without dropping its reference; with that contract, the tcf_proto_put at lines 210-211 is the single designed put.
tcf_block_release() guards IS_ERR(block), so passing the ERR_PTR from line 90-92 to line 215 is safe.
tcf_chain_get() treats chain_index as a hash key; no array indexing is performed with it.
netlink_ns_capable(net->user_ns, CAP_NET_ADMIN) is passable by a user in their own user+net namespace, so the function is reachable by unprivileged-but-namespace-capable callers.
limitations: Uninitialized 'name' read: with TCA_KIND omitted, lines 67 -> 79 pass uninitialized stack bytes into tcf_proto_is_unlocked(name); taint and reachability are concrete, but impact is limited to an rtnl-locking decision and any wrong-choice race or helper-side out-of-bounds string walk depends on unshown code, so this is an unconfirmed CWE-457/CWE-200 robustness concern, not a confirmed vulnerability.

Double-put/UAF hypothesis at lines 206-211: 'err && tp_created' followed by tcf_chain_tp_delete_empty() and then tcf_proto_put(tp) is safe only under the unshown helper's refcount contract; if that contract differs, a double put would occur, and exploitability additionally requires a classifier change() to return an error after a successful insert (no such in-snippet source exists). Unconfirmed.

Replay livelock: the loop at lines 220-227 re-executes the handler while a concurrent flush keeps chain->flushing true (line 121); this is a CPU-availability hypothesis requiring persistent out-of-scope concurrent state, not a confirmed attacker-only trigger.
nla_get_u32(tca[TCA_CHAIN]) length safety at line 96 depends on the unshown rtm_tca_policy validation; the policy is not part of the shown code.

verdict.summary: Stack-based out-of-bounds write in spell_suggest: the suggestion-listing loop copies the bad word remainder with vim_strncpy(wcopy + stp->st_wordlen, su_badptr + st_orglen, su_badlen - st_orglen) into the 204-byte stack buffer wcopy[MAXWLEN+2]. sug.su_badlen is the bad-word length derived from attacker-controlled buffer text (unbounded, e.g., a long word or long visual selection) and is not clamped anywhere in the shown code; the guard at line 134 only checks positivity of the length, not its magnitude, so a bad word longer than MAXWLEN with a prefix-replacing suggestion overruns the buffer.

evidence.reason: Sink: writes up to (su_badlen - st_orglen) chars plus NUL at offset st_wordlen into wcopy[204]. su_badlen originates from attacker-controlled buffer text (line 78) via spell_find_suggest (line 88) and unbounded visual-selection badlen (lines 40-45); no cap exists in the shown code. Guard at line 134 covers only su_badlen > st_orglen, so e.g. su_badlen=1000, st_orglen=0, st_wordlen=5 passes and writes 1001 bytes, overflowing the 204-byte stack buffer (CWE-787/CWE-121).
Overflow target: fixed-size stack array of MAXWLEN+2 (204) bytes that the line 135-137 append writes past when su_badlen exceeds roughly MAXWLEN.

Taint source of the uncontrolled length: badlen is the full selection span on one buffer line, with no bound relative to MAXWLEN; it is passed to spell_find_suggest (line 88) and ultimately determines sug.su_badlen used as the write length at line 137.

assumptions: MAXWLEN is 202, so wcopy is 204 bytes.
vim_strncpy(dst, src, len) writes at most len characters and then a NUL terminator (len+1 bytes total).
stp->st_wordlen (suggested word length) does not exceed MAXWLEN.
spell_find_suggest sets su_badlen to the full bad-word length without clamping it to MAXWLEN.
limitations: Reachability partly depends on unshown spell_find_suggest: it must return su_badlen > MAXWLEN and at least one suggestion with st_orglen < su_badlen (a prefix-replacing suggestion); this matches the real upstream bug fixed in Vim 9.0.1969, but the suggestion-generating branch is not in the shown code.
Integer overflow of ++badlen at line 45 would require a selection span near INT_MAX (implausible line lengths); not confirmed.

STRLEN(line) - stp->st_orglen at line 215 could underflow (huge allocation) only if st_orglen exceeded the remaining line length, which contradicts the su_badlen/line invariant; robustness concern, not a confirmed finding.
Negative precision in the '%.*s' snprintf calls would require invariant violation of su_badlen/st_orglen; not independently confirmed.

verdict.summary: No confirmed reachable vulnerability. The Opt_name path bounds param->size to 1..63 before the validation loop, whose strict inequality keeps every string[i] read inside the allocation; all string-owning branches NULL param->string after transfer, and the subsys index/shift and isalnum() usage are constrained by kernel compile-time invariants rather than attacker input.

evidence.reason: The size_t param->size (attacker-derived string length) is first capped at 63 by the guard on line 67, and the loop on line 70 uses strict inequality i < param->size, so the maximum reachable index is size-1 <= 62, strictly inside the parser-provided allocation; the loop reads never exceed the buffer and there is no off-by-one.

The loop index i comes from for_each_subsys, bounded by the compile-time constant CGROUP_SUBSYS_COUNT (< 31), so the signed int shift (1 << i) and the write into the u16 subsys_mask stay in range; the bound is a kernel invariant, not attacker-controlled input.

Ownership of the parser-allocated string is transferred to ctx->name and param->string is cleared, matching the fs_parse contract so the caller does not free a pointer that remains referenced; no dangling pointer or double-free is created in the shown code.

assumptions: fs_parse guarantees param->key and param->string are non-NULL NUL-terminated buffers and param->size equals the byte length of param->string (framework invariant).
MAX_CGROUP_ROOT_NAMELEN is 64, making the allowed maximum name length 63.
This is kernel code; ctype macros in include/linux/ctype.h mask arguments to unsigned char, and for_each_subsys bounds i by the compile-time CGROUP_SUBSYS_COUNT.
limitations: char c = param->string[i] can be negative for bytes >= 0x80 and passing it to isalnum(c) is undefined per ISO C; safe in this kernel build due to the unsigned-char cast, but a userspace/libc port could read before the ctype table (unconfirmed, out of scope).
(1 << i) is signed-int undefined only if i >= 31, which would require a kernel configuration with 32+ subsystems; that is a compile-time invariant, not attacker-reachable.
Downstream consumers of ctx->name, ctx->release_agent, and fc->source (e.g., cgroup1_get_tree, cgroup_show_options) are outside the shown code and their bounds were not analyzed.
The correctness of the size cap relies on fs_parse setting param->size from the actual string length; a mismatch between size and the real strlen is not observable in the shown code.

verdict.summary: do_tag() was audited for index/pointer safety: tagstack indices are bounded to [0, TAGSTACKSIZE-1] by the push/shift logic, DT_POP/DT_TAG index arithmetic is clamped, and every matches[] dereference is guarded by cur_match = num_matches - 1 within the num_matches > 0 branch. No attacker-reachable memory-safety flaw is demonstrable purely from the shown code.

evidence.reason: The push path writes tagname at tagstack[tagstackidx]. After the full-stack shift, --tagstackidx yields TAGSTACKSIZE-1; otherwise tagstackidx equals the previous tagstacklen <= TAGSTACKSIZE-1. The write index is provably in [0, TAGSTACKSIZE-1], so this sink is fully guarded.

Reached from the new-tag path (tagstackidx in [0, TAGSTACKSIZE-1]), DT_TAG no-arg path (clamped to tagstacklen-1), and other-tag path (--tagstackidx clamped to >= 0). In every reachable branch tagstackidx < tagstacklen <= TAGSTACKSIZE, so the index is in-bounds.

All later matches[cur_match] dereferences (parse_match, matches[cur_match][0] & MT_IC_OFF, jumpto_tag) are executed only inside the num_matches > 0 branch after this clamp, with cur_match adjusted to num_matches - 1, plus the prompt path validates i <= num_matches. The index is bounded by the allocated matches array.

No confirmed vulnerability: tagstack[tagstackidx] is in-bounds per Phase 2, and the ptrdiff tagp.user_data_end - tagp.user_data is assumed non-negative only because parse_match (not shown) is responsible for producing ordered pointers. If parse_match could yield user_data_end < user_data, the size underflow would be a flaw, but reachability depends on non-shown code, so it is recorded as a limitation.

assumptions: count is non-negative because Vim's ex-command parser only accepts digit sequences for the count argument; a negative or INT_MIN count passed by a caller would make tagstackidx -= count / tagstackidx += count - 1 arithmetic depend on caller invariants.
curwin->w_tagstackidx and w_tagstacklen maintain 0 <= tagstackidx <= tagstacklen <= TAGSTACKSIZE; the function itself preserves this invariant at end_do_tag.

find_tags() and vim_strsave()/vim_strnsave() honor their contracts: find_tags initializes new_num_matches/new_matches outputs (so a FAIL return leaves defined values), and allocation failures abort rather than returning NULL with partial writes.
matches[] entries are non-NULL and num_matches reflects the actual allocation size.
limitations: If parse_match() returned user_data_end < user_data for a crafted tags file, vim_strnsave() would receive an underflowed huge size_t (potential over-read); parse_match is not in the shown code, so reachability is unconfirmed.

If find_tags() could return FAIL without setting *num_matches/*matchesp, the subsequent FreeWild(new_num_matches, new_matches) and matches = new_matches would consume uninitialized values; this depends on non-shown code.

Integer overflow in tagstackidx += count - 1 or tagstackidx -= count requires a count value outside the range Vim's parser produces (e.g., INT_MIN or negative), which the shown code does not defend against; treated as a robustness concern, not a reachable flaw.
The static matches/num_matches state is not thread-safe, but Vim's execution model is single-threaded.

verdict.summary: No confirmed reachable vulnerability. All sampled sizes/ratios are computed in double precision with guards (lines 14, 28) that keep later denominators positive, the random cursor is null-checked (line 35), and the only dangerous operation (*bucketUnpacker at lines 120/132) requires a caller-side precondition not shown in the analyzed code.

evidence.reason: Guard on the non-timeseries path: fall-through implies numRecords > 100, so the denominator numRecords * 0.05 used later at line 62 is strictly positive and bounded away from zero; sampleSize (attacker-influenced) is only used in a double comparison, not in any memory operation.

The only division that lacks a positive-denominator guard: with numRecords == 0 and sampleSize == 0 it evaluates 0/0 = NaN, but std::min's operator< makes NaN < 1.0 false and yields 1.0, so the clamp produces a deterministic benign ratio; IEEE-754 double division is defined behavior, so no UB or memory-safety impact.
The nullable getRandomCursor() result is explicitly checked before being moved into MultiIteratorStage at line 44, so no null pointer reaches the plan tree from this input.

assumptions: numRecords is trusted collection metadata (count including orphans), not attacker-controlled, per the comment at lines 48-49.
sampleSize is validated (non-negative, bounded) upstream by the $sample aggregation stage parser.
The caller of createRandomCursorExecutor constructs bucketUnpacker engaged whenever the target namespace is a timeseries buckets collection.
gTimeseriesBucketMaxCount is a positive server-maintained parameter.
IEEE-754 double semantics apply: division by zero yields inf/NaN without trapping.
limitations: *bucketUnpacker (lines 120, 132) is dereferenced without checking that the boost::optional is engaged; if any caller passes a disengaged optional for a timeseries-buckets collection this is undefined behavior (CWE-476). It is not reported as a vulnerability because the precondition is established by code not shown, which is out of scope for reachability.

Threshold arithmetic converts long long to double at lines 14, 28, 62, and 113; for |numRecords| or |sampleSize| above 2^53, precision loss could in edge cases bypass the plan-selection ratio guards. Impact is limited to choosing a suboptimal $sample plan (performance), with no memory-safety sink.

In the timeseries branch, a zero or negative numRecords can produce NaN/Inf in the intermediate division (lines 112-114); this is IEEE-defined and clamped to a benign constant, and negative sampleSize is rejected by the upstream pipeline. Robustness concern only.

verdict.summary: g_socket_client_connected_callback dereferences the shared connect state `data` (attempt->data) without a NULL check on both the connect-failure path (clarify_connect_error (error, data->connectable, ...) and set_last_error (data, ...)) and the success path (data->socket = ...; data->connection = ...), even though the function itself treats data == NULL as an expected state (comment at line 12, the late `if (data)` guard at lines 37-43, and sibling attempts' data being cleared at line 55). A connect result delivered after the shared task has already completed/been cancelled can therefore dereference a NULL pointer and crash the process (availability DoS).

evidence.reason: Sink: `data` (from attempt->data, line 6) can be NULL per the documented invariant (line 12) and per the same path's own NULL handling at lines 42-43, yet `data->connectable` and `data` are dereferenced here before any NULL check. The only guard (`if (data)`, lines 37-43) executes after these dereferences, so data == NULL reaches this sink and causes a NULL pointer dereference (CWE-476).

Sink: on the connect-success path these lines dereference `data` unconditionally. The shown code establishes data == NULL as an expected callback state (line 12 invariant, line 55 sibling data clearing, lines 42-43 NULL handling), and the guard at line 13 only returns when data != NULL, so a late success callback with data == NULL dereferences NULL here.

Source of the NULL state: this shown code clears `attempt->data` for pending sibling attempts, so their later invocations of this same callback run with data == NULL, reaching the unguarded dereferences at lines 31-32 and 48-49.

evidence.snippet:
/* data is NULL once the task is completed */
  if (data && g_task_return_error_if_cancelled (data->task))
evidence.reason: Documents the attacker-independent invariant that data can be NULL in this callback, and shows the guard is only effective when data != NULL; when data == NULL control falls through toward the dereferences at lines 31-32 and 48-49.

assumptions: The async operation holds a reference that keeps `attempt` (user_data) valid while this callback runs.
`attempt->data` becomes NULL only via paths equivalent to those shown (task completion / sibling cancellation), and attempts are heap-allocated and freed by connection_attempt_unref.
`protocol` is a NUL-terminated internal string, so its use as a `%s` argument with a literal format string is safe.
limitations: The exact interleaving that delivers data == NULL together with a non-cancelled connect_finish failure (lines 29-32) or a connect_finish success (lines 48-49) depends on async cancellation/refcount machinery not shown here (connection_attempt_remove, task completion, connection_attempt_unref); if cancellation always precedes data clearing, the dereference would be unreachable and the issue would be a defensive-hardening concern.
Reentrancy / use-after-free in the sibling-cancellation loop (lines 51-57) via g_cancellable_cancel signal handlers cannot be confirmed from the shown code.
No integer/bounds or format-string defects are present in the shown code; those candidates were examined and rejected.

verdict.summary: st21nfca_connectivity_event_received trusts attacker-controlled skb lengths: it allocates only skb->len - 2 bytes but copies up to 16 aid and 255 parameters bytes into the fixed struct members, and the params_len guard at L47 underflows in unsigned arithmetic so it never rejects oversized values, producing a kernel heap out-of-bounds write (and out-of-bounds reads past the skb payload) reachable from crafted NFC HCI EVT_TRANSACTION frames.

evidence.reason: Sink: params_len (attacker-controlled u8 from skb->data[aid_len+3], line 44) and aid_len (from skb->data[1], line 30) determine a 0..255-byte copy into transaction->params, whose containing allocation is only skb->len-2 bytes (line 26). For len=130, aid_len=5, params_len=255 the write ends at offset ~272 while the allocation is 128 bytes, overflowing the kmalloc object (CWE-787); the source skb->data+9 also reads past the 130-byte payload (CWE-125).

The only guard bounding params_len is broken: (skb->len - 2) - sizeof(struct nfc_evt_transaction) is evaluated in unsigned arithmetic and wraps to ~SIZE_MAX whenever skb->len - 2 < sizeof(struct) (true for all realistic NFC frames, e.g. len=130: 128 - 274 wraps). params_len (0..255) always satisfies the comparison, so the check never rejects an oversized length and the memcpy at lines 50-51 always executes.

The only skb length gate uses a conjunction, so it returns -EPROTO only when BOTH skb->len < 7 AND data[0] != 0x81. A short malformed frame with data[0]==0x81 (e.g. len=6) or len=1 passes the gate and reaches skb->data[1], skb->data[aid_len+2], skb->data[aid_len+3], and the memcpy source offsets beyond the payload, enabling the out-of-bounds reads (CWE-125) and the undersized-allocation writes (CWE-787).

The allocation size is attacker-controlled skb->len - 2 (e.g. 128 bytes for len=130), while the code then writes the fixed struct members aid[16], aid_len, and up to 255 params bytes into it. The object is smaller than the struct being written, so the memcpy at lines 50-51 overflows it; for len=2 the allocation is 0 bytes (dereferenced ZERO_SIZE_PTR) and for len<2 the size underflows to ~4 GiB.

assumptions: NFC_MIN_AID_LENGTH is 5, as stated in the function's own spec comment (lines 18-20: AID length 5 to 16).

struct nfc_evt_transaction contains fixed members aid[16], aid_len, params[256] (per the comment PARAMETERS 0 to 255) and params_len, so sizeof(struct) ~= 274 and offsetof(params) >= 17; the overflow conclusion holds for any layout where params is placed after aid[16]+aid_len.
devm_kzalloc(len-2) with len-2 <= 128 returns an object from the kmalloc-128 slab, so a write ending at offset 272 crosses the object boundary by ~144 bytes.
The caller (NFC HCI core) passes the received event skb through; the shown code itself imposes no additional upper bound on skb->len.
limitations: The out-of-bounds reads from skb->data may remain inside the skb's larger linear buffer allocation for some packet sizes (skb->len bounds only the payload), so CWE-125 is reported as secondary; the heap write overflow (CWE-787) does not depend on this caveat.

For skb->len < 2 the allocation-size underflow at line 26 most likely fails with -ENOMEM or yields a ZERO_SIZE_PTR; that path is a DoS/robustness concern absorbed into the broken-gate finding rather than a separate memory-corruption finding.
The default switch case (lines 55-57) returns without kfree_skb(skb), leaking the skb; recorded as robustness only.
The exact maximum skb->len offered by the st21nfca HCI transport is outside the shown code; the demonstrated overflow uses len=130, which only requires that a 130-byte HCI event payload can arrive.

verdict.summary: No attacker-triggerable memory-safety or security flaw is confirmable within the shown code. The loop consuming qfl is guarded against a NULL/short qf_next chain (lines 71-73), qftf strings are validated via tv_get_string_chk with an invalid_val fallback (lines 58-63), and ml_delete(lnum + 1) (line 81) targets a line number that stays consistent with the buffer's line count on every loop-exit path. Residual concerns (user 'quickfixtextfunc' side effects invalidating qfl/qfp, qf_count-vs-chain and qf_start invariants, qf_buf_add_line failure semantics) depend on unshown code or framework invariants and are recorded as limitations.

evidence.reason: The only pointer advance in the display loop is NULL-guarded before the next iteration dereferences qfp->qf_fnum (lines 66, 69). Even if qfl->qf_count (line 51) exceeds the actual qf_next chain length, iteration terminates here instead of dereferencing a dangling/NULL qfp; qfp is non-NULL at loop entry via qfl->qf_start (line 34) or old_last->qf_next/old_last (lines 39-42).

The only user-influenced value consumed as a string is obtained through tv_get_string_chk, which returns NULL instead of a dangerous pointer for non-string values; the NULL result is checked and latched into invalid_val so subsequent iterations fall back to default text. No unvalidated string is passed to a sink.

lnum is derived solely from loop progress: bounded by qfl->qf_count (line 51), incremented once per successful qf_buf_add_line (lines 65-70). On every exit path (full loop, FAIL break at line 67, NULL-chain break at line 73) the buffer holds exactly lnum error lines plus one trailing empty line, so lnum + 1 is always the last valid physical line; no out-of-range line number is generated.

assumptions: qfl->qf_start is non-NULL whenever qfl->qf_count > 0, and the qf_next chain contains exactly qf_count reachable items; this structural invariant is maintained by unshown list-building code (qf_add_entry/qf_set_entries).

old_last, when non-NULL, is a live qfline_T owned by qfl (or by Vim's retained qf_old_* previous list), so old_last->qf_next and old_last->qf_fnum are valid reads; the caller contract also guarantees buf == curbuf when old_last == NULL.
qf_buf_add_line appends exactly one physical line per successful call and fails atomically without inserting a line (ml_append_buf semantics in Vim).
linenr_T and long are 64-bit on the target platform, so (long)(lnum + 1) and (long)qfl->qf_count are width-preserving casts with no narrowing.
limitations: Potential use-after-free if the user-supplied 'quickfixtextfunc' invoked via call_qftf_func (line 46) frees/rebuilds the quickfix list before the loop reads qfl->qf_count (line 51) or qfp->qf_fnum (lines 66, 69): reachability depends on unshown call_qftf_func behavior and the user function being attacker-controlled, so it cannot be confirmed from the shown code.

A NULL/use-after-free deref at qfp->qf_fnum (lines 66, 69) would require qf_start == NULL with qf_count > 0 or a chain shorter than qf_count; the guard at lines 72-73 covers short chains, and the fresh-fill start (line 34) is unguarded only if the unshown list-construction invariant is violated.

ml_delete(lnum + 1) (line 81) would delete the wrong line only if qf_buf_add_line failed non-atomically or inserted partial/extra lines; that semantics is unshown and is an unchecked-allocation scenario, out of scope.

In the incremental branch (lines 39-43), if the buffer's line count is smaller than qf_count while old_last->qf_next == NULL (e.g., user autocmds deleted qf-buffer lines), the loop re-adds old_last, producing a duplicate displayed entry - a display-logic robustness issue, not memory safety.
call_qftf_func and qf_buf_add_line are not shown, so any flaw located inside them (memory errors, bad line-count updates) cannot be attributed here.

verdict.summary: In ax25_release(), the AX25_STATE_3/AX25_STATE_4 case dereferences ax25->ax25_dev at the sink without the NULL check that the same function applies to the identical pointer at the tail (line 76). A SOCK_SEQPACKET AX.25 socket whose device was detached while in connected state triggers a kernel NULL-pointer dereference (local DoS).

evidence.reason: Sink: ax25->ax25_dev (read at line 14, admitted NULL by the guard at line 76) is dereferenced without a NULL check. Trigger: close() on a SOCK_SEQPACKET socket with ax25->state in {AX25_STATE_3, AX25_STATE_4} and ax25->ax25_dev == NULL (device detached while connected). Result: NULL-pointer dereference, kernel oops/panic.

Supporting anchor: the identical pointer read at line 14 is explicitly NULL-guarded at the tail before timer/device teardown, proving the shown code treats ax25->ax25_dev as nullable at release time; the STATE_3/STATE_4 case (line 40) omits this guard entirely.

assumptions: Kernel helper contracts hold: lock_sock/release_sock pairs, sock_hold/sock_put, del_timer_sync, dev_put_track, and ax25_dev_put behave as documented; AX25_STATE_3/4 denote connected/awaiting-disconnect states; sk_to_ax25(sk) returns the attached ax25_cb.
The NULL-device condition originates in the device-unregistration path (code outside the shown snippet), which is the lifecycle event the line 76 guard exists to handle.
limitations: Use-after-free of the ax25_cb in the STATE_0/STATE_1-2/else paths: ax25_destroy_socket (lines 22, 32, 74) precedes the tail's del_timer_sync reads of ax25 (lines 77-81); whether the control block is freed depends on ax25_destroy_socket/ax25_cb_put refcount semantics not shown, so it is unconfirmed.
ax25->sk dereference at line 31 after the unlocked ax25_disconnect at line 29 depends on ax25_disconnect's body (not shown) and is unconfirmed.
Device reference/tracker pairing in dev_put_track/ax25_dev_put (lines 82-83) depends on where the device reference was acquired (not shown) and is unconfirmed.

A fully attacker-controlled trigger for the NULL-device state may require an additional capability (e.g., CAP_NET_ADMIN) or a race with device removal; the crash is the primary confirmed impact, not privilege escalation.

verdict.summary: qh_help treats the attacker-controlled buffer buf as a NUL-terminated C string in strcmp (lines 5, 12), qh_find_handler (line 22), and nsock_printf_nul '%s' (lines 25, 29) while never using the supplied len, allowing out-of-bounds reads and client-visible disclosure/DoS when the received message lacks a NUL terminator.

evidence.snippet: static int qh_help(int sd, char *buf, unsigned int len)
evidence.reason: The caller supplies the buffer's length via len, but len is never read anywhere in the function; this is the only size information available and it is discarded, so buf is subsequently used as an unbounded C-string.

First unbounded C-string scan of the attacker-controlled buf. The NULL guard does not check NUL-termination or bound by len; a message of len non-NUL bytes (e.g., all 'A') passes the guard and strcmp reads past the end of the buffer.
Second unbounded strcmp over buf with no length or termination validation, reachable for any non-NULL buf that failed the line 5 comparison.
Name lookup scans the same unterminated buf as a C-string; an over-read here is reachable for the same attacker message, independent of whether a handler matches.

evidence.snippet: nsock_printf_nul(sd, "No handler named '%s' is registered\n", buf);
evidence.reason: '%s' sink re-scans buf until a NUL byte and echoes the bytes to the client over sd, converting the over-read into both an out-of-bounds access and a potential information disclosure / remote crash.

evidence.snippet: nsock_printf_nul(sd, "The handler %s doesn't have any help yet.", buf);
evidence.reason: Second '%s' sink on the same unterminated attacker-controlled buf, reached when a handler exists; identical unbounded read to line 25.

assumptions: buf is the client-supplied command payload for a socket-backed query handler (implied by sd plus the qhandlers/qh_find_handler framework), i.e. attacker-controlled.
qhandlers is a NULL-terminated list and registered handler name/description fields are valid C strings (trusted registration invariant).

The caller communicates the buffer's extent only via len and does not necessarily append a NUL terminator; otherwise the unused len parameter would be dead code and the C-string operations would be in-bounds.
limitations: The caller of qh_help is not shown; if the dispatcher always NUL-terminates buf within its allocation, the out-of-bounds read cannot be triggered and the finding degrades to a hardening concern.
Potential unbounded recursion/reentrancy through qh->handler(sd, "help", 4) (line 27) cannot be confirmed because the handler implementations are not shown.
No format-string vulnerability is present: all format strings are literals and buf is only ever passed as a %s argument.
No integer/width-conversion or loop-bound issues were found; the only loop is bounded by the trusted handler registry.

verdict.summary: In kvmppc_rtas_hcall, the guest-controlled field args.nargs (read from guest memory at L16) is used at L28 as an unbounded index into the host stack array args.args[] (&args.args[be32_to_cpu(args.nargs)]) with no bounds check. Any nargs >= ARRAY_SIZE(args.args) (e.g. 16, 0x100, 0xFFFFFFFF) forms an out-of-bounds host-stack pointer that is stored in args.rets and passed to the registered RTAS handler at L35, which writes results through args->rets per the RTAS ABI. A malicious guest can thereby trigger host-kernel stack out-of-bounds access: reliable host DoS and potential privilege escalation.

evidence.reason: Sink: args.nargs is a guest-controlled u32 (read at L16 with no value validation; L18 only checks the read return code). It indexes the fixed host-stack array args.args[] without any bound check; nargs >= ARRAY_SIZE(args.args) (e.g. 16, 0x100, 0xFFFFFFFF) forms an out-of-bounds pointer that is stored in args.rets, per Phase 3 the taint flows L16 -> L28 and the failure is confirmed.

Taint origin: the entire struct rtas_args (token/nargs/nrets/args/rets) is copied from guest physical memory at the guest-chosen address from L13; args.nargs, the value later used as the unchecked index, is fully attacker-controlled.

Consumption: with a valid registered token, the handler is invoked at L35 with &args whose args.rets already holds the out-of-bounds pointer from L28; per the RTAS result ABI (fixup purpose documented at L21-L26), the handler writes return values through args->rets, turning the OOB pointer into a host-stack out-of-bounds write (CWE-787).

assumptions: args.args is a small fixed-size array (16 entries per the RTAS ABI; the upstream fix gates with ARRAY_SIZE(args.args)); the shown code applies no bound at all, so any finite bound is exceeded by the 32-bit nargs.

Handlers invoked at L35 write their result values through args->rets (the reason the L27-L28 fixup and L44 restore exist per the comment at L21-L26), so the OOB rets pointer is dereferenced by kernel KVM handler code.
kvm_read_guest returns nonzero for any partial/failed read, so on the success path args is fully initialized and the struct copy itself does not over-read the host buffer.
limitations: The actual dereference of the out-of-bounds args.rets occurs inside handler code not present in the shown snippet; the confirmation rests on the fully shown OOB pointer formation at L28 (UB by itself) plus the documented RTAS result-write contract.

An out-of-bounds read variant (handlers reading args.args[i] for i < nargs with nargs beyond the array) is plausible but not independently confirmed from the shown code, so only the write path (CWE-787) and its root cause (CWE-129) are reported.

With very large nargs the resulting write likely faults and panics the host (DoS); moderate nargs (16..~32) aliases adjacent stack locals. Precise control over which stack slot is clobbered is bounded by the fixed element step, but a host crash is reliably triggerable.

verdict.summary: No attacker-reachable memory-safety flaw is confirmable within the shown code under strict three-part reachability analysis. The unguarded ax25->ax25_dev dereference at line 40 would be a NULL-pointer read if a socket could reach AX25_STATE_3/4 with a NULL device, but that combination is decided by out-of-scope state-machine transitions and kernel bind/connect invariants, so it fails reachability. Potential use-after-free/double-destroy around the release_sock/lock_sock windows and the trailing dev reference drops depend on helper implementations entirely absent from the shown code. These are recorded as limitations, not vulnerabilities.

evidence.reason: Dereferences ax25->ax25_dev without a NULL check even though the same field is explicitly tested for NULL at line 76 (if (ax25_dev)). The dereference is only dangerous if state == AX25_STATE_3/4 can co-occur with ax25_dev == NULL; both the state transitions and the device assignment occur in code not shown, and the kernel bind/connect invariant normally requires a device for an established connection. Taint and sink are real, but reachability cannot be established from the shown code, so this is a robustness concern (CWE-476 unconfirmed), not a confirmed vulnerability.

The socket lock is dropped between release_sock (19) and lock_sock (21), during which ax25_disconnect(ax25, 0) runs on ax25 and ax25_destroy_socket(ax25) follows after relocking. A use-after-free or double-destroy would require a concurrent path (timers, interrupts, or another release, none shown) to free ax25 in that window, or ax25_destroy_socket to release state this function touches afterwards (lines 76-83). All concrete failure modes depend on helper semantics and concurrency outside the shown code, so the UAF hypothesis (CWE-416) fails part 2 and is recorded as a limitation.

assumptions: sock_hold(sk) at line 10 is balanced by sock_put(sk) at line 83, keeping sk alive for the function's entire body (kernel socket-layer contract).
sk_to_ax25(sk) at line 13 is a valid container_of because sock->sk for an AX.25 socket always embeds an ax25_cb (protocol dispatch invariant).
AX25_STATE_3/4 (established connection) is only reachable through bind/connect paths that set ax25->ax25_dev to a live device; that invariant is maintained outside the shown code.
AX25_VALUES_PROTOCOL is a compile-time constant index smaller than the values[] array size, so line 40 cannot index out of bounds.
limitations: NULL-pointer dereference at line 40 (ax25->ax25_dev->values[AX25_VALUES_PROTOCOL]) is an unconfirmed CWE-476 robustness concern: reachability of state AX25_STATE_3/4 with ax25_dev == NULL is not provable from the shown code and conflicts with the kernel bind/connect invariants.
Potential use-after-free / double-destroy of ax25 across the release_sock/lock_sock windows (lines 19-22, 28-32) is an unconfirmed CWE-416 hypothesis requiring concurrent paths not shown.

Potential double device-reference drop (lines 76-78 following ax25_destroy_socket calls at 22/32/74) is an unconfirmed refcount-underflow/UAF hypothesis that depends on the unshown internals of ax25_destroy_socket/ax25_cb_put.
refcount bookkeeping correctness of sock_hold/sock_orphan/sock_put and of dev_put_track/ax25_dev_put relative to helper destroy semantics was not verifiable within the shown scope.

verdict.summary: No confirmed, reachable, attacker-triggerable vulnerability in the shown code. All tagstack indices derived from the user-supplied 'count' and from 'cur_match' are re-clamped by guards before array access (empty-stack check lines 167-176; DT_POP clamps lines 183-200; DT_TAG clamps lines 261-277; cur_match clamps lines 314-322 and 536-551), and the shift loop (lines 141-148) stays within TAGSTACKSIZE. Remaining concerns (signed-overflow UB for extreme counts, unvalidated find_tags failure outputs, non-empty match-string assumption, stale tagstack pointer after window switches) depend on contracts or behaviors outside the shown code and are recorded as limitations.

evidence.reason: User-supplied 'count' (Phase 1, no validation) is subtracted from tagstackidx. Both outcomes are covered: negative results are clamped to 0 before tagstack[tagstackidx] (line 204), and results >= tagstacklen exit via goto. No concrete count value leaves tagstackidx outside [0, tagstacklen), so the subsequent tagstack[tagstackidx] access (line 204) cannot go out of bounds.

'count - 1' is added to tagstackidx with no validation, but both overflow branches clamp before the read at line 278: values >= tagstacklen become tagstacklen-1, and values < 0 exit. tagstacklen == 0 is precluded by the empty-stack guard (lines 167-176), so the access at lines 278-279 always uses an index in [0, tagstacklen).

cur_match is clamped to [0, num_matches-1] in the num_matches > 0 branch before every use of matches[cur_match] (lines 560, 586, 628); combined with the floor clamp at lines 314-322 it can never be negative. The only residual failure mode is a find_tags FAIL leaving new_num_matches/new_matches uninitialized (lines 436-472), which is a contract of find_tags outside the shown code.

Index cur_match is provably in [0, num_matches) at this point (evidence above). The byte read at offset 0 is safe only if find_tags guarantees non-empty match strings; that invariant is not shown and is recorded as a limitation rather than a finding.

assumptions: Constants TAGSTACKSIZE (fixed tag-stack capacity), MAXCOL == INT_MAX, IOSIZE (IObuff capacity), and MT_IC_OFF are defined outside the snippet with their standard Vim values.
Window invariants hold at entry: 0 <= curwin->w_tagstackidx <= curwin->w_tagstacklen <= TAGSTACKSIZE.
find_tags/parse_match/jumpto_tag return non-empty, NUL-terminated, singly-owned tags and initialize their out-parameters, per their (not shown) contracts.
count originates from the Ex-command parser and is a normal small non-negative value in practice; extreme values are only reachable via long-to-int truncation in the caller.
limitations: find_tags() error handling: its return value is ignored in the shown code and new_num_matches/new_matches are used unconditionally (lines 436-472); if find_tags leaves them uninitialized on FAIL, this is an uninitialized-pointer/UB bug, but the contract is outside the shown code and unconfirmed.

Signed-overflow UB for extreme count values in 'tagstackidx -= count' (line 183), 'tagstackidx += count - 1' (line 261), and 'cur_match +=/-= count' (lines 311-312); no concrete value passes the subsequent clamps into an out-of-bounds access, so this is a robustness concern only.
matches[cur_match][0] (line 586) assumes find_tags never returns an empty match string; not verifiable in the shown code.

tagstack/tagstackidx staleness after jumpto_tag may change curwin (lines 628-662); entry lifetime changes would require autocommand side effects in not-shown code, so a use-after-free there is an unconfirmed hypothesis.
max_num_matches = cur_match + 1 (line 415) is overflow-safe only because of the preceding clamp at lines 314-315; if that clamp were ever bypassed by future edits this would break.

verdict.summary: No confirmed, reachable, attacker-triggerable vulnerability in the shown code. The function treats attacker-influenced buf as a NUL-terminated C string (strcmp, %s) without ever using the len parameter, but bounds/termination of buf are guaranteed by the unshown dispatcher; the internal qh->handler(sd, "help", 4) call is safe under a read-only handler contract and its safety otherwise depends on unshown handler code. These are robustness/hardening concerns, not confirmed vulnerabilities.

assumptions: buf is a valid, non-NULL pointer to a NUL-terminated, in-bounds buffer supplied by the query dispatcher, and len matches the received byte count.
qhandlers is a well-formed NULL-terminated list of handler structs registered by the program; qh->name and qh->description are trusted static strings.
qh_find_handler and qh->handler implement the registered-handler contract, and handler buffers are read-only (const) as in the upstream design.
nsock_printf and nsock_printf_nul are safe variadic output wrappers.
limitations: OOB read (potential CWE-125): strcmp at lines 5 and 12, qh_find_handler at line 22, and %s at lines 25 and 29 scan buf without any bound from len. The failure requires buf to lack a NUL terminator within its backing object, a property of the unshown caller/framing, so this is an unconfirmed robustness concern, not a confirmed vulnerability.

Line 27 passes the read-only string literal "help" with hardcoded length 4 to qh->handler; if any handler writes into its input buffer or requires a larger readable region, this internal call could fault. The handler signature/behavior is not shown, so this cannot be confirmed.
Line 5 dereferences buf via !*buf; a NULL or dangling buf would fault, but buf is valid by caller convention and no attacker path in the shown code produces that state.
The observed behavior for "help help" (prints "doesn't have any help yet.") is a functional quirk with no security impact.

verdict.summary: Off-by-one out-of-bounds read in rpa_read_buffer: when the parser position equals the end pointer, the guard `if (p > end)` permits p == end and `len = *p++` dereferences one byte past the buffer end.

evidence.reason: Attacker-controlled parse position p (= *data, line 4) reaches line 7; the guard only rejects p > end, so p == end passes. Line 10 then dereferences *p, reading one byte past the end of the buffer. The correct guard for the length-prefix read is p >= end, since line 10 consumes at least one byte. This is reachable when prior parsing consumes exactly the whole attacker-supplied buffer, and the failure is an off-by-one OOB read (CWE-125).

assumptions: end is a valid one-past-end pointer for the buffer that *data points into, and *data is within [start, end] (buffer start/ownership is a caller invariant, not shown).
len reads exactly one byte, so len is in [0, 255]; pointer arithmetic p + len and the update *data += 1 + len cannot overflow or truncate.
limitations: The copy region check `if (p + len > end)` at line 11 is sufficient for the memcpy at line 15 (p + len <= end covers len bytes); no OOB write is reachable, so impact is limited to a 1-byte read.
p_malloc failure at line 14 would NULL-dereference at line 15 (memcpy); treated as an unchecked-allocation-failure robustness concern, not a confirmed attacker-triggerable vulnerability.
Return value 0 is ambiguous between parse failure and a legitimate zero-length buffer, which could desync a caller that treats 0 as an error; caller-dependent, unconfirmed.
Reachability of p == end depends on the parser framing advancing *data to exactly end, which is implied but not literally shown in this snippet.

verdict.summary: scm_mkdir is a thin wrapper around the POSIX mkdir syscall. The only attacker-influenced values are path and mode: path is converted inside the trusted STRING_SYSCALL macro (out of scope), and mode is either the constant 0777 or a validated unsigned int from scm_to_uint, whose range contract (0..UINT_MAX, exception otherwise) fully covers the later mkdir call. The mode_t assignment is width-preserving on the target POSIX platforms. No memory-safety, bounds, integer, or authz flaw is reachable within the shown code.

assumptions: STRING_SYSCALL is a trusted framework macro that safely validates/converts the SCM path into a null-terminated C string and manages its lifetime; its definition is not part of the shown code.
scm_to_uint enforces the Guile contract: it returns a value in [0, UINT_MAX] and raises a Scheme exception for negative, non-integer, or oversized arguments.
The target platform is a conventional POSIX system where mode_t and unsigned int are both 32-bit, so the unsigned int -> mode_t conversion is value-preserving.
SCM_SYSERROR raises a Scheme exception based on errno rather than returning a value.
limitations: Any memory-safety or encoding flaw inside the unshown STRING_SYSCALL expansion cannot be evaluated from the shown code and was not asserted.

On hypothetical platforms where mode_t is narrower than unsigned int, the assignment at line 13 could truncate an attacker-supplied mode; this is not applicable to the assumed target and is not demonstrable from the shown code.
A TOCTOU window between argument conversion and the mkdir syscall (line 15) is inherent to POSIX directory creation and is not a flaw attributable to this wrapper.

Allowing permissive modes such as #o777 or setuid bits is standard POSIX mkdir semantics decided by the caller (masked by umask per the docstring), not an input-validation vulnerability in the shown code.

verdict.summary: No confirmed, reachable, attacker-triggerable vulnerability in do_viewlog. The only candidate memory-safety concern, buf[n] = 0 at line 14, is fully covered by the fread size bound sizeof(buf)-1 = 511 (max index 511 within char buf[512] at line 11). Log content is escaped via escapeHTML before being embedded in the response, and every StringBuffer_append uses a constant format string. Access is gated by an is_readonly check (lines 2-5).

evidence.snippet:
while ((n = fread(buf, sizeof(char), sizeof(buf) - 1, f)) > 0) {
                                buf[n] = 0;
evidence.reason: buf is declared char buf[512] (line 11), so valid indices are 0..511. fread's size argument is sizeof(buf)-1 = 511, so n ranges over [0, 511]; the maximal write buf[511] = 0 stays within bounds. The guard fully covers the write, so no off-by-one or out-of-bounds access is reachable from any file content.

assumptions: Run.flags and Run.files.log are trusted daemon configuration set at startup, not per-request attacker input.
escapeHTML reliably escapes HTML metacharacters such as &, <, >, and ", so textarea-embedded log content cannot break out; its implementation is outside the shown code.
is_readonly(req) correctly reflects the authenticated user's privilege level, and the SC_FORBIDDEN path terminates the handler for read-only users.
limitations: If the daemon logs substrings derived from HTTP input (e.g., usernames or request paths), the log content delivered here may carry attacker-influenced text; whether this becomes stored XSS depends on escapeHTML's escaping coverage, which is not shown, so it is an unconfirmed hardening concern, not a confirmed vulnerability.

The log file is read without a per-request cap beyond 511-byte chunking; memory use per chunk is bounded in the shown code, so a slow-loris-style amplification concern depends on caller/HTTP-layer behavior outside this function.

fopen(Run.files.log, "r") resolves the path at request time; a symlink swap or log-rotation race could disclose an unintended file, but that requires filesystem write access outside this function and is out of scope.

Disclosure of the log to any authenticated non-read-only user is the designed purpose of the _viewlog page; whether the broader monit user model permits unintended subjects depends on is_readonly and code not shown.

verdict.summary: Within the shown code, fix_dl_name allocates exactly dl->length + so_ext_len + 1 bytes and the copies fit exactly (memcpy of dl->length bytes; strcpy of so_ext_len chars plus NUL at offset dl->length). The || short-circuit prevents evaluating dl->str + dl->length - so_ext_len when dl->length < so_ext_len, so no size_t underflow is reachable. The integer-overflow, unchecked-alloc_root, and my_strcasecmp over-read concerns all require out-of-scope caller values or invariants not established in the shown code, so they are recorded as limitations rather than confirmed vulnerabilities.

evidence.reason: For any finite dl->length (size_t, >= 0 per its type), the allocation is dl->length + 3 + 1 bytes; memcpy writes dl->length bytes at offset 0 and strcpy writes 3 chars + NUL at offset dl->length, ending exactly at the allocation bound. There is no off-by-one for finite lengths. The only failure mode is size_t wrap requiring dl->length > SIZE_MAX - 4, which no operation in the shown code can produce, so the heap-overflow hypothesis is not reachable within this analysis.

assumptions: SO_EXT is a string literal such as ".so", so sizeof(SO_EXT) - 1 == 3.
The caller supplies a LEX_STRING whose dl->length accurately reflects the number of readable bytes at dl->str and, where required, is NUL-terminated within that length.
limitations: dl->length + so_ext_len + 1 (line 8) and dl->length += so_ext_len (line 12) could wrap for dl->length near SIZE_MAX, causing an undersized allocation and heap overflow; however, no shown code path produces such a length, so this is an unconfirmed hypothesis dependent on an out-of-scope caller.

Unchecked alloc_root failure (line 8) would yield NULL dereferenced by memcpy/strcpy on lines 9-10; this is an unchecked-allocation robustness concern, not a confirmed attacker-triggerable vulnerability.
my_strcasecmp on dl->str + dl->length - so_ext_len (line 5) could over-read if dl->str is not NUL-terminated within dl->length; the NUL-termination invariant is not established in the shown code.

verdict.summary: Two attacker-reachable flaws in gst_flxdec_chain: (A) a crafted FLX_FRAME_TYPE chunk with flxfh.size < FlxFrameChunkSize underflows 'flxfh.size - FlxFrameChunkSize' (line 112) to a ~4 GB length passed to gst_adapter_take, whose NULL result is then dereferenced by FLX_FRAME_TYPE_FIX_ENDIANNESS (line 113), crashing the process; (B) 'flxdec->size * 4' (line 124), where size = width*height from the file header (line 78), overflows 32-bit arithmetic for dimensions such that width*height >= 2^30, undersizing the output buffer that later receives the full 32-bit frame in flx_colorspace_convert (line 140), enabling a heap-based buffer overflow.

evidence.reason: flxfh.size is copied from attacker-controlled adapter bytes at line 98 and is not required to be >= FlxFrameChunkSize. A value such as 4 underflows '4 - 16' to 0xFFFFFFF0 (4294967280) in guint32 arithmetic, so gst_adapter_take receives a huge length when the adapter holds ~0 bytes after the line-109 flush.

The only guard before the subtraction only ensures flxfh.size <= avail; since the while condition (line 90) guarantees avail >= FlxFrameChunkSize, any flxfh.size in [0, FlxFrameChunkSize-1] (e.g. 4) passes this guard yet causes the line-112 underflow.

chunk is the NULL (or aborted) result of gst_adapter_take on the oversized underflowed length and is dereferenced here without a NULL check, converting the line-111/112 underflow into a NULL-pointer crash (DoS).
width/height are unvalidated attacker header fields (lines 22-23, 36-37). Their product (max 4,294,836,225) feeds both the frame allocations and, 46 lines later, 'flxdec->size * 4'.

For 32-bit guint 'size', 'size * 4' wraps when size >= 2^30 (e.g. width=32768, height=32768: buffer size 0 instead of 2^32 bytes; max dimensions yield 4,294,443,012 instead of 17,179,344,900), allocating an undersized output buffer.

The full size*4-byte 32-bit frame is written into map.data, whose backing buffer was allocated with the wrapped value from line 124, producing a heap out-of-bounds write of (roughly 2^32 * (floor(size*4/2^32))) bytes.

assumptions: flxdec->size is a 32-bit guint (the explicit '(guint)' casts on line 78 and the gst-plugins-good GstFlxDec definition), so 'flxdec->size * 4' at line 124 uses 32-bit wraparound arithmetic.

FlxFrameChunk.size is a 32-bit unsigned field and FlxFrameChunkSize equals the chunk-header size (16) mapped/flushed at lines 97/109, making 'flxfh.size - FlxFrameChunkSize' underflow for flxfh.size < 16.
FLX_FRAME_TYPE_FIX_ENDIANNESS dereferences its argument, so a NULL chunk crashes.
gst_adapter_take returns NULL (GLib precondition) rather than aborting for oversized requests; with fatal assertions enabled it aborts instead — a crash in either mode.
The adapter contents (and thus all flxfh/flxh fields) are the attacker-controlled media bytes pushed via buf at line 14.
Line numbers refer to the code block as presented, numbered from line 1.
limitations: Out-of-bounds read when flxfh.size < FlxFrameChunkSize + FlxFrameTypeSize: 'chunk + FlxFrameTypeSize' (line 129) may point past the taken chunk, but the actual read occurs inside flx_decode_chunks (not shown); unconfirmed here.
Writes beyond frame_data/delta_data (size bytes, lines 81-82) depend on the internal bounds of flx_decode_chunks reading chunk data; that function is not shown, so not confirmed.

Unchecked allocation failure / resource exhaustion: header width*height near 4,294,836,225 forces ~4.29 GB g_malloc calls (lines 81-82); per analysis rules, unchecked allocation failure is a robustness concern, though it reinforces the DoS potential.

Possible non-termination (infinite loop) in the default branch when flxfh.size < FlxFrameChunkSize (e.g. 0): gst_adapter_flush at line 154 consumes fewer than the 16 mapped bytes (0 bytes for size 0), so avail never decreases and the while loop at line 90 spins; also causes parser desynchronization.
The exact out-of-bounds write inside flx_colorspace_convert (line 140) is not shown; the confirmed defect is the shown integer overflow at line 124 producing an undersized allocation.

verdict.summary: tipc_crypto_key_rcv copies an attacker-controlled 32-bit keylen from the message payload into a kmalloc(size) buffer (size = msg_data_sz(hdr), u16) before the consistency check size == TIPC_AEAD_ALG_NAME + sizeof(__be32) + keylen, enabling a remotely triggerable kernel heap out-of-bounds write (CVE-2022-0435).

evidence.reason: Line 24 loads keylen as an unvalidated attacker-controlled u32 from the message payload; line 27 uses it as the memcpy length into skey->key, whose capacity is only size - TIPC_AEAD_ALG_NAME - sizeof(__be32) (size <= 65535 from line 6). Any keylen > size - 20 overflows the kmalloc(size) object from line 17 before line 30 can reject the mismatch.

evidence.snippet:
/* Allocate memory for the key */
	skey = kmalloc(size, GFP_ATOMIC);
evidence.reason: The destination object for the later memcpy is allocated with attacker-controlled size from msg_data_sz(hdr) (line 6, u16, max 65535), establishing the capacity that keylen is never checked against.

This is the only validation comparing size with 20 + keylen, but it executes after the memcpy already wrote keylen bytes; it can only free the corrupted object, not prevent the out-of-bounds write on lines 26-27.

assumptions: TIPC_AEAD_ALG_NAME == 16 and sizeof(__be32) == 4 (net/tipc/crypto.h), so struct tipc_aead_key has alg_name[16], keylen (4 bytes), and flexible array key[] at byte offset 20.
tipc_aead_key_size(skey) == TIPC_AEAD_ALG_NAME + sizeof(__be32) + ntohl(skey->keylen).
msg_data_sz(hdr) returns a u16 data length; no truncation occurs when widening u16/u32 to size_t.
limitations: Reading *(data + TIPC_AEAD_ALG_NAME) (line 24) and keylen bytes from data + 20 (lines 26-27) can read past the end of the message payload; whether a message with data size < 20 can reach this handler depends on caller-side length validation not shown, so this OOB-read/infoleak aspect is an unconfirmed hypothesis.
Accessing data + TIPC_AEAD_ALG_NAME as __be32 may be unaligned depending on skb layout; treated as a robustness concern, not a confirmed vulnerability.
Precise exploitation impact (which adjacent kmalloc object is corrupted) depends on slab state and is not needed to confirm the overflow.

verdict.summary: do_viewlog reads the log file and appends each chunk verbatim into an HTML <textarea> without escaping (lines 12-15). Attacker-influenced log content containing </textarea><script>... executes as stored XSS in the browser of any non-readonly admin who views /_viewlog.

evidence.reason: Sink: buf holds raw bytes read from Run.files.log (line 13) and is appended into the HTML page with no neutralization, so log content is interpreted as HTML/script by the viewer's browser.

Context for the XSS: the unescaped log chunk is embedded between the opening <textarea> (line 12) and closing </textarea> (line 18); a chunk such as '</textarea><script>...' breaks out of the textarea and executes in the admin's session. Reachability requires only a non-readonly account (line 2), Run_Log set with Run_UseSyslog clear (line 7), and a readable log file (line 9).

assumptions: The /_viewlog response is served as text/html, so an injected script tag executes in the viewer's browser.
Run.files.log is an admin-configured path; the path itself is not attacker-controlled.
StringBuffer_append(res->outputbuffer, fmt, ...) follows printf-style semantics, so '%s' with buf as a vararg does not interpret log bytes as format directives.
limitations: Attacker control of the log file contents depends on deployment: entries originating from program-check output or external log sources can carry attacker-influenced text, while purely framework-generated entries would not; this is the main uncertainty in the XSS verdict.
The read loop does not check ferror(); a read error only ends the loop early (truncated output) - a robustness concern, not a memory-safety issue.
The entire log file is buffered into res->outputbuffer; a very large log could cause memory/CPU exhaustion, but StringBuffer's capacity behavior is framework-internal, so this is unconfirmed.
A chunk containing an embedded NUL byte truncates display of that chunk; no security impact.

verdict.summary: fix_dl_name evaluates dl->str + dl->length - so_ext_len without ensuring dl->length >= so_ext_len. For dl names of length 0-2 the size_t subtraction underflows so my_strcasecmp reads out of bounds before the buffer, enabling server crash (DoS) or exposure of heap bytes through an OOB read.

evidence.reason: so_ext_len is sizeof(SO_EXT) - 1 = 3 (line 3). dl->length is an unvalidated size_t input with no lower-bound guard; when dl->length < 3 the subtraction underflows (e.g., dl->length == 0 yields an effective address of dl->str - 3) and my_strcasecmp dereferences out-of-bounds bytes until a mismatch or NUL byte is reached.

assumptions: SO_EXT is the literal ".so", so so_ext_len == 3.
dl->str points to a buffer holding at least dl->length readable bytes for the memcpy path; this does not protect the line-4 read, which for dl->length < 3 starts before the buffer.
my_strcasecmp reads both arguments byte-by-byte until a byte difference or a NUL terminator.
limitations: The immediate callers (INSTALL PLUGIN ... SONAME / --plugin-load parsing) are outside the shown code; triggering requires a natural short input (length 0-2), which is not a contract violation of this snippet.

Integer overflow in dl->length + so_ext_len + 1 (line 7) could cause an undersized allocation followed by a heap overwrite, but only if a caller supplies length near SIZE_MAX; no such source is visible, so it is recorded as a robustness concern rather than a confirmed finding.
Whether the bytes before dl->str are unmapped (crash) or readable (garbage consumed by the comparison) is heap-layout dependent; both outcomes are out-of-bounds reads.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability. The attacker-controlled ticket length (ticklen, read from 2 bytes at line 57) is validated by the guard `ticklen + 6 != n` at line 59 before allocation/copy, and since the message length n is capped at 16384 by the ssl_get_message call at line 11, the only reachable value at the memcpy/EVP_Digest sinks is ticklen = n - 6, which exactly matches the bytes remaining at p. No integer overflow, no out-of-bounds read/write, and no digest-buffer overflow is reachable. This is the patched form of the historical CVE-2014-3513 code.

evidence.reason: This guard fully bounds the only attacker-controlled size: ticklen (from n2s at line 57, range 0..65535) must equal n - 6 to proceed. Because n is capped at 16384 by the ssl_get_message max_len argument at line 11, any ticklen that passes this check is ≤ 16378, i.e. exactly the number of bytes remaining at p after the 6-byte header. The memcpy at line 73 and EVP_Digest at line 86 therefore stay strictly inside the received message; the guard also cannot overflow (ticklen + 6 ≤ 65541 < INT_MAX).

Sink size check: with the guard at line 59 enforced, ticklen == n - 6, and p == init_msg + 6 (line 23 plus the 4-byte n2l at line 56 and 2-byte n2s at line 57). The source range covers exactly the tail of the n-byte message and the destination was allocated with the same ticklen bytes at line 68, so the copy is in-bounds both sides.

assumptions: ssl_get_message honors its max_len argument 16384 (line 11) and guarantees init_msg contains exactly the n returned bytes when ok is set.
s->session->session_id is a 32-byte array (SSL_MAX_SSL_SESSION_ID_LENGTH) and the digest outputs used (SHA-256=32 bytes, SHA-1=20 bytes) fit within it.
n2s reads exactly 2 bytes into the signed int ticklen, limiting its range to 0..65535 with no sign or narrowing issue.
limitations: The historical vulnerable variant of this function (OpenSSL before 1.0.1i, CVE-2014-3513) lacked the `ticklen + 6 != n` guard; the shown code contains the guard, so that specific over-read is not reachable from the given code.

If a caller or transport layer returned an n larger than the actual init_msg buffer despite the 16384 cap, memcpy/EVP_Digest could over-read; this depends on an out-of-scope framework invariant and is not confirmed here.

Behavior of OPENSSL_malloc(0) and the session-cache callbacks invoked at lines 37-42 were not assessed for DoS; they are framework configuration concerns, not attacker-length-dependent flaws in the shown parsing logic.

verdict.summary: parse() mmaps an attacker-controlled ELF file (line 23) and dereferences attacker-derived offsets, indices, counts and string pointers with no bounds validation against the mapping size: e_shoff/e_phoff/e_shstrndx (lines 176-178, 822-824), e_shnum/e_phnum loops (182-183, 265, 828, 911), strlen/strcmp/%s reads on unbounded name pointers (254, 335, 338, 363), and the dynamic-table block that uses uninitialized dynstr/dynamic locals and unbounded sh_offset/sh_size/count (330-350). A crafted file reliably triggers out-of-bounds reads (crash/DoS); the uninitialized-index use is CWE-457 feeding the same OOB set.

evidence.reason: e_shoff/e_phoff (32-bit) and e_shstrndx (16-bit) are attacker-controlled bytes from the mapped file (Phase 1) and are used to form pointers and an array index with no comparison against st.st_size from line 23. Concrete trigger: 4 KB ELFCLASS32 file with e_shoff=0 and e_shstrndx=0xFFFF dereferences shdr[65535] at elf_map + 65535*40 (~2.6 MB past the mapping) at line 178 -> OOB read / SIGSEGV (CWE-125).

64-bit clone of the same missing bounds validation: attacker-controlled e_shoff/e_phoff/e_shstrndx index into the shdr/phdr arrays with no size check; a large e_shoff or e_shstrndx dereferences beyond the mmap at line 23 -> OOB read (CWE-125).

evidence.snippet:
for (int i = 0; i < ehdr->e_shnum; i++) {
            name = elf_map + shstrtab.sh_offset + shdr[i].sh_name;
evidence.reason: e_shnum can be up to 0xFFFF and shdr[i] is read at e_shoff + i*sizeof(entry) with no bound on the last index relative to the mapping size, so the maximum i=0xFFFF-1 can place the read far past st.st_size. name is then a pointer built from two unbounded attacker offsets (shstrtab.sh_offset + sh_name) consumed by strlen/strcmp/printf later (lines 254, 322, 335) -> OOB read (CWE-125).

If the string is positioned so that the attacker's non-NUL bytes run to the end of the last mapped page (bytes beyond EOF within the page are zero, so a NUL must exist by the page end unless the pointer itself is past the mapping), the read crosses into unmapped memory and faults -> OOB read (CWE-125). verdict.summary: ecc_256_modp touches only rp indices 0..7 (the 2*p->size == 8 limb workspace), with the loop guard n >= p->size keeping every in-loop offset rp+n-4 >= rp+0 for the contract-required p->size == 4. p and rp are trusted library-internal values; attacker-influenced numeric contents affect only limb magnitudes, never sizes or indices. No tainted input reaches a bounds, pointer, or arithmetic sink, so no confirmed vulnerability; the absence of an in-function p->size >= 4 check is a caller-invariant robustness concern only.

evidence.reason: Loop-bound guard: n starts at 2*p->size-1 = 7 and decreases by 1 while n >= p->size = 4, so the body runs exactly 4 times (n = 7,6,5,4) and terminates at n = 3. Every index used inside the body, rp[n-4], rp[n-3], rp[n-2], stays within 0..5, and the pre-loop reads rp[7], rp[6] plus the tail writes rp[2], rp[3] stay within the 8-limb rp buffer.

Lowest-touching sink: at the minimal loop value n = p->size = 4, rp + n - 4 == rp + 0 and the 2-limb multiply writes rp[0..1]; at n = 7 it writes rp[3..4]. All indices are within the 2*p->size == 8 limb workspace supplied by the integrator, so no out-of-bounds access is reachable; the same holds for cnd_sub_n (n-3) and cnd_add_n (n-4..n-3).

assumptions: mp_limb_t is 64-bit (GMP_NUMB_BITS == 64) for this build; the 32-bit split operations u1<<32 / u1>>32 and the fixed tail writes rp[2], rp[3] are consistent only with p->size == 4.
The caller obeys the documented Nettle contract: rp provides exactly 2*p->size limbs of workspace, and p is the SECG P-256 modulus struct with p->size == 4 and p->m valid for 4 limbs.
mpn_submul_1, cnd_sub_n, cnd_add_n follow GMP/Nettle semantics (0/1 borrow/carry) and are not attacker-influenced.
limitations: No in-function validation that p->size >= 4 or that rp has 2*p->size limbs; a caller violating the contract (e.g., p->size < 4) would make rp + n - 4 or rp[n-2] underflow. This is unreachable from attacker input in the shown context and is a defensive-hardening concern, not a confirmed vulnerability.

If built with 32-bit limbs (p->size == 8), the hardcoded rp[2]/rp[3] tail writes and u1<<32 shifts would be invalid for the layout; that configuration mismatch is out of scope for the analyzed code's intended build.
assert(q2 < 2) is compiled out under NDEBUG; a violation would only skew arithmetic results, with no memory-safety impact identified.

Callers pass a valid, non-NULL KSSL_CTX (e.g., allocated by kssl_ctx_new in OpenSSL).

KRB5_KT_NOTFOUND is reported as rc=1 (keytab available) even when the host principal entry is absent; if callers interpret 1 as 'host key present', they may proceed and fail later — a robustness/logic concern with no memory-safety impact in this function.

verdict.summary: Off-by-one in the initial bounds check: `if (p > end)` admits `p == end`, so `len = *p++` dereferences one byte past the end of the readable input region. The state is attacker-reachable (e.g., a frame whose 1+len bytes exactly consume the buffer, leaving *data == end, or an empty input). evidence.reason: The guard protecting the dereference at line 10 allows the boundary case p == end (`>` instead of `>=`). With *data == end, zero bytes remain but execution continues to the unchecked dereference. The attacker-introduced length byte and buffer framing make *data == end an ordinary, attacker-craftable state.

Sink of the confirmed one-byte out-of-bounds read: when p == end passes the line 7 guard, `*p` reads the byte at address `end`, one past the last readable byte. The read value is used only to evaluate line 11, which always returns 0 on this path, so the failure is a CWE-125 OOB read rather than a corruption or disclosure.

assumptions: `end` is an exclusive bound (points one past the last readable byte), consistent with the line 11 check `p + len > end`.
`p` and `end` refer into the same buffer object, so the pointer comparisons are defined except for the boundary flaw described.
`p_malloc(pool, len)` returns an allocation of at least `len` bytes when it succeeds.
limitations: Reaching the vulnerable state requires the caller to invoke the function with `*data == end`, i.e., after a prior successful read consumed the whole buffer (line 17 can set `*data == end`) or with an empty input; the caller's read loop is not shown, so the second call is an inferred usage pattern.
Impact is bounded: the function always returns 0 before `memcpy` on the p == end path, so the over-read byte is never disclosed through `*buffer`; a crash requires `end` to lie on an unmapped page.
`p_malloc`'s return value is not checked; on allocation failure `memcpy(NULL, p, len)` would dereference NULL. Recorded as an unchecked-allocation robustness concern, not a confirmed vulnerability.
Behavior for a caller that passes `*data > end` (or pointers from different objects) is undefined by C and treated as a caller contract issue, out of scope.

verdict.summary: No confirmed attacker-triggerable vulnerability in scm_mkdir. The explicit-mode path converts mode with scm_to_uint and passes it to mkdir; any values that would not fit mode_t are silent-truncated, but all permission bits live in the low 12 bits and the OS masks the creation mode to 07777, so no permission boundary is crossed. The umask(0)-read pattern (lines 14-15) is a thread-safety robustness concern whose exploitation depends on concurrent threads outside the shown code, and is reported as a limitation.

evidence.reason: Mode sink: scm_to_uint(mode) produces unsigned int in [0, UINT_MAX], implicitly converted to the mode_t parameter without a visible range check. Truncation only removes bits above the mode_t width; the permission bits are within the low 12 bits, and the OS masks creation modes to 07777, so this is silent truncation without demonstrated security impact (demoted to limitation per the rules).

umask is zeroed to read the previous value; the effective mkdir mode is passed explicitly (0777 ^ mask), so this branch's own result is unaffected. A separate thread creating a file in the two-syscall window would see umask 0, but that requires concurrent execution and external file-creation behavior not shown or controllable here — recorded as a limitation, not a confirmed vulnerability.

assumptions: scm_to_uint raises an out-of-range exception for negative or >UINT_MAX Scheme integers (Guile numeric-conversion invariant; not visible in the shown snippet).
STRING_SYSCALL's path conversion (scm_to_locale_string) rejects malformed strings with embedded NUL bytes, so c_path is a well-formed C string at the mkdir call.
The OS filesystem layer masks directory creation modes to S_IRWXUGO|S_ISVTX (07777) and applies the process umask, bounding the security effect of any mode value.
limitations: Silent truncation of mode when mode_t is narrower than unsigned int (e.g., 16-bit mode_t platforms): values above mode_t range are accepted by scm_to_uint and truncated; low permission bits are preserved and the kernel masks to 07777, so no concrete security impact is demonstrated (robustness concern only).

Reading the umask via umask(0)/umask(mask) temporarily clears the umask process-wide; a concurrent thread creating a file in that window would do so with umask 0. Not a confirmed vulnerability because it requires concurrent execution and other threads' file-creation activity outside the shown code.

Whether mode is attacker-controlled depends on the calling Scheme program (not shown); from the C function's perspective, mode is already range-validated by scm_to_uint, so no validation gap is confirmed in this code.

verdict.summary: In Item_equal::create_pushable_equalities, left_item is assigned before the checker test and retains the last rejected item when the field iterator is exhausted, so the if (!left_item) guard never detects 'no eligible item'; with a constant present, the function clones and pushes an equality built from an item that failed the caller's pushdown checker, bypassing the pushability gate.

evidence.reason: left_item is assigned at line 14 before the rejection test at line 15, so a continue leaves it pointing at the rejected item. If every item is rejected and the iterator is exhausted, left_item is non-NULL (the last rejected item) and the line 20 guard passes, failing to detect that no eligible item was found.

Sink of the bypass: with right_item non-NULL (line 23) and all items rejected by the checker, this line clones the ineligible left_item and the resulting Item_func_eq is pushed at lines 31-34, creating a pushable equality the caller's checker explicitly rejected.

assumptions: Item_equal field-list members and get_const() items are parser/optimizer-validated Item objects derived from the user's SQL.
NULL returns from build_clone and nonzero returns from push_back represent OOM and are handled by early return true.
limitations: End-to-end attacker reachability depends on an optimizer caller passing a checker that can reject every field item of an Item_equal that simultaneously holds a constant; the checker/caller semantics are not shown, so this is a confirmed code-level guard flaw but only a plausible exploit scenario.
No memory-safety, integer, or lifetime vulnerability was found; allocations are mem_root-based and NULL-checked, and no bounds/index arithmetic exists.
The observed impact is optimizer correctness (wrong pushdown/wrong results), not a demonstrated confidentiality, integrity, or availability security mechanism.

verdict.summary: No confirmed attacker-triggerable vulnerability in sys_setrlimit. The rlim array index is bounded by RLIM_NLIMITS, the user copy is size-exact, and the NOFILE/NR_OPEN and CAP_SYS_RESOURCE authorization checks are present. The RLIMIT_CPU zero-soft-limit fixup can store rlim_cur=1 with rlim_max=0 (breaking the cur<=max invariant), and secs_to_cputime can wrap for huge limits, but both only affect the calling process and have no confirmed privilege or memory-safety impact in the shown code.

evidence.reason: Attacker-controlled rlim_cur==0 with rlim_max==0 passes the cur>max check (lines 11-12) and the CAP_SYS_RESOURCE check (lines 14-16, since 0 is not > old_rlim->rlim_max), is rewritten to 1 at line 31, and stored at line 35 as (cur=1, max=0), violating the invariant enforced at lines 11-12. Taint and reachability hold, but impact fails: no shown sink uses the violated invariant and the only consequence is a stricter self-imposed CPU limit on the calling process, so this is a robustness quirk, not a confirmed vulnerability.

assumptions: RLIM_NLIMITS equals the declared size of current->signal->rlim, so rlim[resource] is in bounds after the line 7 check.
copy_from_user failure (nonzero return) is treated as EFAULT (lines 9-10) and new_rlim is only used on success.
rlim_cur/rlim_max are unsigned long and cputime_t is 64-bit on the analyzed configuration.
Default RLIMIT_CPU is typically RLIM_INFINITY, so a request of (cur=0, max=0) needs no capability, making the line 24-32 fixup reachable.
capable(CAP_SYS_RESOURCE) and security_task_setrlimit follow the kernel's trust boundaries.
limitations: The RLIMIT_CPU zero-soft-limit fixup stores rlim_cur=1 with rlim_max=0, breaking the cur<=max invariant; downstream consumers (getrlimit, fork, fd-allocation, exec) are not shown, so any security impact there is unconfirmed.

secs_to_cputime(rlim_cur) at line 51 can wrap for very large rlim_cur when it_prof_secs==0 (line 51 guard), producing an early self-SIGXCPU; the impact is confined to the calling process and no privilege boundary is crossed.

Concurrent threads sharing current->signal could race the check-then-store of rlim; demonstrating a capability bypass requires caller-side interleaving not provable from this single syscall body, so it is treated as an unconfirmed robustness concern.
Interactions with kernel subsystems not shown (e.g., RLIMIT_NOFILE enforcement during fd allocation) were not analyzed.

verdict.summary: No attacker-reachable memory-safety or logic vulnerability is confirmable within the shown function.
