A blob of 8-9 bytes (or 4-11 on 32-bit) passes every guard, and line 42 then reads bh->flags at byte offsets 8-9 out of bounds, disclosing adjacent memory through *hdrflags.

evidence.reason: The guard compares length against sizeof(bh), a pointer (8 on LP64), not sizeof(blobheader) (12 with the totlen@0/min_version@4/version@5/hdrsize@6/flags@8 layout). Any length in [8,9] on LP64 (or [4,11] on 32-bit) passes, although later dereferences need up to 10 bytes, so the bound is insufficient for the accesses it is meant to protect.

With an attacker-supplied 8-byte buffer where totlen==htonl(8) and bytes 6-7 equal 0x000C, lines 8, 15, 23, and 33 all pass, and this line reads bh->flags at offsets 8-9 - 1 to 2 bytes past the end of data. The out-of-bounds value is written to *hdrflags and returned to the caller, an OOB read (CWE-125) with information-disclosure impact.

assumptions: 64-bit build assumed for sizeof(bh) == 8; the flaw is wider on 32-bit (sizeof(bh) == 4, so lengths 4-11 pass the guard).
blobheader layout assumed as totlen@0 (4 bytes), min_version@4 (1), version@5 (1), hdrsize@6 (2), flags@8 (2), sizeof == 12 with padding.
The caller passes a buffer of at least `length` bytes, matching the implicit contract the line-8 guard claims to enforce.
limitations: Unaligned access from the cast at line 5 could fault on strict-alignment architectures (e.g., ARM) only if the caller supplies a misaligned buffer; caller buffer alignment is not visible in the shown code, so this is unconfirmed.
NULL dereferences of data/dataoffset/hdrflags/hdrversion would require a caller violating its contract; out of scope for the shown code.
The OOB window is small (1-2 bytes on LP64; larger on 32-bit), so a crash requires the adjacent page to be unmapped; the primary confirmed impact is memory disclosure via *hdrflags.

verdict.summary: NULL pointer dereference in load_buffer: if get_prelink_info_range_from_mach0 returns NULL (attacker-controlled MACH-O without kernelcache prelink metadata), the code jumps to the beach label where 'obj->cache_buf = NULL;' dereferences the still-NULL obj (declared NULL at line 11, only assigned at line 18), crashing the process on a crafted file.

evidence.reason: Attacker-controlled file bytes make get_prelink_info_range_from_mach0 return NULL while main_mach0 is non-NULL (line 5). obj is still NULL here (declared at line 11, assigned only at line 18), so the unconditional goto beach reaches line 67 with obj == NULL.

Sink: unconditional NULL pointer dereference. Every path reaching beach (lines 15, 21, 31, 41) has obj == NULL (never assigned or freed-and-nulled by R_FREE), so line 67 writes through NULL, causing SIGSEGV and denial of service on a crafted input (CWE-476).

assumptions: R_FREE(p) is the standard radare2 macro that frees and sets the pointer to NULL (used at lines 20, 29, 30, 38, 39, 40, 52).
r_buf_ref(buf) succeeds because buf is a valid RBuffer supplied by the bin loader framework.
MACH0_ and RKernelCacheObj type definitions and MACH0_(new_buf) semantics follow the standard radare2 kernelcache plugin.
limitations: The identical NULL dereference at line 67 is also reachable via allocation failure (R_NEW0 at line 18 returning NULL, lines 19-21); per analysis rules, unchecked-allocation-failure paths are treated as a robustness concern, not a separate vulnerability.
r_rebase_info_new_from_mach0 may return NULL but is only used as a boolean at line 58 in the shown code; no dereference exists in this scope.
Parser internals of MACH0_(new_buf), get_prelink_info_range_from_mach0, and r_cf_value_dict_parse are not shown; any further memory-safety issues inside them are out of scope for this analysis.
Impact is a crash-only denial of service (local, when opening a crafted file); no memory-corruption or code-execution primitive is confirmed from the shown code.

verdict.summary: njs_object_iterate_reverse never validates the caller-supplied indices args->from/args->to. The byte/ASCII string path computes p = string_prop.start + from and dereferences it (and decrements p below the buffer when to < 0), the array fast path guards only from < array->length but not from >= 0, and the UTF-8 path runs njs_utf8_prev/njs_string_new on positions derived from the same unvalidated range. Out-of-range indices (from >= length, or to <= -1) yield out-of-bounds heap reads before/after string and array buffers.

evidence.reason: args->from (int64_t, unvalidated at lines 14-15) selects the byte offset p into the string window [start, start+string_prop.size). There is no from <= length-1 check in this branch, so for an ASCII string with length 4 and from == 4, to == 0, the first iteration passes p == end to njs_string_new which reads *p (1 byte past the heap buffer). With to <= -1, p-- at line 97 walks p below start and line 86 reads before the buffer on the extra iteration.

The reverse loop (from += 1 at line 20; while (from-- > to) at line 22) reaches index -1 when to <= -1, e.g. from_orig = 0, to = -1. The guard covers only the upper bound: -1 < array->length is true, so njs_is_valid(&array->start[-1]) dereferences one element before the allocation, and handler(..., &array->start[-1], -1) can propagate that out-of-bounds pointer. Missing lower-bound check on the unvalidated args->from/args->to inputs.

For from == length and to == 0 the loop runs length+1 iterations; after processing the first character, the final iteration calls njs_utf8_prev(p) with p at the buffer start (line 109), scanning before the buffer if the helper does not clamp, and line 112 forms a string from pos with length p - pos derived from those out-of-bounds positions. The from/to inputs are never validated in the shown function.

assumptions: array->start has exactly array->length valid elements, and string_prop describes the valid byte window [string_prop.start, string_prop.start + string_prop.size).
njs_string_offset/njs_utf8_next/njs_utf8_prev follow njs semantics (offset returns the from-th character pointer, utf8_prev scans backward one character without a documented start clamp).
handler and args->value are trusted integration points; only the numeric index inputs need validation in this function.
limitations: The caller chain is not shown: whether any real njs caller can pass from >= length or to <= -1 to this function is unverifiable from the snippet. If every caller guarantees 0 <= to <= from <= length-1, these OOB paths are unreachable in practice and the issue reduces to defensive hardening.
The UTF-8 branch finding depends on njs_utf8_prev not clamping at the buffer start; that implementation is not shown.
from += 1 and i = from + 1 perform signed overflow at INT64_MAX (UB), but require an absurd caller value and no concrete memory impact is confirmed.
njs_string_new result is discarded ((void) cast, 'This cannot fail.'); an allocation failure would be a separate robustness concern, not confirmed here.
idx (double) compared to to/from (int64_t) at line 147 has precision edge cases (e.g., NaN/very large indices) but no memory-safety impact in the shown code.

verdict.summary: check_passwd compares raw binary key/digest material with strncmp, which terminates at the first NUL byte in either operand. When the stored digest/key begins with 0x00, any attacker-supplied password whose computed key/digest also begins with 0x00 is accepted after a truncated (effectively zero-length) comparison, bypassing the password check.

evidence.reason: passwd1_sum is the non-NUL-terminated binary PBKDF2 output (keylen bytes) derived from attacker-controlled passwd at lines 43-44, and key is a raw slice of the stored blob (line 39). strncmp stops at the first 0x00 in either operand: if both the stored key and the computed key start with 0x00, only a zero-length comparison occurs and strncmp returns 0, so line 49 sets ret = 1 and the wrong password is accepted regardless of the remaining keylen-1 bytes. Primary CWE-697, secondary CWE-287.

Same defect in the raw-digest path: passwd1_sum is the digest of attacker-controlled passwd computed at line 51, and passwd2_sum is the stored digest (line 26). strncmp over hash_len bytes of binary data truncates at the first 0x00 in either digest, so when both digests begin with 0x00 any password whose digest also begins with 0x00 is accepted via line 57, bypassing the check.

assumptions: read_env_passwd and read_default_passwd honor their length argument and write at most hash_len bytes into passwd2_sum (their bodies are outside the shown code).
digest_digest writes exactly digest_length(d) bytes and pkcs5_pbkdf2_hmac_sha1 writes exactly keylen bytes into passwd1_sum.
Compile-time macros satisfy 0 <= PBKDF2_SALT_LEN < PBKDF2_LENGTH (values not shown).
The caller guarantees that passwd points to at least length bytes.
limitations: The bypass is probabilistic: it requires the stored key/digest to begin with 0x00 (~1/256 chance for a random hash) and the attacker to find a candidate whose derived output also begins with 0x00 (expected ~256 verification attempts); caller-side attempt limiting/rate limiting is not shown.
Any memory-safety issue inside read_env_passwd/read_default_passwd cannot be confirmed from the shown code.
If PBKDF2_SALT_LEN >= PBKDF2_LENGTH, keylen <= 0 and the strncmp count at line 48 wraps to a huge size_t causing an out-of-bounds read; this depends on unshown config macros and is unconfirmed.
hash_len * 2 at line 22 could overflow int only under pathological configuration values and is not attacker-controlled.
In the digest path, a calloc failure at lines 23-24 returns -ENOMEM without digest_free(d), leaking d; OOM-only and not attacker-reachable in practice.
The strncmp comparisons are not constant-time (CWE-208 timing side channel); minor for a local console and not independently confirmed as exploitable.

verdict.summary: No confirmed, reachable vulnerability within the shown code. The only directly attacker-controlled input (S3 response-* query parameters) is validated before being emitted as an HTTP header: anonymous callers are rejected (line 112) and any value containing control characters is rejected (line 122), which blocks CR/LF header injection. Candidate issues — (a) unvalidated object metadata used as HTTP header names/values (lines 150, 165, 155->208), and (b) unguarded pointer arithmetic bl.c_str() + bl_ofs in dump_body (line 218) — cannot be tied to attacker-controlled values within the shown code (metadata sanitization and offset computation happen in unshown layers), so they are recorded as robustness limitations, not vulnerabilities.

evidence.reason: val is attacker-controlled query-param text (line 108) destined for HTTP header values (line 129/131). This guard fully covers CR/LF-bearing inputs, so the header-injection sink is not reachable with a control-character value; no finding.

name/value originate from stored object metadata attrs (client-influenced but populated by the unshown upload layer). No control-character validation exists here; whether attrs can hold CR/LF depends on code outside the snippet, so this is an unconfirmed response-splitting hypothesis (limitation), not a confirmed vulnerability.

evidence.snippet: int r = dump_body(s, bl.c_str() + bl_ofs, bl_len);
evidence.reason: bl of length bl.length() is indexed by caller-supplied off_t bl_ofs/bl_len with no in-function bounds check; overflow (bl_ofs > bl.length()) or underflow (negative bl_ofs) would be an OOB read/UB. The offending values originate in the unshown caller (RGWGetObj::execute), so reachability is not established within the shown code; recorded as a limitation.

assumptions: str_has_cntrl rejects all RFC 7230 control characters (c < 0x20, 0x7F), including CR (0x0D) and LF (0x0A), as the in-code comment states.
resp_attr_params is a static whitelist whose p->http_attr values are compile-time constants, so response header names cannot be attacker-chosen.
s->auth.identity and s->info.args are valid framework-supplied state (identity non-null).
attrs is populated and sanitized by the object-fetch/upload layer; the shown function relies on that invariant.
bl_ofs/bl_len are maintained by the caller to lie within [0, bl.length()] and describe a valid slice of bl.
limitations: If the unshown upload/metadata path ever allowed CR or LF bytes in stored object metadata values, lines 150/165/199 would emit unvalidated HTTP header values (response splitting, CWE-113); and an unvalidated content-type attr (lines 155-156 -> 208) could inject headers. Not confirmable from the shown code.
A stored metadata key that survives upload with CR/LF would reach dump_header at line 165 as a header name; HTTP header-name parsing at PUT time is assumed (not shown) to prevent this.
Out-of-bounds read at line 218 if a caller violated the bl_ofs/bl_len contract (includes negative offsets and bl_ofs+bl_len > bl.length()); out of scope for this snippet (CWE-125 unconfirmed).
total_len/metadata_bl length arithmetic (lines 33, 54) and (long long) cast are unvalidated but overflow only for unrealistically large metadata; not security-relevant in scope.

verdict.summary: TransposeShapeFn derives an unbounded 64-bit rank from attacker-controlled shape metadata (NumElements of input(1)) and uses it, without any upper-bound validation, to size std::vector allocations (dims.resize(rank), and AsInt64's internal vector) and to bound 32-bit loop counters. A tiny malicious graph declaring input(1) as a vector of huge size (e.g., [3000000000]) with unknown input rank yields rank >= 2^31, causing multi-gigabyte allocation/memory exhaustion (CWE-789) and, when the allocation succeeds, int32/int counter overflow leading to out-of-bounds dims[i]/data[i] access (CWE-190).

evidence.reason: Taint source: perm_elems (line 5) is NumElements(perm_shape), i.e., an attacker-controlled shape declaration of input(1). A fully-known vector shape such as [3000000000] makes ValueKnown true and rank = 3000000000 with no upper-bound check; this value flows to line 32.

Sink: dims is std::vector<DimensionHandle> (approx. 8 bytes/element); resize(rank) allocates 8*rank bytes from attacker-controlled rank before any validation. Reachability: input rank unknown, perm_shape=[3000000000] known, perm==nullptr -> line 9 falls through, line 23 guard (rank<2) fails, so line 32 attempts a ~24GB allocation -> bad_alloc/OOM/termination (CWE-789). WithRank at line 33 would reject huge rank but runs only after this allocation.

Loop bound compares 32-bit int32_t i with unbounded 64-bit rank: for rank > INT32_MAX the condition i < rank never fails; i overflows to negative and data[i]/dims[i] index out of bounds (CWE-190; OOB read at line 50, OOB write at line 55). Also note the in_idx >= rank guard at line 51 does not reject negative in_idx, which reaches c->Dim at line 55.

Same overflow pattern with a plain 32-bit int counter against unbounded int64 rank (reachable with perm==nullptr and a huge declarative perm_shape): for rank >= 2^31 the counter wraps and dims[i] is written out of bounds at line 59 if the line-32 allocation succeeded.

assumptions: When perm != nullptr, c->input_tensor(1) is assumed to have a shape matching the input(1) shape handle, so rank == perm_elems == perm->NumElements() (framework invariant).
c->Dim(input, negative_or_large_idx) is assumed to bounds-check and return UnknownDim internally (behavior not shown in this code).
c->Value() returns a non-negative value when ValueKnown is true, and c->Rank() returns a non-negative bounded value when RankKnown is true.
limitations: An out-of-bounds read inside AsInt64 (reading rank elements from a smaller tensor) would require rank > perm->NumElements(), i.e., a violation of the input-tensor/shape-handle invariant; not confirmable from the shown code.

The OOB dims[i]/data[i] accesses from the 32-bit counter overflow require rank >= 2^31 AND successful allocation of the multi-GB dims/data vectors (overcommit or very large RAM); on typical systems the line-32 allocation fails first, so the confirmed impact is memory-exhaustion DoS and the memory-corruption impact is environment-dependent.

Negative in_idx values bypass the in_idx >= rank guard and reach c->Dim; the consequence (likely incorrect shape results) depends on c->Dim's internal bounds handling and is not memory-unsafe in the shown code, so it is not reported as a vulnerability.
The crash mechanism relies in part on uncaught std::bad_alloc; the primary issue is the attacker-controlled allocation size (CWE-789) rather than allocator failure of a bounded request.

verdict.summary: No attacker-reachable memory-safety or authorization flaw is provable from the shown code. The only attacker-controlled flow (the promise resolution value) reaches fixed-size, type-checked operations (L13-16, L37-38, L58, L80). The unchecked frame/scope dereferences (ctx->await at L18-19, scope write at L37) are keyed by VM-internal invariants established outside this function; the memory-error early return (L67-68) is an OOM-only leak path. These are recorded as limitations, not confirmed vulnerabilities.

evidence.reason: Candidate UAF/null-deref assessed and rejected: ctx/ctx->await come from vm->top_frame->function->context (L11), a VM-internal value installed by the await-setup machinery, not from attacker input. No condition in the shown code can invalidate it; exploitation depends on promise-reaction lifetime code not shown, so reachability (part 2) fails.

Candidate OOB scope write assessed and rejected: the destination is selected by ctx->index, a compile-time/bytecode-derived value (trusted, no arithmetic applied), while value (attacker-controlled) is a fixed-size njs_value_t copied in full. OOB would require a bad index/level invariant from code not shown; taint and reachability fail for the shown code.

Robustness path assessed, not a confirmed vulnerability: on VM memory error the function returns without njs_async_context_free(vm, ctx) and without settling ctx->capability, leaking ctx and leaving the async promise pending. Reaching it requires the VM itself to fail allocation; it is a resource-leak/DoS robustness concern, not an attacker-triggerable memory-safety flaw.

assumptions: njs_arg(args, nargs, 1) follows the standard njs njs_argument contract and returns &njs_value_undefined when nargs <= 1 (macro body not shown), preventing an OOB read at L13.
ctx, ctx->await, ctx->index, ctx->pc, and ctx->capability are established by the await-setup/bytecode machinery outside this function and remain valid while the reaction callback executes.
njs_scope_value(vm, ctx->index) resolves against the currently active local level, and the index range is guaranteed by the bytecode compiler (implementation not shown).
njs_value_t copies are fixed-size and njs_function_call with nargs=1 expects a 1-element array, satisfied by value and &vm->retval.
limitations: Use-after-free/null-deref of ctx->await (L18-19, used through L45) cannot be triggered by any condition inside the shown code; it depends on promise-reaction registration/lifetime code not shown (unconfirmed CWE-416/476).
Out-of-bounds write via *njs_scope_value(vm, ctx->index) = *value (L37) depends on bytecode-derived index/level invariants not shown (unconfirmed CWE-787).
Memory-error early return (L67-68) skips njs_async_context_free and leaves the capability unsettled; reachable only under VM OOM, so it is a robustness/resource-leak concern (unconfirmed CWE-401).
A fulfilled Error object is routed to the reject path (L13-16), diverging from ECMAScript await semantics; no security impact is confirmed.

verdict.summary: ReadOneMNGImage contains two attacker-reachable memory-corruption bugs. (1) MNG MAGN magnification: when magn_methy==0 (or magn_methx==0) and the magnification factor is >=2, the row/column expand loop writes more pixels than the magnified image was allocated (magnified_height/magnified_width computed with 32-bit png_uint_32 truncation), so GetAuthenticPixels(large_image,0,yy,...) is called with yy == large_image->rows, causing a heap out-of-bounds write (CWE-787) or NULL dereference. (2) MNG DEFI: object_id of exactly MNG_MAX_OBJECTS (or any value > MNG_MAX_OBJECTS, which is clamped to MNG_MAX_OBJECTS) is used to index the 256-element MngInfo arrays exists/frozen/invisible/x_off/y_off/object_clip after a `>`-only guard, causing in-struct heap out-of-bounds read and write (CWE-787/CWE-125).

evidence.reason: magnified_height is computed with 32-bit png_uint_32 arithmetic from the attacker-controlled MAGN factors (magn_mt, magn_mb, magn_my) and the attacker-controlled row count. For magn_methy==0 the else-branch formula gives mt+mb+(rows-3)*my+1, but the actual row loop below emits mt+(rows-2)*my+mb rows; the loop overruns by my-1 rows, and the 32-bit truncation of the products (e.g. 67000*65535) can wrap, producing a small allocation while the loop still writes the unwrapped count.

The loop's y==0/rows-1 branches use magn_methy<=1 semantics whenever magn_methy is 0, while the height formula used the else branch; with rows=4, methx=2, methy=0, mt=1, mb=1, my=2 the loop writes 1+2+2+1=6 rows into a 5-row large_image (yy reaches 5), so GetAuthenticPixels(large_image,0,5,...) at line 1743 accesses row 5 of rows 0..4 — out of bounds. The only guard is a debug-only assert, so release builds perform the OOB row write.

object_id is a 16-bit value parsed from attacker-controlled bytes at line 377. The guard uses strict >, so object_id == MNG_MAX_OBJECTS (e.g. p[0]=1, p[1]=0) is not clamped, and any value >= 257 is clamped to exactly MNG_MAX_OBJECTS. The loop bounds in the same function (line 813: i >= MNG_MAX_OBJECTS -> continue; line 835: i < MNG_MAX_OBJECTS) establish that the valid index range is [0, MNG_MAX_OBJECTS), making index MNG_MAX_OBJECTS out of bounds.

Sink write with object_id == MNG_MAX_OBJECTS (256) into the 256-element (assumption anchored by the CLIP/SAVE loops at lines 813/835) exists[] array: heap OOB write one slot past the array, corrupting adjacent MngInfo members. The same index reaches the OOB read at line 395 and the wider OOB writes at lines 416-420 (x_off/y_off) and 435 (object_clip, 32 bytes).

assumptions: MNG_MAX_OBJECTS == 256 and the MngInfo arrays (exists, invisible, viewable, frozen, x_off, y_off, object_clip) have 256 elements; the shown CLIP guard (line 813, i >= MNG_MAX_OBJECTS -> continue) and SAVE loop (line 835, i < MNG_MAX_OBJECTS) confirm MNG_MAX_OBJECTS is the exclusive bound.
MNG_MAX_LOOPS >= 256 so the loop_level values 0..255 derived from chunk[0] in LOOP/ENDL stay in bounds.
The chunk allocation includes MagickPathExtent (~4096 bytes) of slack, so reads past the payload length in TERM/FRAM/MOVE/BASI are in-bounds uninitialized reads, not OOB.
The MAGN magnification path is compiled unconditionally inside `if (mng_type)`, independent of MNG_INSERT_LAYERS/MNG_OBJECT_BUFFERS build flags.
Embedded PNG dimensions (image->rows/image->columns) pass through ReadOnePNGImage unchanged and can be 4 or larger.
limitations: TERM (p[2..9]) and FRAM/MOVE clip-box reads can read past the chunk payload when length guards are looser than the fields; they stay within the length+MagickPathExtent allocation, so this is an uninitialized-data robustness concern, not memory-unsafe.
MHDR width/height parsing `(p[0] << 24)` is signed-int UB for bytes >= 0x80, but the subsequent 65535 limit check prevents misuse of the resulting values.
MngInfoDiscardObject receives 16-bit object ids from DISC/SEEK without a shown bounds check; its body is outside the provided code, so any OOB there is unconfirmed.
global_plte allocation failure is not checked before the fill loop (lines 500-509); per the rules, unchecked allocation failure is not reported as a vulnerability.

png_uint_32 truncation in magnified_width/magnified_height can wrap for large rows*factor products, arbitrarily enlarging the Finding-1 overrun; the wrap alone is not independently demonstrated to reach a sink without the methy==0/methx==0 loop-formula mismatch.
Short reads (EOF) mid-chunk leave the chunk tail uninitialized; downstream code may use that slack data, a robustness/info concern with no OOB.

verdict.summary: Stack-based buffer overflow in inbound_cap_ls: the server-supplied CAP LS payload (extensions_str) is split into tokens and each recognized token is appended to the fixed 256-byte stack buffer via unbounded strcat with no length check. A server sending >=19 copies of a known capability (e.g., 'multi-prefix', 13 bytes each) writes past buffer[255] (cumulative 9 + 19*13 = 256, NUL at index 256), corrupting the stack; the overwrite grows with every additional token.

evidence.snippet: char buffer[256];	/* buffer for requesting capabilities and emitting the signal */
evidence.reason: Fixed 256-byte stack buffer (valid indices 0-255) is the overflow target; its capacity is never compared against the cumulative length of the strcat appends performed later in the function.
Seeds the buffer with 9 bytes (8 chars + NUL at index 8), leaving only 247 bytes for all subsequent appends; every later strcat reduces the remaining capacity with no check.

Iteration count is the token count of the attacker-controlled extensions_str array produced by g_strsplit (line 15); it is unbounded, so the number of appends (and thus total bytes written to the 256-byte buffer) is attacker-selected.

Representative sink (same pattern at lines 25, 35, 40, 45, 50, 59, 64, 70, 79): appends a fixed 13 bytes for every token equal to 'multi-prefix' with no bounds check. 19 repetitions yield 9 + 19*13 = 256 bytes, writing the terminating NUL at index 256, beyond the buffer; the same token via g_strsplit is a separate element each time, so repetition directly multiplies the write.

assumptions: extensions_str carries the CAP LS payload received from the IRC server over the network; the function is the inbound CAP handler and echoes recognized tokens into a 'CAP REQ' string, confirming the parameter is server-supplied capability data.
prefs.hex_irc_cap_server_time and the serv fields used (loginmethod, password, have_cert) are trusted client configuration and are not part of the vulnerability.
Line numbers and snippets are transcribed from the code as provided.
limitations: The exact caller that extracts extensions_str from the raw IRC line is not shown; no truncation of the payload is visible, and even a conventional 512-byte IRC line limit still permits the ~247+ bytes of recognized tokens needed to overflow, so this does not undermine the finding.

A well-behaved server that sends each capability once with a short list does not trigger the overflow; the trigger requires enough recognized tokens (e.g., 19 x 'multi-prefix', 21 x 'away-notify', or 11 x 'znc.in/server-time-iso'), which an attacker-controlled server can emit trivially.
If an upstream layer imposed an invariant bounding recognized-token bytes to <=247 this would be unreachable, but no such invariant exists in the shown code.

verdict.summary: In do_i2c_md, the display length parsed from attacker-controlled argv[3] is stored in 32-bit uint and then copied to signed int nbytes with no range check. A length whose uint value has the high bit set (e.g. 0x80000000) makes nbytes/linebytes negative, and that negative length is passed to dm_i2c_read()/i2c_read() together with the fixed DISP_LINE_LEN-byte stack buffer linebuf. The I2C API converts the length to an unsigned message length, so the driver reads ~2^31 bytes into a 16-byte stack buffer, causing a stack-based out-of-bounds write.

evidence.reason: argv[3] is attacker-controlled command-line input parsed by hextoul with no upper-bound validation; the returned unsigned long is stored into 32-bit uint length and so can take any value up to 0xFFFFFFFF, later becoming the signed nbytes.

uint length (up to 0xFFFFFFFF) is converted to signed int nbytes; for length >= 0x80000000, nbytes is negative, so the ternary's true branch (cap at DISP_LINE_LEN) is not taken and linebytes becomes negative. linebuf is declared with only DISP_LINE_LEN bytes.

Sink: negative linebytes (e.g. -2147483648 for length 0x80000000) is passed as the read length together with the 16-byte linebuf. Per the I2C API the length becomes an unsigned message length (0x80000000), and the driver writes that many bytes into linebuf, overflowing the stack buffer. Reachable via `i2c md <chip> <addr> 0x80000000` with a valid I2C device on the bus.

assumptions: int and uint are 32-bit on U-Boot targets; hextoul returns unsigned long, which truncates to uint on assignment (LP64 builds).
DISP_LINE_LEN is 16 (defined outside the shown snippet), making linebuf a 16-byte stack buffer.
dm_i2c_read/i2c_read propagate the length parameter to an I2C transfer whose message length field is unsigned (I2C driver API contract).
limitations: The actual out-of-bounds write occurs inside the I2C driver/API, which is not shown; a driver that validates or caps the message length could truncate or fail the transfer, though the negative-length computation and the fixed-size buffer are fully in the shown code.
The DM path requires i2c_get_cur_bus_chip() to succeed (lines 52–56); otherwise the function returns before the read sink is reached.
Positive-but-huge lengths such as 0x7FFFFFFF cause an enormous number of bus reads and console prints (availability/robustness concern) with no memory-safety impact.
Inputs whose truncated uint value is below 0x80000000 (e.g. values that wrap to small numbers on LP64 builds) do not trigger the overflow.

verdict.summary: No vulnerability is confirmable within the shown code alone. The stack arrays x_cur/x_new (size XFRM_MAX_DEPTH) are indexed by nx_cur/nx_new, which grow up to num_migrate; the only gate on num_migrate is xfrm_migrate_check (line 13), whose bound enforcement is not shown. If that check does not enforce num_migrate < XFRM_MAX_DEPTH, an attacker-influenced count yields a stack out-of-bounds write (CWE-787) — this matches the upstream CVE-2017-11600 pattern — but reachability depends on unshown code, so it is recorded as a limitation.

evidence.reason: Both index targets are fixed-size arrays of XFRM_MAX_DEPTH entries; valid indices are 0..XFRM_MAX_DEPTH-1. Any write at index >= XFRM_MAX_DEPTH is out of bounds, so the arrays bound the loop's write indices only if num_migrate (the loop-derived count) stays below XFRM_MAX_DEPTH.

This is the only gate between the attacker-influenced num_migrate and the loop that writes x_cur/x_new. Its body is not part of the shown code, so whether it rejects num_migrate >= XFRM_MAX_DEPTH cannot be verified; a guard exists but its bound is not demonstrated, and the failure condition cannot be concretely tied to a shown pass-through value.

The loop runs i < num_migrate times and each matching iteration increments nx_cur and nx_new by exactly one, so the maximum index written equals num_migrate - 1. If num_migrate >= XFRM_MAX_DEPTH reaches this loop, lines 25 and 29 write past x_cur/x_new; whether xfrm_migrate_check prevents that is unshown, so the overflow is an unconfirmed hypothesis here rather than a confirmed, in-scope reachable vulnerability.

assumptions: XFRM_MAX_DEPTH is a small positive compile-time constant (6 in the upstream kernel), though not defined in the shown code.

In the real subsystem, xfrm_migrate is reached from the netlink handler xfrm_user (XFRM_MSG_MIGRATE), where m and num_migrate are derived from userspace-controlled attributes; callers are expected to provide exactly num_migrate valid entries.
Called helpers other than the bounds question (xfrm_policy_migrate, xfrm_states_put/delete, km_migrate) are assumed correct, as their bodies are not shown.
limitations: Stack out-of-bounds write into x_cur[nx_cur]/x_new[nx_new] (CWE-787, secondary CWE-121) if num_migrate >= XFRM_MAX_DEPTH (e.g., 6 or 7 when the constant is 6) passes xfrm_migrate_check at line 13; the guard's bound is not shown, so reachability cannot be confirmed within the provided code. This is the historical CVE-2017-11600 pattern, fixed upstream by adding 'num_migrate < 0 || num_migrate >= XFRM_MAX_DEPTH' to xfrm_migrate_check.
Handling of negative or oversized num_migrate inside xfrm_policy_migrate (line 39) is not shown; the shown loop harmlessly skips for negative counts, but helper behavior is out of scope.
Duplicate/xfrm_migrate_state_find returning the same state for multiple entries would be a logic concern only; counts remain bounded by num_migrate, so no memory-safety effect in the shown code.

verdict.summary: No attacker-reachable memory-safety, lifetime, integer, or input-validation vulnerability is confirmed in the shown code. The only unvalidated input reaching memory operations is a typed njs_value_t; all indices and pointers (nargs, ctx->index, frame/scope pointers) are engine-internal invariants. The nargs guard absence, scope-write bounds, NULL-frame deref, and the memory-error leak are recorded as limitations, not confirmed findings.

evidence.reason: Write sink at offset ctx->index into the scope bases installed at lines 27-29. ctx->index is compiler-emitted from validated bytecode, so no attacker-controlled value can select an out-of-range slot; no concrete index violating the frame allocation can be demonstrated from the shown code, so this is not a confirmed CWE-787.

Argument fetch with no visible nargs bounds check. Reachability of an OOB read requires the internal promise-resolution machinery to invoke this native with nargs < 2; nargs is runtime-fixed, not attacker-controlled, and no out-of-contract caller is shown, so taint/reachability cannot be confirmed.

Early return on memory error bypasses njs_async_context_free(vm, ctx) at line 74, leaking the async context. This is an engine-internal resource-lifetime robustness concern without attacker-controlled input or memory-corruption impact, so no CWE is assigned.

assumptions: njs_arg is assumed to be the engine's guarded macro (e.g., returning &njs_value_invalid when nargs <= index); its body is not shown.
njs_async_ctx_t fields (await, index, pc, capability) are initialized by the engine and remain pointer-valid for the lifetime of the pending await.
ctx->index is compiler-emitted and lies within the resumed frame's local/temp/closure scope allocation.
vm->levels is sized to admit all NJS_LEVEL_* indices, and the resolved frame's scope bases at lines 27-29 are non-NULL and correctly sized.
limitations: If njs_arg were an unchecked &args[1] and a caller invoked this native with nargs < 2, line 12 would be an OOB read (CWE-125); no such caller appears in the shown code and the argument count is fixed by the runtime.
An out-of-bounds scope write at line 34 (CWE-787) is unconfirmed: ctx->index is bytecode-validated, so no concrete index/value that violates the frame's allocated scope can be produced.

A NULL or stale dereference of ctx->await (lines 17-18) or vm->top_frame->function->context (line 10) would require the engine to violate its own async-context invariant; classified as robustness, not a reachable attacker vector.

The ret == NJS_ERROR memory-error path (lines 57-60) frees nothing, leaking ctx (CWE-404-style resource leak); impact is limited to engine-internal state and is not attacker-controllable memory corruption.
The routing of a fulfilled Error value from njs_is_error to the reject path (lines 13-15) is semantically unusual but has no identified memory-safety consequence in the shown code.

verdict.summary: The row_remapping int64 tensor is validated only for rank and size (num_rows_), never for value range. Unchecked values flow into min_old_row/max_old_row and drive the slice-generation loop (`while (row_start <= max_old_row)`), whose iteration count is bounded only by the attacker-supplied value and whose length expression `max_old_row - row_start + 1` can overflow int64 when max_rows_in_memory_ <= 0. A crafted remapping (e.g., containing INT64_MAX) causes a non-terminating loop / unbounded tensor_slices growth, i.e., process hang or memory exhaustion (DoS).

evidence.reason: Sink for the DoS: `max_old_row` is derived from attacker-controlled `row_remapping(i)` (lines 25-33) with no bound against `tensor_shape.dim_size(0)` (line 79) or any value-range check, so the loop condition (line 117) permits arbitrarily many iterations; each iteration grows `tensor_slices` (line 125) and advances `row_start` (line 126) by an unvalidated length. A `row_remapping` containing a large (e.g., 2^40) or `INT64_MAX` value passes the only checks (lines 8-17, 111) and triggers hang/OOM before the bounds-checking `SliceTensorShape`/`LookupSlice` calls (lines 146-153) are ever reached.

Integer-overflow site (CWE-190): with `max_rows_in_memory_ <= 0` (explicitly supported by the comment on line 120) and `max_old_row = INT64_MAX`, `row_start = 0` from attacker-supplied `row_remapping` values, the int64 expression wraps after the first iteration; `row_start += slice_length` (line 126) wraps to `INT64_MIN`, subsequent iterations compute `slice_length = 0`, and `while (row_start <= max_old_row)` (line 117) never terminates while `tensor_slices` grows without bound (line 125) — resource exhaustion / hang.

assumptions: Op inputs (`row_remapping`, `col_remapping`, checkpoint path/metadata, `initializing_values`) are treated as attacker-controllable per the TensorFlow op-boundary threat model; the only constraints are those enforced by the shown `OP_REQUIRES` checks.

`num_rows_`, `num_cols_`, and `max_rows_in_memory_` are op attributes fixed at graph construction; the DoS holds regardless of `max_rows_in_memory_` (unbounded iteration count vs. int64-overflow path), so no specific attribute default is required.
`LookupSlice`/`SliceTensorShape` (lines 146-153) reject out-of-bounds slices, but they run only after the slice-generation loop at lines 111-127 has already executed/overflown.
limitations: Candidate B: `int` loop counters vs. `int64_t` sizes at lines 157, 175, 216-217 can overflow/wrap only for dims or attributes > 2^31 (a tensor of roughly 8 GB or larger), which is not a realistically confirmed reachable condition — robustness concern only, no CWE listed.

Candidate C: `old_tensor_name` (lines 68-71) lacks the `NumElements() == 1` check that `ckpt_path` has (line 63); whether `scalar<tstring>()()` on an empty/non-scalar tensor is memory-unsafe depends on `Tensor::scalar` semantics in framework code not shown here — unconfirmed.
`RemapVectorToMap` (lines 18-19, 52-53) is not shown; any out-of-bounds behavior inside it (e.g., indexing `id_present` by remapping value) is out of scope for this analysis.

The output-write path is not memory-unsafe: lines 190-192 fully guard `output_matrix(new_row, new_col)` at line 199, and `initializing_values` reads are guarded at lines 219-223 with the exact-consumption check at lines 230-235.

verdict.summary: ljpeg_start computes the segment length as len = (data[2]<<8|data[3]) - 2 from attacker-controlled file bytes without validating it. A crafted length of 0 or 1 (bytes 0x00 0x00 or 0x00 0x01) yields len = -2 or -1, which converts to a near-SIZE_MAX size_t count for fread(data, 1, len, ifp) (line 16). fread then copies the entire remaining file into the fixed 0x10000-byte stack buffer 'data', overflowing it when the file contains >= 65537 further bytes (stack-based buffer overflow, potential RCE/crash).

evidence.reason: Sink: attacker-controlled len (line 14) is passed as fread's count after int->size_t conversion. With length bytes 0x00 0x00 (len=-2) or 0x00 0x01 (len=-1) the count becomes huge, so fread writes the whole remaining file into the 0x10000-byte data buffer (line 4), overflowing the stack once the file supplies >= 65537 more bytes; the tag-only guard at line 15 does not restrict len.

Taint source: data[2..3] come from fread at line 12 over the attacker-controlled file stream ifp; subtracting 2 yields the range -2..65533 with no bounds/negativity check, directly feeding the overflowing fread at line 16 after the tag guard at line 15 passes (e.g., tag bytes FF C0).

assumptions: ifp is a FILE* positioned on attacker-controlled file content (untrusted image input), which is the standard usage for this raw/JPEG header parser.
The int-to-size_t conversion of a negative value is defined behavior (modulo 2^N) and yields a very large count for fread.
struct jhead member sizes, make_decoder_ref, merror, dng_version and zero_after_ff are not defined in the snippet; the confirmed finding does not depend on them.
limitations: Unchecked fread returns (lines 9, 12, 16) allow stale/uninitialized data[] reads at lines 19-24 and 33-37 (CWE-457 candidate); attacker control of the stale bytes is nondeterministic, so it is not confirmed as exploitable.
Out-of-bounds writes to jh->huff/jh->free at lines 42-45 (indices up to 5) cannot be confirmed because the struct jhead layout is not shown.
make_decoder_ref(&dp) at line 30 may advance dp past data+len and read past the buffer; its implementation is not shown, so past-end reads are unconfirmed.
If the file is smaller than 65537 bytes after the length prefix, the line-16 overflow does not occur; the finding requires a payload of >= 65537 bytes.

verdict.summary: In mobi_decode_infl, the delete branch decrements pos (line 41) without a lower-bound check; a crafted rule drives pos to -1, so decoded[-1] is read (line 49) and, if the byte matches, memmove writes one byte before the decoded buffer (line 53), causing a heap out-of-bounds read and conditional one-byte heap underflow write from attacker-controlled rule data.

evidence.reason: pos is decremented with no lower-bound check. pos can legitimately be 0 (initial *decoded_size == 0, or reset via line 13/39 and prior deletes), so attacker rule byte 0x03 followed by a char byte yields pos = -1, which the line-45 guard (checking only d + l <= decoded + INDX_INFLBUF_SIZEMAX) does not catch.

With pos = -1 (from line 41: initial size 0, rule = {0x41, 0x03, 0x41}), l = size + 1 = 1 and d + l = decoded + size passes the guard at line 45, so this line deterministically reads decoded[-1], an out-of-bounds heap read (CWE-125) driven by attacker rule bytes.

When pos = -1, d = decoded - 1, s = decoded, and l = *decoded_size + 1; the line-45 guard passes, so memmove writes (at least) one byte to decoded[-1], a heap underflow write (CWE-787). The write executes whenever the byte read at line 49 equals the attacker-chosen c.

Secondary end-of-buffer read: after size reaches INDX_INFLBUF_SIZEMAX and pos == size with dir == '>', the line-45 guard (>) accepts equality, so the memmove source range decoded[pos+1 .. size] reads decoded[INDX_INFLBUF_SIZEMAX], one byte past the allocation (CWE-125).

assumptions: decoded points to an allocation of exactly INDX_INFLBUF_SIZEMAX (or larger), and the line-32 insert guard maintains *decoded_size <= INDX_INFLBUF_SIZEMAX.

mobi_decode_infl may be invoked in fresh-decode mode with *decoded_size == 0; the shown code's own guards explicitly handle size == 0 (line 31-32), so this is the natural in-contract starting state, not a caller contract violation.
rule is a NUL-terminated byte stream of attacker-controlled length.
limitations: The heap underflow WRITE at decoded[-1] (line 53) only executes if the garbage byte at decoded[-1] equals the attacker's rule byte (uncontrolled heap-layout predecessor); the OOB READ at line 49 is deterministic regardless.

The end-of-buffer read (second evidence item) requires filling the buffer to INDX_INFLBUF_SIZEMAX, i.e. an INDX_INFLBUF_SIZEMAX-length rule; feasible in principle for a large attacker file but not confirmed for any specific value of the constant shown here.

The while loop (line 7) reads rule until a zero byte; if a caller ever passes a non-NUL-terminated rule, the loop itself would over-read rule. This depends on an out-of-scope caller invariant, so it is a robustness concern, not a confirmed finding.
The debug_print calls (lines 23, 33, 46, 50) print decoded as %s and may read past the logical data if it is not NUL-terminated; log-path only, not reported.

verdict.summary: No reachable memory-safety vulnerability is confirmed in mobi_decode_infl. Both dangerous branches guard pos (>= 0), l (>= 0, i.e. pos <= *decoded_size), and the buffer end; the guarded expressions d + l (insert) and s + l (delete) both algebraically reduce to decoded + *decoded_size + 1, so each check bounds every read/write against decoded + INDX_INFLBUF_SIZEMAX independently of pos. Remaining concerns (pointer arithmetic formed before the guards, uninitialized one-byte read in delete within the allocation, unbounded rule length, and caller-supplied size) are caller-contract or robustness issues, not attacker-reachable faults in the shown code.

evidence.snippet: if (pos < 0 || l < 0 || d + l > decoded + INDX_INFLBUF_SIZEMAX) {
evidence.reason: Insert-branch guard fully covers the subsequent memmove (line 32) and decoded[pos] = c (line 33). With l = *decoded_size - pos (line 27), d + l = decoded + *decoded_size + 1, so the size term depends only on *decoded_size: pos < 0 excludes negative indexes, l < 0 excludes pos > *decoded_size, and the end-pointer check permits writes only up to index INDX_INFLBUF_SIZEMAX - 1. No concrete (pos, *decoded_size) pair passes this guard yet writes out of bounds.

evidence.snippet: if (pos < 0 || l < 0 || s + l > decoded + INDX_INFLBUF_SIZEMAX) {
evidence.reason: Delete-branch guard bounds the decoded[pos] read (line 45) and the memmove (line 49). With l = *decoded_size - pos (line 40), s + l = decoded + *decoded_size + 1; the guard therefore keeps every read (largest index *decoded_size) and every write (largest index *decoded_size - 1) inside the INDX_INFLBUF_SIZEMAX-byte allocation for all pos <= *decoded_size with pos >= 0. The pos-- at line 37 cannot create an out-of-bounds access because a resulting pos == -1 is rejected by pos < 0 before any dereference.

The only position-decrement source. c in 11..19 subtracts 1..9 per command, so pos can only go negative through repeated commands; every subsequent insert (line 28) or delete (line 41) re-validates pos < 0 before any memory operation, and no arithmetic on pos can overflow int without ~2^31 consecutive move commands from an unbounded (out-of-scope) rule stream.

assumptions: decoded is allocated with at least INDX_INFLBUF_SIZEMAX bytes; the code compares all end pointers against decoded + INDX_INFLBUF_SIZEMAX, so this is the function's own stated contract.
rule is NUL-terminated by the caller; line 7 (while ((c = *rule++))) has no other termination condition.
Initial *decoded_size is within [0, INDX_INFLBUF_SIZEMAX]; every read/write index is derived from it and validated against INDX_INFLBUF_SIZEMAX.
int is 32-bit; pointer arithmetic and comparisons on in-bounds and one-past-end pointers behave conventionally.
limitations: Lines 25-27 and 38-40 compute decoded + pos (and decoded + pos + 1) before the pos < 0 guard at lines 28/41; with a negative pos this is out-of-bounds pointer arithmetic (UB in the strict language sense), though no dereference or memmove occurs before the guard, so no memory access is reachable.

The delete branch moves l = *decoded_size - pos bytes (one more than a strict delete needs) and reads the byte at old index *decoded_size; the guard keeps this read inside the allocation and the copied byte falls past the new logical end, so there is no exposure.
No bound is imposed in the shown code on rule's length; a non-NUL-terminated rule (caller contract) or a rule long enough to overflow pos (≈2^31 move commands) is not established as reachable.
debug_print at lines 29/42/46 passes decoded as %s although it may not be NUL-terminated on error paths; at most a log-only issue, not attacker-controlled formatting.

When *decoded_size == INDX_INFLBUF_SIZEMAX the checks reject deletes as well as inserts (n + 1 > INDX_INFLBUF_SIZEMAX in both branches), a logical/DoS robustness quirk rather than a memory-safety fault.

verdict.summary: In DecodeImageAPNG, attacker-controlled IHDR dimensions up to cMaxPNGSize (2^30) are multiplied in 32-bit unsigned arithmetic at lines 53-54: rowbytes = w*4 and imagesize = h*rowbytes wrap (e.g., w=2^30 -> rowbytes=0/imagesize=0; w=h=2^30-1 -> imagesize=4). The resulting undersized heap buffer is installed into frameRaw.p (line 56) with row pointers computed from the wrapped stride (line 58); a crafted APNG frame that decodes successfully then reaches the copy loop (lines 107-126), which reads up to 4*w0 bytes per row from the undersized buffer, causing heap OOB reads (with matching OOB writes inside the libpng processing path).

evidence.reason: Taint source: w/h are taken from attacker-controlled IHDR bytes (lines 40-41). The only constraint is w,h <= cMaxPNGSize (2^30) at line 43, which does not protect the 32-bit multiplications at lines 53-54: the maximum legal w=2^30 makes w*4 wrap to 0 (mod 2^32).

Confirmed overflow and undersized allocation: unsigned 32-bit products wrap. For w=h=2^30-1, imagesize=4; for w=2^30, rowbytes=0 and imagesize=0, so frameRaw.p is a 0-byte heap block. Row pointers at line 58 use the wrapped stride (j*4294967292 == -4j mod 2^32), placing even row 1 at p-4, outside the allocation.

Confirmed OOB-read sink: f = frameRaw.rows[y] points into the undersized frameRaw.p (size 0 or 4 bytes) via the wrapped stride, while the loop reads f[4*x+0..3] for x<w0 (up to 4*w0 bytes per row). A crafted A-GIF-like fcTL w0=h0=16 frame on a w=h=2^30 canvas passes the frame-placement guard (x0+w0<=w, y0+h0<=h, no 32-bit wrap since each field <= 2^30) and the successful-decode branch reaches these reads out of bounds.

assumptions: cMaxPNGSize is the file-scope constant 1u << 30 (2^30) referenced at lines 43 and 151; it is defined outside the shown snippet.

processing_start / processing_data / processing_finish implement a normal libpng pipeline and return nonzero on decode error, so the successful-decode branch at line 76 (if (!processing_finish(...))) is reachable for a well-formed crafted APNG.
64-bit build: sizeof(png_bytep) == 8 and size_t is 64-bit, so h * sizeof(png_bytep) at line 57 does not wrap in 32 bits (on a 32-bit build it would also wrap).

libpng is configured (outside the shown code) with user limits up to cMaxPNGSize; if it rejected ~2^30-wide images instead, the decoder would exit with errorstate and the overflow would be unreachable in practice, which is why confidence is 0.8.
limitations: fcTL is parsed at lines 142-149 (reads chunk.p+12..+33) without a chunk-size check in the shown code; whether a short fcTL can reach these OOB reads depends on read_chunk's unshown validation — unconfirmed.

The fdAT branch (lines 179-181) computes chunk.size-16 and chunk.size-4 without a size check; underflow for short chunks would feed a huge length to processing_data — unconfirmed because read_chunk is not shown.

Line 78 divides delay_num*1000 by attacker-controlled delay_den (line 147) with no non-zero check shown; delay_den==0 yields SIGFPE. Kept as a robustness concern because reaching it depends on the unshown processing_finish success semantics.
Unchecked operator new at lines 56-57 (and inside the libpng wrappers) can throw std::bad_alloc for multi-GiB sizes, terminating the process; allocation-failure handling is not shown.

The OOB-write side (libpng writing decoded rows into the undersized frameRaw.p) occurs inside the not-shown processing_data path; only the undersized allocation and the OOB read in the shown copy loop are directly confirmable from this snippet.
io->dec_pixels += w0*h0 (line 103) wraps 32-bit arithmetic but is accounting-only, with no confirmed memory-safety impact.

verdict.summary: No reachable, attacker-triggerable vulnerability found in fastrpc_dma_buf_attach. All inputs are framework/allocator-internal; kzalloc failure and dma_get_sgtable failure are fully handled before any use of the scatterlist; list insertion is serialized under buffer->lock. Remaining concerns (unbounded attachment list growth, detach-side cleanup) depend on code outside the snippet and are recorded as limitations.

evidence.reason: All arguments to dma_get_sgtable come from trusted allocator fields (buffer->dev/virt/phys/size, Phase 1). The ret < 0 guard fully covers the failure path: a->sgt is never dereferenced after failure and a is freed, so no uninitialized-scatterlist or double-free is reachable within the shown code.

List insertion of the freshly allocated and initialized attachment is fully serialized by buffer->lock and list_add cannot fail; no untrusted index, size, or pointer is involved, so no memory-safety impact is reachable here.

assumptions: dmabuf->priv is set by the exporter at allocation and remains valid for the dmabuf's lifetime (framework invariant).
The DMA-BUF framework validates the buffer/attachment pairing and serializes attach calls via dmabuf->lock before calling this callback.
buffer->dev, buffer->virt, buffer->phys, and buffer->size are coherent values written once at allocation and not attacker-modifiable.
attachment->priv is freshly zeroed by the framework for each attachment.
limitations: Unbounded growth of buffer->attachments is not bounded inside this snippet; whether an attacker can drive unlimited successful attaches depends on framework fd limits and on detach behavior outside the shown code (resource-exhaustion hypothesis, not confirmed).
Freeing of a and a->sgt and list removal occur in the not-shown fastrpc_dma_buf_detach; any use-after-free/double-free scenario there cannot be confirmed from this snippet.
Races with other buffer users (map/unmap/release) are outside the shown code; within the snippet, list access is already serialized by buffer->lock.

verdict.summary: The shown code is a test callback whose inputs are static, trusted test-table data. All memory-sensitive operations (backing-store parsing, XML serialization, buffer management) occur inside unshown libvirt functions, and the shown code performs no pointer arithmetic, indexing, or narrowing conversions. Inputs are validated/compared via exact guards (L11-12, L14, L22, L34). No confirmed, reachable, attacker-triggerable vulnerability exists.

This guard establishes that reaching the STRNEQ at L34 implies data->expect is non-NULL (otherwise the function returns). It also fully covers the 'unexpected success' branch, using %s with char-pointer arguments, so no NULL or format-string issue is reachable.

Both operands are NUL-terminated strings whose non-NULL status is guaranteed by the earlier guards (L19-20, L22-26); the comparison performs no index arithmetic, and all fprintf conversions match their argument types. No vulnerability is confirmed at this sink.

data->backing and data->expect are static, trusted test-table strings, not runtime attacker input.
virStorageSourceNewFromBackingAbsolute, virDomainDiskSourceFormat, virBufferContentAndReset, and STRNEQ behave per their documented contracts (their implementations are not shown).

Allocation failure or internal overflow inside virDomainDiskSourceFormat / virBufferContentAndReset (L28-29) is framework-internal and unconfirmed; no CWE is assigned.
Line 19-20 returns success when src is NULL even if data->expect is non-NULL, silently skipping the expected-output comparison; this is a test-accuracy issue with no security impact.

verdict.summary: No confirmed, reachable vulnerability in the shown code. The only in-scope arithmetic (negating int32 zero_point at lines 4-5) is safe under the documented TFLite zero-point range invariant; the missing input2-type check, unvalidated scale, and potential OOB inside the reference kernels all depend on caller/framework code not shown, so they are recorded as unconfirmed hypotheses rather than findings.

Verified as NOT confirmed: the failing value INT32_MIN presupposes a model loader accepting a zero_point outside the TFLite int8/uint8 invariant, i.e., reachability depends on code not shown.

Candidate sites for type confusion / OOB: input2 and output buffers are reinterpreted as input_dtype without in-function type, shape, or allocation-size checks. Verified as NOT confirmed: all indexing and size arithmetic is inside the unshown reference kernels, and a mismatch requires the unshown caller to violate its type-equality and shape/buffer invariants.

assumptions: TfLiteTensor.params.zero_point has type int32_t, so `auto` at lines 4-5 is int32_t.
The TFLite quantization invariant holds: zero_point is in [0,255] for kTfLiteUInt8 and [-128,127] for kTfLiteInt8, and scale is positive and < 1 for these quantized comparison kernels.
The caller (not shown) enforces input1->type == input2->type, computes requires_broadcast from the operand shapes, and guarantees data buffers match declared shapes and element sizes.
limitations: CWE-190 signed overflow on -zero_point (lines 4-5) is unconfirmed: reaching INT32_MIN requires an out-of-range zero_point, which depends on model-loading validation not present in the shown code.

The line-3 guard checks only input1->type; missing input2->type/output->type validation is a defense-in-depth gap whose exploitability depends on the unshown dispatcher violating its type-equality contract.

Unvalidated params.scale passed to QuantizeMultiplierSmallerThanOneExp (lines 10-15) is unconfirmed: the callee's behavior for non-positive/NaN/>=1 scale and any upstream scale validation are not shown.

Potential OOB in BroadcastComparison4DSlowWithScaling/ComparisonWithScaling (lines 26-34) cannot be confirmed because the kernel implementations are not shown; loop-bound vs. buffer-size verification is out of scope.
requires_broadcast (line 25) is trusted from the caller; a stale/mismatched flag with unequal shapes would mislead the chosen kernel, but that path depends on unshown caller computation.

Every dereference of attacker-influenced pointers (main_mach0, prelink_range, obj, prelink_info) is protected by an explicit NULL check on the direct control path, and no index arithmetic or raw buffer access occurs in this function. The cleanup path nulls obj's cache ownership before returning and frees main_mach0/fbuf exactly once; R_FREE nulls its pointers in the earlier failure branches, so the if (obj) guard at line 67 prevents any double-free. The only lifetime defect visible here is the missing rebase_info free.

MACH0_(new_buf) copies the opts struct rather than retaining a pointer to the stack variable.

verdict.summary: ComparisonQuantized validates only input1->type; input2->type is never checked, yet input2's raw buffer is reinterpreted with the element type tag derived from input1 via GetTensorData<input_dtype>(input2). An attacker-controlled TFLite model can supply tensors of mismatched types so that input2's data is read and compared under the wrong type, producing incorrect comparison results (type confusion).

evidence.reason: This is the only type guard in the function; it constrains input1->type but never input2->type. The tainted, unvalidated input2->type therefore flows downstream to both reinterpretation sinks, so the guard does not cover the dangerous operation on input2.

Broadcast-path sink: input2's buffer is accessed with the input_dtype tag inherited from input1 even though input2->type was never checked, enabling type confusion (e.g., input1 kTfLiteInt8 with input2 kTfLiteUInt8) whenever the line-3 guard is taken.

Non-broadcast sink: with input1->type == kTfLiteInt8 and input2->type == kTfLiteUInt8 (same shape, requires_broadcast == false), line 31 reinterprets input2's bytes as int8; e.g., uint8 bytes {200,210,220} are read as {-56,-46,-36}, so semantically equal values compare unequal. The tainted type tag reaches this sink with no in-scope validation.

assumptions: input_dtype (the template parameter) is instantiated from input1's tensor type at the kernel dispatch site that is not shown in this snippet.
Tensor type, shape, and quantization parameters originate in the TFLite model/graph and are treated as attacker-controlled in the untrusted-model threat model.
The reference_ops::*WithScaling functions are assumed to read within their tensors' buffers when the accessed type matches the tensor's declared type; their internals are outside the shown code.
limitations: Exploitability of the type confusion depends on the framework layer not enforcing input1->type == input2->type before this kernel runs; such upstream validation is not shown, which caps confidence at 0.6.

Negating zero_point (lines 4-5) is undefined behavior if zero_point == INT32_MIN, but reachability requires upstream to accept out-of-range quantization parameters and no security impact in the shown code was identified; recorded as an unconfirmed robustness concern, not a vulnerability.

An out-of-bounds read in the non-broadcast arm (lines 29-32) would require the caller to pass requires_broadcast == false with input tensors of different element counts, violating the caller contract not shown here; unconfirmed, not reported.
No memory corruption (OOB read/write, heap/stack overflow) is confirmed within the shown code; Candidate A's impact is restricted to incorrect type interpretation and wrong comparison results.

verdict.summary: In the SET_ENCODINGS branch, a 4-byte frame with attacker-chosen limit==0 falls through the `limit > 0` early-return guard, so the loop executes once and performs a 4-byte out-of-bounds read (read_s32) and write (memcpy) at data[4..7], beyond the validated 4-byte message; with a tightly sized backing buffer this corrupts heap memory. A secondary 1-byte over-read exists in the QEMU AUDIO default branch when len==4.

evidence.reason: With len==4 and attacker-chosen limit==0 (data[2..3]), the guard at line 28 is false and the loop runs with i=0: read_s32(data,4) reads data[4..7] and memcpy writes data[4..7] while only data[0..3] are valid, exceeding the frame by 4 bytes in both directions.
The `limit > 0` check only protects the early return; a 4-byte SET_ENCODINGS frame with limit==0 reaches the unguarded loop below, providing the concrete failing input (type=2, pad=0, n_encodings=0).

After len==2 returns 4 (line 86), the next invocation has len==4; an attacker-chosen audio submessage id (data[2..3], line 88) outside ENABLE/DISABLE/SET_FORMAT reaches this default branch and read_u8(data,4) reads 1 byte past the valid frame.

assumptions: The caller delivers exactly the frame sizes this function returns (1, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 20, 4+limit*4, 8+dlen), so only those len values occur on re-invocation.
read_u8/u16/u32/s32 perform unconditional absolute reads from data at the given offsets.
data points to a writable buffer whose valid content is exactly len bytes.
limitations: Whether the 4-byte OOB write at data[4..7] crosses an allocation boundary (observable heap corruption) depends on the caller's buffer sizing, which is not present in the shown code.

Partial-frame lengths (e.g., SET_PIXEL_FORMAT with 2<=len<17, KEY_EVENT with 2<=len<8) are unreachable because the caller accumulates exact frame sizes, so the missing intermediate checks are not attacker-reachable here.
CUT_TEXT's 8+dlen wrap (e.g., dlen=0xFFFFFFFF returns 7) can desync frame accounting, but the shown code never reaches client_cut_text with the wrapped value, so no OOB is confirmed on that path.
Large limit (SET_ENCODINGS, up to 65535) or large dlen (CUT_TEXT, up to 2^32-8) force large read-size requests and possible memory-exhaustion DoS in the caller; caller handling is out of scope.
The 1-byte over-read in the AUDIO default branch only leaks a byte into the server log before vnc_client_error disconnects the client.

verdict.summary: The int64_t values of the attacker-controlled row_remapping tensor are never range-checked. A single value INT64_MAX flows into max_old_row, making `max_old_row - row_start + 1` overflow to a non-positive slice_length; row_start then wraps and the `while (row_start <= max_old_row)` loop never terminates while `tensor_slices.push_back(slice)` grows the vector without bound, causing a hang and unbounded memory growth (denial of service).

evidence.reason: Sink. With row_remapping={INT64_MAX} and num_rows_=1, line 9 passes and lines 20-29 set min_old_row=max_old_row=INT64_MAX, so line 106 enters the loop. Iteration 1: slice_length = INT64_MAX - INT64_MAX + 1 = 1, then line 121 computes INT64_MAX+1 which overflows to INT64_MIN. Iteration 2: slice_length = INT64_MAX - INT64_MIN + 1 wraps to 0, so row_start stays INT64_MIN forever; line 112 is always true and line 120 pushes a TensorSlice on every iteration with no bound, producing an infinite loop and unbounded memory growth.

Taint source. row_remapping is an op input tensor (attacker-controlled) whose values are int64_t with no range validation; the only constraint is that its size equals num_rows_, so INT64_MAX is accepted and later used to compute min_old_row/max_old_row (lines 20-29).

Value transport. An unvalidated non-negative row_remapping value (e.g. INT64_MAX) is copied verbatim into max_old_row, which then drives the slicing loop; no upper bound against tensor_shape.dim_size(0) or any other limit is applied.

evidence.snippet:
OP_REQUIRES(context,
                      new_row < num_rows_ && new_col < num_cols_ &&
                          new_row >= 0 && new_col >= 0,
                      errors::Internal(strings::StrCat(
                          "new_row=", new_row, " and new_col=", new_col,
                          " should have been less than num_rows_=", num_rows_,
                          " and num_cols_=", num_cols_,
                          " and non-negative. This should never have happened "

evidence.reason: Negative result: the write at line 194 is fully covered by the guard at lines 185-193, which bounds both new_row and new_col (and their signs) before the write and aborts the kernel on violation, so no out-of-bounds write is reachable through the remapping map values.

assumptions: row_remapping, col_remapping, initializing_values, ckpt_path, and old_tensor_name are op input tensors; treating model/checkpoint-supplied tensors as attacker-controlled follows the TensorFlow untrusted-graph/checkpoint threat model.
num_rows_, num_cols_, and max_rows_in_memory_ are op attributes treated as framework-provided; the confirmed finding does not depend on attacker control of these attributes.
The unshown helper RemapVectorToMap is assumed to size row_id_present/col_id_present to the input vector length and to build the old-ID -> new-ID maps without out-of-bounds access.
Signed int64_t overflow is undefined behavior per the C++ standard but wraps on all platforms TensorFlow supports; the concrete observed failure is the non-terminating loop.
ckpt_path/old_tensor_name must resolve via BundleReader/LookupDtypeAndShape to a valid rank-2 DT_FLOAT tensor for the slicing loop to be reached.
limitations: The int loop indices (line 20 `int i`, line 152 `int row`, line 170 `int old_col`, lines 211-212 `int i`/`int j`) can overflow if sizes exceed INT_MAX; this would cause OOB reads/writes, but requires >2^31-element tensors (>=16 GB for int64 inputs) and is impractical, so it is recorded as a robustness concern, not a confirmed finding.

No validation exists that remapping values lie within the old tensor's row range; out-of-range slices are expected to fail via OP_REQUIRES_OK on SliceTensorShape/LookupSlice, but those library internals are not shown, so any memory-level effect is unconfirmed.
Any out-of-bounds behavior inside the unshown RemapVectorToMap (e.g. indexing by old_id without checks) is out of scope for this analysis; the shown code checks sizes before calling it (lines 9, 43).
The checkpoint file access via attacker-controlled ckpt_path/old_tensor_name is the designed function of this op and was not assessed as a path-traversal/arbitrary-file-read finding.

Cell leakage of uninitialized output memory (cells skipped because remap_cols maps fewer columns than the source tensor) depends on unshown map-building semantics of RemapVectorToMap and is unconfirmed.

verdict.summary: No reachable, attacker-controlled memory-safety, lifetime, or input-validation vulnerability is present in the shown code. The fixed buffers are either size-capped by construction (strport, addr via passed sizeof) or guarded after an in/out length API (naddr_len > sizeof(naddr)), the addrinfo loop closes each created fd exactly once on every path, and the sole post-freeaddrinfo use of ptr is a NULL comparison of the local variable, not a dereference.

evidence.reason: *port is an unsigned short (0-65535), so the largest rendered value is "65535" plus NUL = 6 bytes, which always fits strport[8]; truncation is impossible and no overflow path exists.

getsockname (line 73) caps its write at the in/out naddr_len <= sizeof(naddr) and this guard aborts on any kernel-reported larger length, so the subsequent net_port_get/net_address_get calls always operate on a fully captured sockaddr; no overflow of naddr or addr[INET6_ADDRSTRLEN] via address data is reachable.

fd lifecycle is sound: the loop-top close (lines 32-33) closes only the previous candidate's socket, continue paths leave the current fd open until the next iteration or the error path's close(fd) at line 93, and a successful bind exits via break (line 60) with exactly one fd returned at line 90; every created fd is closed exactly once, ruling out double-close and leak within the function.

assumptions: getaddrinfo returns a non-NULL result list when it returns 0 (POSIX contract); on ret < 0 the function returns before using servinfo.
union net_sockaddr is large enough for both AF_INET and AF_INET6 sockaddr structures (its size is the cap passed to and checked against getsockname).
net_address_get honors the size argument passed at line 86, and net_port_get writes only the 16-bit port.
limitations: ptr still holds a dangling value after freeaddrinfo(servinfo) (line 63); the shown code only compares it at line 65, which is not a dereference, but any future code dereferencing ptr there would be a use-after-free (CWE-416).

addr is uninitialized stack memory (line 9); if net_address_get failed to populate it, line 88 would log a partially uninitialized buffer (potential info leak). The helper's behavior and the restricted AF_INET/AF_INET6 family set are outside the shown code, so this is unconfirmed.

socket() at line 35 receives the caller's unmasked type flags (e.g., SOCK_NONBLOCK); invalid flags simply fail the call, and callers intentionally pass such flags, so this is a robustness/contract concern rather than a confirmed vulnerability.

The truncation check at line 79 runs after getsockname has already copied (truncated) data into naddr; it correctly prevents subsequent use of a truncated address, so this is defensive ordering, not a flaw.

verdict.summary: No attacker-triggerable vulnerability is confirmable within the shown code. The argument-copy loop (lines 35-40), the `c->ci[1]` write (line 50), and the `c->ci--` pop (line 42) can only fail under contracts of helpers/callers that are not shown (`mrb_stack_extend`, `fiber_switch_context`, callinfo layout/headroom) or under a purely theoretical integer overflow of `len+2`; per the three-part confirmation rules these are robustness hypotheses, not confirmed findings.

evidence.reason: `len` (caller-supplied `mrb_int` argument count) reaches the sink unvalidated: `e = b + len` bounds the loop that writes `c->stbase[1..len]` plus `stbase[0]` at line 45 (len+1 slots), while the only guard is `mrb_stack_extend(mrb, len+2)` whose allocation/overflow behavior and post-`fiber_switch_context` target context are not shown. A negative `len` makes `e < b`, skipping the loop (line 38) with no write. A concrete in-scope value that passes the visible guards and overruns cannot be named (requires len beyond stack capacity or `len == MRB_INT_MAX-1` overflow), so this fails the reachability leg and stays a limitation.

Writes one callinfo slot above the current `c->ci` with no visible check that `c->ci+1 < c->ciend`; an out-of-bounds write would require resuming a fiber whose callinfo array is full, an unseen framework invariant. Taint (attacker-influenced `len`/`a`) does not control `c->ci` position, so this is an unconfirmed CWE-787 hypothesis.

The decrement assumes the dummy callinfo sits above `c->cibase` so that the later reads `c->ci->proc` and `c->ci->pc` (line 56) stay in bounds; if the dummy were `c->cibase` itself the pointer would underflow the array. The layout is an unseen invariant, so this is a limitation, not a confirmed finding.

assumptions: `fiber_check`/`fiber_check_cfunc` validate `self` and reject fibers executing C code, so `c` is a valid `mrb_context*` when the dangerous branches are reached.
`fiber_switch_context(mrb, c)` switches the current context so the subsequent `mrb_stack_extend`, `c->stbase`, `c->ci`, and `c->cibase` refer to the target fiber `c` (mrb->c == c).
`mrb_int` is a signed integer (32- or 64-bit); `len` is an argument count normally derived outside the shown code (`mrb_get_args` / VM `ci->n`) and is bounded by the calling VM stack.
`mrb_stack_extend(mrb, room)` grows the target context's stack (or raises) so that `ci->stack + room` fits within `stend`.
limitations: Copy-loop OOB (lines 35-40): `len` beyond the fresh fiber's capacity or `len >= MRB_INT_MAX-1` (wrapping `len+2`) would make `while (b<e) *b++ = *a++` write past `c->stend`; the concrete failing caller value and a failing `mrb_stack_extend` are not derivable from the shown code (out-of-scope caller / unchecked allocation / theoretical worst case) - unconfirmed CWE-787 / CWE-190.
`c->ci[1].stack[0] = value` (line 50): no guard ensures `c->ci+1` is within the callinfo array; safety depends on an unseen callinfo-headroom invariant - unconfirmed.
`c->ci--` (line 42) followed by `c->ci->proc`/`c->ci->pc` dereferences (line 56): safety depends on the unseen dummy-callinfo layout - unconfirmed.
`c->cibase->n = len` (line 44): silent truncation would occur if `n` is a narrower integer type; no security impact is demonstrated in the shown code.
Negative `len`: the copy loop is a no-op (line 38) but `len` still flows into `fiber_result` (line 48) and `c->cibase->n` (line 44); no memory-safety effect is provable in the shown code.

verdict.summary: Attacker-supplied MAT files can (1) wrap the 32-bit multiplication used to compute ldblk (row byte count) for miINT16/32/64/miSINGLE/miDOUBLE cells (e.g. SizeX=0x20000000 with miDOUBLE yields ldblk=0), producing a heap buffer at line 270 that is inconsistent with image->columns and is then passed to pixel import, enabling an out-of-bounds read in the import path or a multi-GiB allocation DoS (CWE-190); and (2) set Frames (line 133) to any u32, including 0 (underflow) or 0xFFFFFFFF, causing the NEXT_FRAME loop (lines 416-421) to iterate an attacker-chosen number of times with an Image allocation per iteration until CPU/memory exhaustion (CWE-835/CWE-400).

evidence.reason: SizeX is an attacker-controlled u32 read from the file at line 119 and is only checked for non-zero (line 243). `8 * MATLAB_HDR.SizeX` is computed in 32-bit unsigned arithmetic and wraps before the `(ssize_t)` cast: SizeX=0x20000000 gives 2^32 mod 2^32 = 0, so ldblk=0; SizeX=0x1FFFFFFF gives ldblk=0xFFFFFFF8 (~4.29e9). The buffer at line 270 is allocated with count=ldblk and element size 8 (so 0 bytes or ~34 GiB), while image->columns=SizeX and ImportQuantumPixels (lines 304/314) consumes SizeX*(depth/8) bytes from it; there is no guard ensuring ldblk == SizeX * bytesPerSample. This is the CWE-190 integer-overflow/undersized-allocation sink.

Frames is read verbatim from the attacker-controlled file as an unvalidated u32 when DimFlag==16 (z==1 or z==3). It is used at line 416 as the loop count for the NEXT_FRAME loop; setting it to 0 or 0xFFFFFFFF makes `--Frames > 0` true for up to ~4.29e9 iterations with no EOF check, no remaining-data bound, and an Image allocation per iteration (line 406), giving unbounded CPU/memory consumption (CWE-835/CWE-400).

This is the unbounded-loop sink: the only exits are `image->next == NULL` after a failed image allocation (line 407) or an exception. With Frames=0xFFFFFFFF from line 133, every iteration returns to NEXT_FRAME (line 180), re-enters the CellType switch, fails its scanline read at EOF (line 295, `goto ExitLoop`), and reaches `done_reading`→`AcquireNextImage` again, allocating one Image per iteration until resource exhaustion (CWE-835/CWE-400).

assumptions: ReadBlobXXXLong/ReadBlobXXXShort return the raw 32-/16-bit values stored in the file (attacker-controlled), and ReadBlob returns 0/short counts at EOF.
size_t is 64-bit (LP64), so the allocation `AcquireQuantumMemory(ldblk, 8)` is ldblk*8 bytes, and `one << image->depth` with depth 64 is a shift by the type width (UB).
z2qtype has at least 4 entries (indices 0..3 are used), matching the upstream mat.c definition.
ImportQuantumPixels reads columns*ceil(depth/8) bytes per row from the supplied buffer and returns its status (behavior not shown in the supplied code).
limitations: The concrete out-of-bounds read caused by the wrapped ldblk executes inside ImportQuantumPixels (and FixSignedValues/CalcMinMax/RotateImage), which are not part of the shown code; the over-read is therefore a high-confidence hypothesis, while the 32-bit overflow and the 0-byte/multi-GiB allocation are confirmed in the shown code (CWE-190).
Exploitation of the wrapped-ldblk over-read also requires SetImageExtent (line 265) to succeed with huge dimensions (e.g. SizeX=0x20000000), which on constrained systems fails cleanly instead.

`image->colors = one << image->depth` (line 242) is undefined behavior for depth==64 (miDOUBLE/miINT64/miUINT64), but on the target ABI the shift masks to 1 and no security impact is demonstrated; left as a robustness concern, not a listed CWE.

NameFlag case 0 seek (lines 160-161) can move past EOF with the result ignored, and reads (167, 178) partially fill `size`; stale/zero values may later be parsed as phantom frame data, but no memory-safety impact is demonstrated.
Object reads are not bounded against MATLAB_HDR.ObjectSize; reads past an object's end only degrade to zero/EOF values with no memory-safety impact in the shown code.

Huge SizeX/SizeY values can cause multi-GiB SetImageExtent/quantum allocations; these fail via the checked ResourceLimitError paths and are treated as resource-exhaustion robustness concerns rather than independent vulnerabilities.

verdict.summary: No confirmed reachable memory-safety flaw in the shown code. The created-fiber stack writes are bounded by mrb_stack_extend(len+2) (indices 1..len copied, max index len < len+2) and mrb_stack_extend(3) (index 1 of 3 reserved slots), and len is clamped to 15 in the packed-array branch; these bounds hold under the standard creation invariant ci->stack == stbase. Candidate OOB write at c->ci[1].stack[0] and negative/huge-len cases depend on callinfo-buffer layout or C-API callers not shown here, so they are recorded as limitations rather than vulnerabilities.

evidence.reason: Copy of len arguments into stbase[1..len]. The guard mrb_stack_extend(len+2) provides capacity >= len+2 slots relative to the created fiber's top callinfo (stack == stbase by the fiber creation invariant), so every written index (max = len) and the block slot (len+1) are in bounds; reachable len values are 0..14 here, and len == 0 makes the loop a no-op. No in-scope value defeats the guard.

For len >= 15 the argument list is packed into one heap array stored at stbase[1]; mrb_stack_extend(3) covers indices 0..2 under the same invariant and only stbase[0] and stbase[1] are written, after which len is clamped to 15 for c->cibase->n at line 51. The read a[0..len-1] in mrb_ary_new_from_values is bounded by the caller-supplied argument array.

Potential write one callinfo past the resumed fiber's current top.
