simplestring_init_str (not shown) allocates target->str and sets target->size to a positive value (SIMPLESTRING_INCR in libmemcached), so lazy-init leaves size > 0.
Calling code may pass any int value for add_len; this snippet imposes no constraint.
limitations: The concrete attacker origin of add_len (e.g. network-parse-derived lengths in calling code) is outside this fragment; if every caller only ever passes validated non-negative lengths, the overflow is unreachable.

Division by zero at line 12 (newsize % incr) when target->size == 0 requires str != NULL with size == 0 at line 6; the shown code sets size = 0 only when realloc returns NULL, which also sets str = NULL (lines 13, 15), so the inconsistent state must originate outside the shown code.

Int narrowing at line 8 and int incr = target->size * 2 at line 9 can mis-size the buffer only when len + add_len + 1 > INT_MAX (requires a pre-existing ~2-4 GB buffer); not needed for the confirmed negative-length path and treated as an unconfirmed worst case.
realloc failure at line 13 leaks the old block and silently truncates data (str = NULL, size = 0); denial-of-service/robustness concern only.
memcpy at line 20 reads add_len bytes from source; an out-of-bounds read occurs if source is shorter than a positive add_len, which depends on an unshown caller contract.

verdict.summary: No vulnerability is confirmable within the shown code. drop_table passes an unvalidated name to maria_delete_table_files and discards both return values, but every security-relevant behavior (name validation, path confinement, memory safety) lives in the caller and in maria_delete_table_files, neither of which is shown; those are recorded as unconfirmed limitations, not findings.

assumptions: name points to a valid NUL-terminated string at the time of the call.
The SQL/handler layer that invokes drop_table validates and normalizes the table name before it reaches this function (external invariant, not shown).
maria_delete_table_files is trusted engine code that performs its own path/bounds handling (external, not shown).
limitations: Path traversal or arbitrary file deletion via a crafted name cannot be confirmed: the shown code imposes no check on name at line 5, but demonstrating a real exploit requires the unshown caller to pass unvalidated attacker input and maria_delete_table_files to lack path confinement, both out of scope.

The return values of ha_close() (line 4) and maria_delete_table_files() (line 5) are discarded with (void), which can mask I/O or cleanup failures; this is a robustness/error-handling concern, not a confirmed security vulnerability.

DBUG_ASSERT(!file || file->s->temporary) (line 3) is compiled out in release builds and only constrains file, never name, so it provides no protection for the sink; however, the misuse it guards against is an internal-contract violation by the caller, not reachable within the shown code.

A NULL name would be dereferenced inside maria_delete_table_files without any NULL check in the shown code, but the resulting behavior is in unshown code and depends on an out-of-scope caller violating the naming contract.

verdict.summary: Out-of-bounds read in get_lisp_indent(): loop 97-101 advances the line pointer by one CHARACTER per iteration (lbr_chartabsize_adv advances by multibyte byte length) while decrementing col (a BYTE offset from pos->col) by 1, so for lines with UTF-8 characters before the matched bracket the pointer lands on the NUL terminator; the unconditional that++ at line 114 then moves it one byte past the NUL, and the first dereference at line 118 (VIM_ISWHITE(*that)) is a heap out-of-bounds read reachable by opening a crafted Lisp file (e.g. a line '(foo é)'), causing a crash/DoS (CWE-125).

evidence.reason: Root cause: col is a byte offset (col = pos->col, line 86, from findmatch on attacker-controlled text), but each lbr_chartabsize_adv call advances that by one CHARACTER's byte length while col is decremented by 1. For line '(foo é)' the ')' is at byte 7; 7 iterations advance 1+1+1+1+2+1+1 = 8 bytes, leaving that on the NUL at index 8 (col==0). The loop therefore terminates with that at the NUL terminator whenever the line has fewer characters than pos->col (multibyte surplus), which is attacker-controllable.

Sink: line 114 executes that++ unconditionally after the overshoot, moving the pointer one byte past the NUL end of the line (e.g. index 9 for '(foo é)', which is beyond the 8 non-NUL bytes + NUL). The first dereference of that out-of-bounds pointer is VIM_ISWHITE(*that) at line 118, a heap out-of-bounds read (CWE-125); with whitespace bytes following (garbage adjacent heap), loop 118-122 reads further out of bounds. Trigger path: pos != NULL and amount == -1 (single-line buffer or unbalanced parens), reaching line 118 with the crafted line.

assumptions: ml_get_curline() returns a NUL-terminated line whose allocation may end exactly at the NUL (ASan/KASAN layout), making the dereference of that+1 an actual out-of-bounds read.
findmatch() returns pos->col as the BYTE offset of a real bracket character on pos->lnum, so 0 <= pos->col < line byte length.
lbr_chartabsize_adv() advances the supplied pointer by the byte length of one full character (1 for ASCII/tab, 2-4 for UTF-8) per call.
VIM_ISWHITE(NUL) evaluates to false (all whitespace loops terminate at an in-bounds NUL).
get_lisp_indent() is invoked by Vim's 'lisp' indentation machinery on buffer text, making the file contents the attacker-controlled input.
limitations: Exact correspondence to the published CVE-2024-45306 (and the advisory's 'use-after-free' wording) could not be verified offline; no UAF is substantiable within the shown code, so only the confirmed OOB read is reported.

Whether the one-past-NUL dereference crashes or merely reads adjacent heap bytes depends on Vim's memline block layout, which is not shown; severity assumes the ASan-verified heap-buffer-overflow case.

The OOB occurs only when the bracket line has fewer (or equally many) characters than the bracket's byte column, i.e. when the UTF-8 byte surplus exceeds the trailing characters; ASCII-only lines land on the NUL in-bounds and are safe.

The first string-skip loop (lines 51-69), the big inner loop (lines 140-162) for in-bounds entry, and the whitespace loops were verified safe by exit-path tracing; integer arithmetic on 'amount' is not used as an index and has no security impact here.

verdict.summary: In handle_returned_header, the header value after the matched 'timelimit_header' prefix is parsed with sscanf("%u") into an unsigned int without any range validation (line 16). A responder-controlled decimal larger than UINT_MAX (e.g. "4294967296") makes the %u conversion overflow, which is undefined behavior per the C standard, and the resulting value is added to time(NULL) to set the security-relevant connection timeout discon_time (line 17), letting the responder corrupt connection lifetime (premature or indefinite disconnects). No memory corruption occurs; impact is timeout/policy corruption (availability).

evidence.reason: Taint: bytes following the matched timelimit_header prefix are fully attacker-controlled network data (Phase 1). Reachability: an attacker-chosen header 'icecast-timelimit: 4294967296\r\n' passes the prefix match at line 13 (the first timelimit_header_len bytes are the configured prefix), so line 16 parses a decimal exceeding UINT_MAX into 'unsigned int limit'; a %u conversion that cannot be represented in the object is undefined behavior, directly anchored to line 16 (Phase 3, Candidate 1). Impact: the corrupted 'limit' flows to line 17, where discon_time = time(NULL) + limit sets the connection timeout to an attacker-influenced value, corrupting the access-time-limit enforcement; primary CWE-190, low severity since the overflow corrupts a scalar timeout value rather than memory.

assumptions: libcurl guarantees header-callback data is a complete header line that is NUL-terminated, with size=1 and nmemb=line length, and per-header length capped by libcurl — this makes the strncasecmp/%s reads in-bounds.
client->auth and auth->state are non-NULL while an auth request is in flight (set by the icecast code that registered this callback with CURLOPT_HEADERFUNCTION).
The target build uses 64-bit time_t; on 32-bit time_t, time(NULL)+limit could wrap, but the effect is duplicated by in-range attacker values.
limitations: bytes = size * nmemb (line 4) could theoretically wrap on size_t, but reaching an overflow would require a header of ~2^64 (64-bit) or ~2^32 (32-bit) bytes, impossible given libcurl's header-size caps and size=1 for header callbacks; a wrap would only reduce the returned count, so this is a robustness concern, not a confirmed vulnerability.

Out-of-bounds reads in strncasecmp (lines 11/13) and the %s source in snprintf (line 22) are unconfirmed: they would require the libcurl header buffer to lack its NUL terminator, contradicting libcurl's documented guarantee; strncasecmp and %s both stop at the first NUL, so no in-code value produces an over-read under the invariant.
The prefix-match guards (lines 11/13/19) guarantee the offsets ptr+timelimit_header_len and ptr+22 are within the received line, so no short-line over-read was confirmed.
discon_time/time_t wrap only matters on legacy 32-bit time_t and adds no attacker capability beyond in-range values; not counted as a finding.
Header-based authentication (client->authenticated = 1, line 12) assumes the auth responder is trusted; a malicious responder is outside the shown trust model.

verdict.summary: mpgviddmx_process writes attacker-controlled numbers of bytes into ctx->hdr_store (L129, L139, L275, L217, L530) without establishing that ctx->hdr_store_alloc covers the write; on the first packet paths none of the shown allocation sites (L70, L305, L350) run, so a 1-4 byte packet (or a mid-stream remainder < 5, or the 3-byte copy_last_bytes paths) performs an out-of-bounds/NULL heap write. The same path can read 1-2 bytes past the end of the input packet when bytes_in_header==1..2 and remain==5..6 (L139). Reachable when parsing untrusted MPEG video, yielding memory corruption and crashes.

evidence.reason: remain is the attacker-controlled packet size (pck_size from gf_filter_pck_get_data at L31, converted at L35). On the first packet, aggregation (L67, requires hdr_store_size!=0) and resume (L84) are both skipped, so no code path in the shown function has allocated or enlarged ctx->hdr_store before this sink; there is no check that hdr_store_alloc >= remain. A first packet of pck_size 1..4 takes this branch and writes 1..4 bytes to an unallocated/undersized heap buffer (CWE-787).

When bytes_in_header==1..2 (set from a prior 1..2-byte packet at L130) and the next packet has remain==5..6 (guard at L128 only enforces remain>=5), this copies 7 or 6 bytes from 'start', which has exactly remain valid bytes (framework invariant): a 1..2-byte out-of-bounds heap read (CWE-125). The destination write of up to 7 bytes at hdr_store+bytes_in_header also has no hdr_store_alloc>=8 guarantee (CWE-787).

Second occurrence of the same unguarded sink: reachable mid-stream when start/remain have been advanced (e.g., remain -= current, L264) leaving a 1..4-byte tail, or via the remain<5 continue at L414. ctx->hdr_store capacity is again not verified before the 1..4-byte write (CWE-787).

assumptions: gf_filter_pck_get_data returns a buffer of exactly pck_size valid bytes (input-packet framework invariant used at L31).
No shown path allocates ctx->hdr_store before the first small-packet write; the only growth sites are L70 (aggregation, skipped while hdr_store_size==0) and L305/L350 (parse-config EOS accumulation).
pck_size < 2^31 so the u32-to-s32 assignment at L35 preserves the value; larger sizes make remain negative and skip the while loop (no memory access).
limitations: The filter/context constructor (not shown) may pre-allocate or pre-size ctx->hdr_store; if it always guarantees capacity >= 8 and the input pipeline never delivers <5-byte packets, the flagged overflows would not trigger. That invariant cannot be validated from this snippet, hence confidence 0.75.

OOB reads/writes at L498/L501 and the integer truncations at L486 ((u32)size), L452/L461/L536 ((s32)size) require gf_m4v_parse_frame to return size > remaining buffer bytes; the parser implementation is not in scope. Release builds also compile out the assert(remain>=size) guards (L450, L459, L534), so this is a robustness concern, not a confirmed finding.
Overlapping memcpy at L139 can occur when start points into ctx->hdr_store (aggregated mode), which is undefined behavior but not a bounds violation.
The u64 byte_offset can underflow (wrap to a huge value) at L155/L252/L496 when the subtracted byte count exceeds byte_offset; this corrupts only output metadata, not memory.
hdr_store_alloc at L305/L349 is cast to u32; a >4GiB accumulated header would truncate the allocation (theoretical; requires ~4GiB of header data).

verdict.summary: No confirmed, attacker-reachable vulnerability in the shown code: the WQ allocation (lines 21-22), the CQE initialization loop bound (line 26) and the PAS/input buffer sizes (lines 31-33, 53-54) are all derived from the same log_cq_size/npages values, so indices and sizes remain mutually consistent for every value reachable through the in-function control flow. The only potentially dangerous input, the parameter cq_size, has no attacker-controlled provenance in the shown code; its worst-case in-function effect (oversized allocation attempt) is cleanly unwound.

evidence.reason: Loop bound is derived from the same WQ whose size was set by log_cq_size at line 16 and allocated at lines 21-22; max index is size-1 < size, so i can never index past the allocated CQE array. Off-by-one: strict '<' comparison covers indices [0, size-1] only.

inlen is int, but npages is bounded by the WQ allocation that succeeded at lines 21-22 (max 2^25 pages for the extreme log_cq_size=31 case, giving inlen ~ base + 2^28). Signed overflow of inlen would require npages >= 2^28, which cannot occur before the earlier allocation fails, and kvzalloc failure is handled at lines 34-37.

evidence.snippet:
cq_size = roundup_pow_of_two(cq_size);
	MLX5_SET(cqc, temp_cqc, log_cq_size, ilog2(cq_size));
evidence.reason: The only external input, cq_size (int), is rounded up and its ilog2 masked into a 5-bit field; even in the worst reachable-in-principle case the resulting log_cq_size (31) only triggers a huge allocation that fails with a clean ENOMEM unwind. No attacker-controlled origin or reaching call path is present in the shown code, so this is not a confirmed vulnerability.

assumptions: Callers of mlx5_fpga_conn_create_cq (e.g., mlx5_fpga_conn_create) pass kernel-internal, non-negative, bounded cq_size; no user-facing origin is shown for cq_size.
mlx5_cqwq_create / mlx5_cqwq_get_size / mlx5_cqwq_get_wqe are mutually consistent: the reported size and the allocated CQE array both derive from the same log_cq_size written at line 16.
mlx5_fill_page_frag_array writes exactly buf.npages descriptors at the pas offset, and pas offset does not exceed MLX5_ST_SZ_BYTES(create_cq_in).
limitations: If an out-of-scope caller passed cq_size >= 2^30 or <= 0, line 15 would truncate the unsigned round-up result into int and ilog2 would yield up to 31, causing mlx5_cqwq_create to attempt an ~137 GiB allocation; the failure is cleanly unwound (ENOMEM at lines 34-37), so this is only a robustness/DoS concern with unreachable evidence in the shown code.

roundup_pow_of_two(0) relies on fls_long(-1)=64 and 1UL<<64, which is undefined shift behavior on some architectures; the resulting cq_size=1 is an arch-dependent robustness issue, not a memory-safety violation.
inlen signed overflow would require npages >= 2^28 (a WQ >= ~16 GiB), which is impossible because the corresponding allocation at lines 21-22 would already have failed.
Attacker-controllable origin for cq_size, if any, resides in unshown caller code; no taint path to the sinks could be confirmed from this snippet alone.

verdict.summary: In do_cmdline(), the loop jump-back path (endwhile/endfor/continue) validates an index read from cstack.cs_line[] only with cs_line[cs_idx] >= 0 before using it as current_line to index lines_ga.ga_data at the breakpoint lookup; the missing upper-bound check against lines_ga.ga_len allows a desynchronized loop index to read past the heap array (wcmd_T.lnum), causing an out-of-bounds read / crash in sourced-file and function-execution contexts.

evidence.reason: This guard bounds current_line only from below (cs_line[cs_idx] >= 0). It never checks cs_line[cs_idx] < lines_ga.ga_len before that value is assigned to current_line at line 446 and used as an index at line 458; the corresponding loop-read path (line 177) does enforce the strict inequality, so the bound here is demonstrably incomplete.

Sink: current_line is attacker-influenced loop state (cs_line[cs_idx], written at line 477 from current_line_before) and is dereferenced into the heap array lines_ga.ga_data without an upper-bound check. Any current_line >= lines_ga.ga_len passes the line-443 guard and reads wcmd_T.lnum out of bounds; in :source/function execution breakpoint != NULL (lines 90-95), so this branch is exercised.

assumptions: FEAT_EVAL is enabled, so the cstack/lines_ga/loop machinery is compiled in.
lines_ga.ga_data is a heap allocation of sizeof(wcmd_T) elements (ga_init2 at line 73).
Executing a sourced file or function makes breakpoint non-NULL via source_breakpoint()/func_breakpoint() (lines 84-95), making the line-453 breakpoint branch reachable.
wcmd_T has at least .line and .lnum fields, as used at lines 220-221, 458, and 496.
limitations: A concrete script that drives cs_line[cs_idx] >= lines_ga.ga_len depends on state transitions inside the unshown do_one_cmd()/get_loop_line()/store_loop_line() (e.g., defining a function inside a loop advancing current_line per the comment at lines 381-382); the shown code alone proves the guard is insufficient, not the exact desync trigger.

The use-after-free hypothesis with cmdline_copy aliasing lines_ga after free_cmdlines() was examined and rejected: line 181 always clears cmdline_copy before re-reading lines_ga, and line 290 re-copies with vim_strsave(), so cmdline_copy never aliases freed loop lines in the shown flow.

The other indexed accesses (lines 220-221 guarded by 177, line 496 guarded by 493) are correctly bounded; cs_idx bounds themselves are enforced by unshown cstack management (do_one_cmd/rewind_conditionals).
Impact is limited to an out-of-bounds read (crash / possible line-number disclosure through the debugger path), not a write, so no CWE-787 is asserted.

verdict.summary: The CoRRE decoder passes fully unvalidated, network-controlled sub-rectangle geometry (x,y,w,h each uint8_t 0..255) to client->GotFillRect (line 32), which fills the client framebuffer. Sub-rectangles extending past the framebuffer edges cause heap out-of-bounds writes with attacker-controlled pixel data; the only guard (line 19) bounds the bulk read size, not the sub-rect geometry.

evidence.reason: x,y,w,h are single bytes read from client->buffer (populated by ReadFromRFBServer at line 19) and flow with no validation or bounds check into GotFillRect at line 32, which writes the rectangle into the client framebuffer. Every value in 0..255 passes the only guard (line 19), which bounds the bulk read size but not the sub-rect geometry; e.g., on a 200x200 framebuffer, a subrect (150,150,150,150) writes rows/columns 200..299 out of bounds (CWE-787).

This guard correctly bounds the bulk read: hdr.nSubrects <= RFB_BUFFER_SIZE/(4+BPP/8) implies nSubrects*(4+BPP/8) <= RFB_BUFFER_SIZE (integer division truncates), so the parse buffer is not over-read and the multiplication does not overflow. It does NOT constrain the sub-rect coordinates/sizes x,y,w,h passed to GotFillRect at line 32, so it cannot prevent the out-of-bounds framebuffer write.

assumptions: client->buffer is allocated with at least RFB_BUFFER_SIZE bytes (standard libvncclient invariant).
client->GotFillRect writes the given rectangle into a heap framebuffer of size width*height*BPP/8.
BPP is one of 8/16/32 and CARDBPP is the matching pixel type; ReadFromRFBServer fills exactly the requested byte count on success.
In the real caller, rx/ry/rw/rh originate from the untrusted RFB message header, but the calling code is not shown here.
limitations: The final memory-corruption impact depends on the not-shown GotFillRect implementation: a caller that installs a clipping or ignoring callback would prevent the OOB write; the shown code nevertheless performs no validation of its own.
Bounds of rx/ry/rw/rh cannot be confirmed from the shown code; caller-side validation is out of scope for this analysis.
Exploitability specifics (heap layout, ASLR, exact overwritten objects) are not assessed; the confirmed issue is the unvalidated geometry at the framebuffer fill sink.

verdict.summary: Integer wraparound: attacker controlled per-header ut32 slide-info counts are summed into ut32 total_slide_infos (line 17) without an overflow check, so e.g. 0xFFFFFFFE + 4 wraps to 2 and sizes the infos heap array (line 24) to 2 entries; the fill loop (line 47) then iterates the unwrapped per-header counts and writes infos[k] (lines 55-58) past the end once k exceeds the wrapped total, producing a heap out-of-bounds write reachable with a small crafted dyld cache.

evidence.reason: Attacker-controlled ut32 n_slide_infos[i] (read from file at 0x13c + hdr_offset, line 14) is accumulated into ut32 total_slide_infos with no overflow check; n_slide_infos[0]=0xFFFFFFFE and n_slide_infos[1]=4 wrap the sum 0x100000002 to 2.
The heap array is sized by the wrapped total (2 entries, ~48 bytes), which is smaller than the true sum of per-header counts used to fill it.
The fill loop is bounded by the unwrapped attacker-controlled per-header counts (0xFFFFFFFE for header 0), not by the wrapped allocation size, so k can exceed the number of allocated entries.

With three crafted valid cache_mapping_slide blocks (nonzero slideInfoOffset/slideInfoSize) at slide_infos_offset, the third iteration sets k=2 and writes infos[2].start/.end/.info at byte offset 48, fully outside the 2-entry (48-byte) allocation; line 54's nonzero guard does not limit k, and no other check compares k to total_slide_infos before the writes.

assumptions: MAX_N_HDR >= 2 so the per-header counts can be summed across at least two headers (the compile-time constant is not shown here; rizin's dyldcache code uses 4).
sizeof(RzDyldRebaseInfosEntry) is at least 24 bytes (start, end, info pointer), so index 2 lands fully outside a 2-element allocation.
The caller populates cache->n_hdr and cache->hdr_offset[] from attacker-controlled dyld cache headers, and a two-header (subcache) layout is normal input.
rz_buf_read_le32_at/rz_buf_fread_at bounds-check their reads against cache->buf and fail on out-of-range offsets.
limitations: ut64 wraparound of infos[k].end = start + entry.size (line 56) and infos[0].end (line 94) can produce end < start; impact depends on downstream range-check consumers not shown in this code.
ut64 wraparound in the offset/size arguments passed to get_rebase_info (lines 58, 95) could shift the parse target, but get_rebase_info's internal handling is out of scope.
Huge non-wrapped totals (e.g., 0xFFFFFFFF) cause oversized calloc; observable behavior is a NULL return (lines 25-27) or a pruned copy, so no memory-safety issue arises without the wraparound.
A hypothetical invalid cache state such as cache->hdr == NULL is a caller contract violation and is intentionally not modeled.

verdict.summary: cgroup_release_agent_write() stores the attacker-supplied buf into cgrp->root->release_agent_path with no capability or authorization check. Any caller that can invoke this write handler (e.g., root in a user namespace with write access to the cgroup v1 release_agent file) can set a path that the kernel later executes as root when the cgroup empties, enabling local privilege escalation / container escape (CVE-2022-0492).

evidence.reason: The attacker-controlled buf (Phase 1, line 2) flows unvalidated to the sink at lines 12-13. The only guard (lines 9-10) tests cgroup liveness, not privilege; there is no capable()/ns_capable()/file_ns_capable() call in the path, so any caller that can invoke the handler, e.g. root inside a user namespace with write access to the cgroup v1 release_agent file, commits its own path into release_agent_path. The kernel executes that path as init-root when the cgroup becomes empty, giving local privilege escalation / container escape (CWE-862, CVE-2022-0492).

assumptions: cgroup_kn_lock_live() pins cgrp so cgrp->root remains valid for the duration of the function.
sizeof(cgrp->root->release_agent_path) is a compile-time constant >= PATH_MAX, as enforced by line 6.
The handler is registered as the write callback for the cgroup v1 release_agent kernfs node (registration code not shown).
limitations: The attacker's precondition of holding write access to the release_agent file (e.g., via a user namespace and a writable cgroup v1 mount) is configured outside this function; the vulnerability is precisely the absent capability check inside it.

An out-of-bounds read via strstrip(buf)/strlcpy source scanning would occur only if the kernfs caller does not NUL-terminate buf (e.g., on a full-page write); that invariant is in unshown framework code, so it is recorded as an unconfirmed robustness concern, not a finding.
strlcpy silently truncates paths >= PATH_MAX and the handler still returns the original nbytes; this causes no memory-safety issue and is noted only for completeness.

verdict.summary: sctp_setsockopt_auth_key allocates exactly optlen bytes, copies optlen bytes into it, and validates the user-supplied sca_keylength against optlen - sizeof(struct sctp_authkey) before the key is consumed. Because sizeof(struct sctp_authkey) equals the key offset (8 bytes), the guard exactly caps the key region at bytes [8, optlen-1], so no out-of-bounds access is reachable. This is the post-fix form of CVE-2007-3105; the vulnerable variant ('sca_keylength > optlen') is not present.

evidence.reason: The user-supplied __u16 sca_keylength (copied at line 19) is rejected whenever it exceeds optlen - sizeof(struct sctp_authkey). Since sizeof(struct sctp_authkey) == offsetof(sca_key) == 8, the key region occupies bytes [8, 8+sca_keylength) inside the optlen-byte allocation; the guard permits only sca_keylength <= optlen - 8, so the last byte touched is at most optlen - 1, strictly inside the buffer. No attacker value that passes this guard can cause an out-of-bounds write or read.

For every reachable input, optlen >= 9, so the later size_t subtraction at line 24 cannot underflow and kmalloc/copy_from_user use the same optlen size. The only way to bypass this guard is a negative optlen (the int <= size_t comparison would then pass), but the kernel setsockopt path guarantees optlen >= 0, making that path unreachable in scope.

assumptions: struct sctp_authkey ends with a flexible (or zero-length) sca_key member, so sizeof(struct sctp_authkey) == offsetof(sca_key) == 8 (4-byte assoc id plus two 2-byte fields), making optlen - sizeof(...) exactly the in-buffer key capacity.
The caller (kernel setsockopt path) guarantees optlen >= 0 before invoking this handler.
The out-of-scope callee sctp_auth_set_key consumes at most sca_keylength bytes starting at sca_key; any different behavior would be outside the shown code.
limitations: Negative-optlen handling relies on the caller invariant; if this function were invoked with optlen < 0 the unsigned comparison would pass, but kmalloc would fail before any copy, so this is only a robustness/hardening concern and is not reported as a vulnerability.
The correctness/security of the unshown callees (sctp_auth_set_key, sctp_id2assoc, sctp_style) is not audited here.

The historical CVE-2007-3105 pattern used the looser bound 'sca_keylength > optlen'; the shown code uses the fixed bound 'optlen - sizeof(struct sctp_authkey)', so that out-of-bounds read is not present.

verdict.summary: hfsplus_find_cat reads an on-disk catalog record into a stack buffer and, after checking only the record-type discriminator, forwards the unvalidated nodeName.length to hfsplus_cat_build_key_uni. A crafted thread record whose declared name length exceeds the bytes actually fetched (or the stack buffer size) causes an out-of-bounds read of kernel stack memory, enabling a denial of service and potential kernel-stack information disclosure.

evidence.reason: Sink: attacker-controlled tmp.thread.nodeName (populated from the on-disk catalog record by hfs_brec_read at line 9) is passed with no length validation. A short thread record (e.g., nodeName.length = 0xFFFF with fd->entrylength = 8) passes the line 14 type-only guard and makes the helper read length * 2 bytes from the stack buffer tmp, exceeding both the fetched bytes and the object bounds (CWE-125).

evidence.snippet:
type = be16_to_cpu(tmp.type);
	if (type != HFSPLUS_FOLDER_THREAD && type != HFSPLUS_FILE_THREAD) {
evidence.reason: This is the only validation before the dangerous dereference: it constrains the record discriminator to two values but places no bound on tmp.thread.nodeName.length relative to fd->entrylength or to the size of tmp, so the guard does not cover the subsequent out-of-bounds read.

assumptions: hfs_brec_read copies at most sizeof(hfsplus_cat_entry) bytes into tmp and exposes the on-disk record length via fd->entrylength.
Attacker reachability assumes a crafted/compromised HFS+ image can be mounted (local attacker, untrusted removable media, or auto-mount).
Line numbers are relative to the supplied snippet, numbered from 1.
limitations: Whether the oversized nodeName.length also yields an out-of-bounds write into fd->search_key (CWE-787) depends on the unshown implementation of hfsplus_cat_build_key_uni and is not independently confirmed.
The extent to which leaked stack bytes reach user space depends on the unshown caller's use of fd/search_key results.

If hfs_brec_read did not cap its copy at sizeof(hfsplus_cat_entry), line 9 itself would be a direct stack overflow; that cap is not visible in the shown code and is treated as an unconfirmed robustness concern.
Reads of uninitialized tmp fields for records shorter than the thread header (use of uninitialized value) are a robustness concern without demonstrated independent security impact here.

verdict.summary: No confirmed, reachable, attacker-triggerable flaw in the shown code. Dimensions are file-controlled but type-bounded (columns <= 2^31-1, rows <= 2^31) so bytes_per_line*rows cannot wrap 64-bit size_t; SetImageExtent (L391) aborts on resource violations; pixel and colormap reads are count-checked; all conversion reads/writes stay within the allocated stride and column extent. Remaining issues (shift-count undefined behavior in the mask loops, the length/8 slack checks, and 32-bit arithmetic overflow) fail reachability or impact and are listed as limitations.

evidence.reason: Attacker-controlled columns/rows (from file width/height at L153-L154 via L369-L370) are validated here; a failure aborts the reader, and together with the 32-bit signed dimension sources this bounds every later product (bytes_per_line*rows at L457 and rows*stride at L463) below 2^64, refuting the integer-overflow/heap-OOB candidate.

bytes_per_line <= 4*columns <= 2^33-4 and rows <= 2^31 (width>0 at L332, height!=0 at L334, 32-bit signed sources at L153-L154), so length max = (2^33-4)*2^31 = 2^64-2^33 < 2^64: no size_t wraparound on 64-bit, and under-sized files either throw here or at the count-checked read (L471-L477).

The buffer stride is MagickMax(bytes_per_line, columns+256), which dominates every scanline stride used later (L513, L712, L758, L818, L858), so the row pointers pixels+(rows-y-1)*bytes_per_line in all conversion cases read within the allocation; NULL allocation and short reads both abort, closing the undersized-buffer and truncated-file paths.

Together with L162-L163, image->colors is capped at 1<<bpp <= 256 for PseudoClass, bounding the colormap allocation (L413-L414), the count-checked colormap read (L427-L433), and the colormap loop writes (L435-L441); a runaway number_colors cannot cause an oversized colormap allocation or out-of-bounds colormap access.

With an attacker-supplied mask such as red_mask=0xFFFFFFFF and compression=BI_BITFIELDS/bpp=32, the loop evaluates (0xFFFFFFFFUL << 32) at sample==32, which is undefined behavior (C11 6.5.7 p3). Taint and reachability exist, but the result flows only into quantum_bits.red (L588) used in scalar pixel-value arithmetic (L770-L774) with no index, pointer, or size impact, so no security mechanism is compromised in the shown code; recorded as a limitation rather than a vulnerability.

assumptions: 64-bit build: size_t/ssize_t are 64-bit and unsigned int/unsigned long (from ReadBlobLSBLong) are 32-bit, matching the MagickOffsetType/ssize_t usage in the snippet.
SetImageExtent (L391) enforces the width/height/area resource limits and returns MagickFalse on violation, which the caller handles by returning (L392-L396).
AcquireVirtualMemory/AcquireQuantumMemory return NULL on overflow or allocation failure, and every such result is checked before use (L465-L466, L486-L487, L415-L416, L411).

QueueAuthenticPixels/GetAuthenticIndexQueue provide pixel/index buffers of exactly image->columns entries per row, so SetPixelIndex writes with indexes+x and indexes+x+1 are bounded by the column loop bounds.
For RLE images, DecodeImage (not shown) writes no more than the passed extent image->columns*image->rows bytes, which the allocated rows x max(bytes_per_line, columns+256) buffer always covers.
limitations: Undefined behavior in the mask bit-shift loops (L553-L613): an all-ones attacker mask can evaluate a shift count of 32 (e.g., L582 with sample==32). It is taint-reachable but only distorts pixel values; no memory-safety consequence is demonstrable in the shown code.

The length guard at L458 compares length/8 to the blob size, allowing a header-claimed length up to ~8x the file; the subsequent count-checked ReadBlob (L471-L477) throws before the data is used, so the residual exposure is bounded resource consumption, not corruption.

On 32-bit builds (size_t 32-bit), multiplications such as image->columns*bmp_info.bits_per_pixel (L456) and bytes_per_line*image->rows (L457) could wrap and likely yield heap out-of-bounds access through the scanline pointers; unconfirmed here because the assumed platform uses 64-bit size_t.
The multi-image loop (L948-L972) can process many frames; per-frame resource use is subject to the library resource limits, but no frame-count cap is visible in the shown code.
DecodeImage internals (RLE decoding) are outside the shown code; the analysis relies on it honoring the passed extent and on the buffer-sizing argument at L484-L490.

verdict.summary: Sign error in the max_len argument of uni_utf8_get_char_n: since the loop guard guarantees p < parser->end, the expression (size_t)(p - parser->end) converts a negative ptrdiff_t into a huge size_t, so a multi-byte UTF-8 sequence cut off at the end of the input chunk is decoded by reading up to 3 bytes past parser->end (out-of-bounds read) on attacker-fragmentable SMTP input.

evidence.reason: The loop guard at line 13 ('p < parser->end') guarantees p - parser->end is negative inside this branch; casting it to size_t yields a huge max_len, so the decoder is not limited to the available bytes. An attacker putting an incomplete UTF-8 sequence at the chunk end (e.g., trailing 0xE2 0x82) causes the callee to read continuation bytes past parser->end.

Establishes the invariant that makes (p - parser->end) negative at the sink (line 19) and shows the intended data window [parser->cur, parser->end) whose bound the decoder over-reads; partial-input parsing is further supported by lines 43-45 which save state.poff and return 0 for incomplete data.

assumptions: uni_utf8_get_char_n treats its second argument as the maximum number of bytes it may read and reads continuation bytes directly without a separately supplied buffer limit (standard Dovecot libcharset semantics).
The parser can be invoked on fragmented input chunks (supported by the parser->state.poff save/resume at lines 43-45), so an attacker controls where a chunk boundary falls.
parser->state.poff is trusted framework state satisfying 0 <= poff <= end-cur.
limitations: The implementation of uni_utf8_get_char_n is not shown; if it internally refused to read beyond the printed argument, the over-read would not occur — however the caller's intended bound is unambiguously defeated by the sign error.

The allocation layout beyond parser->end is not shown; if the underlying buffer always has slack beyond the current chunk, the over-read may stay within the allocation (still a logical out-of-bounds read relative to the parsed window), and a crash depends on page-boundary placement.

Leaked bytes are only used for parse validation, not copied to the client, so no direct information disclosure is confirmed; the primary impact is memory-safety violation and potential denial of service.
Severity is capped at medium because the maximum over-read is bounded (up to 3 bytes) and crash behavior depends on buffer layout.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability. The thread-record name length is validated to 0..255 (line 19) before it reaches the key builder at line 24, which bounds the unicode payload to the 510-byte field size and the key length to 6+2*255=516 (fits u16). The record read is bounded by sizeof(hfsplus_cat_entry), and tmp is only treated as a thread after the type check at line 14.

evidence.reason: On-disk nodeName.length (u16) is the tainted input. This guard rejects every value >= 256, the only values that could make the downstream key builder at lines 24-25 exceed the 510-byte unicode field or produce a key beyond the 516-byte catalog maximum. Accepted values 0..255 keep the copy at <= 2*255 = 510 bytes and key_len = 516, so the guard fully covers the subsequent sink.

Sink consuming the validated name. After the guard at line 19, nodeName.length <= 255, so the helper receives at most 255 unicode characters (510 bytes, exactly the field size) and produces key_len 6+2*255=516 that fits u16; no value passing the guard can cause an out-of-bounds access here.

The stack buffer tmp is filled with a copy bounded by sizeof(hfsplus_cat_entry); the kernel helper errors on records larger than the requested size, so the subsequent field reads at lines 13, 19, and 24 stay within tmp.

assumptions: hfs_brec_read copies at most rec_len bytes and returns -EIO when the on-disk record exceeds it, per kernel btree helper contract.
hfsplus_cat_build_key_uni copies at most 2*length bytes from nodeName.unicode into fd->search_key, and fd->search_key has capacity for the maximum catalog key (516 bytes).
HFS_NAMELEN is 255 and the catalog B-tree maximum key content length is 516 bytes, so length 255 is valid by design (hence the guard is > 255, not >= 255).
limitations: hfsplus_cat_build_key_uni and hfs_brec_find are not shown; if the key builder used an unguarded strncpy/memcpy with a length-255 name and no NUL bytes, a 2-byte read past the unicode field could occur, but such behavior is not confirmable from the shown code.

hfs_brec_find's comparison of a 516-byte key depends on the catalog B-tree header's key-size fields; a corrupt header shrinking that bound could cause out-of-bounds reads inside hfs_brec_find, which is outside this function.
cnid originates from on-disk data via callers but is used only as a 4-byte key field with no arithmetic, so no concrete overflow is demonstrable in the shown code.
No loops exist in this function; iteration bounds are not applicable.

If hfs_brec_read could copy fewer than sizeof(hfsplus_cat_entry) bytes without erroring, trailing union bytes would be uninitialized; the shown checks only read the record's minimum prefix, so no uninitialized read is demonstrable here.

verdict.summary: jp2_decode contains two reachable memory-safety flaws driven by attacker-controlled JP2 boxes: (1) the BPCC consistency check is warning-only, so a BPCC box declaring fewer components than the codestream causes a heap out-of-bounds read of bpcs[]; (2) the CMAP direct-mapping path stores channo into chantocmptlut with no bound against the image component count, and the CDEF/non-CDEF passes then pass that value to jas_image_setcmpttype as a component index, causing an out-of-bounds component access.

evidence.reason: The only guard on the BPCC component count is a warning and does not terminate; it permits bpcc->numcmpts (box-declared array length of bpcs[]) to be smaller than jas_image_numcmpts(dec->image), which the subsequent loop uses as its bound.

Sink: bpcs[i] is indexed by i < image numcmpts while the bpcs array has only bpcc->numcmpts elements. Concrete failure: codestream with 3 components and BPCC box with numcmpts=1 (and differing component dtypes so !samedtype) reads bpcs[1] and bpcs[2] out of bounds. CWE-125.

Root cause: for directly mapped channels the LUT value is the channel number channo, which is only bounded by cmap->numchans (via dec->numchans at lines 233-234) and never validated against jas_image_numcmpts(dec->image). The validated cmapent->cmptno is ignored.

Sink (CDEF path): channo is checked < dec->numchans (line 309), but the LUT value it indexes is used as a component number without checking < numcmpts. CMAP with numchans=5 (all direct, cmptno=0), PCLR numchans=1, codestream with 2 components, and a CDEF entry with channo=4 passes all guards and calls jas_image_setcmpttype with component index 4, out of bounds. CWE-787.

Sink (no-CDEF path): iterates all dec->numchans (attacker cmap->numchans) and passes chantocmptlut[i] as a component index with no bound against numcmpts. Same crafted CMAP/PCLR/codestream as above gives values 2,3,4 for a 2-component image, causing out-of-bounds component access in jas_image_setcmpttype. CWE-787.

assumptions: bpcs[] is allocated with exactly the BPCC box's numcmpts elements by the box parser (JP2/JPX structure invariant).
cmap->ents[] and cdef->ents[] are allocated with numchans elements by the box parser, so reads bounded by the box's own numchans are in bounds.
pclr->lutdata[] has numchans*numlutents elements, making lutdata[cmapent->pcol + i*pclrd->numchans] in bounds under the pcol < numchans guard.
jas_image_setcmpttype dereferences cmpts_[cmptno] and does not bounds-check when called, i.e., the caller is required to pass a valid component number.
jas_alloc2 performs overflow-checked multiplication.
The image component count (jas_image_numcmpts) is positive for all analyzed loops because of the guard at lines 141-144.
limitations: Line 212 assert(dec->image->cmprof_) could abort on attacker input only if jas_cmprof_createfromiccprof returns NULL; that condition is in out-of-scope code, and the assert is compiled out under NDEBUG, so it is an unconfirmed DoS hypothesis.
Line 268 cdefd = &dec->cdef->data.cdef performs UB (would-be NULL member access) when CMAP is present without CDEF, but cdefd is only used inside #if 0, so no confirmed runtime impact.

Line 274 lutents = jas_alloc2(pclrd->numlutents, sizeof(int_fast32_t)) is unchecked; a NULL return would cause a NULL-pointer dereference. This is an allocation-failure robustness concern, not a confirmed attacker-triggerable memory-safety issue.
The 32-bit product in pcol + i*pclrd->numchans could theoretically wrap only for box sizes near 2^32, which is not realizable within box-length constraints; robustness concern only.
IHDR numcmpts mismatch (lines 135-138) is warning-only, and COLR ICC internals (jas_iccprof_createfrombuf) are not analyzed because their code is not shown.
